News.title: Couple’s wedding day saved by bride’s grandad’s mobility scooter after groom breaks leg & ankle in drunken stag do fall
News.content:
A GROOM who broke his leg and ankle on his stag do got married sat in a mobility scooter borrowed from his bride’s grandad.

Andy Sheldon, 47, used it to help him get around with wife Lisa, 42, on their big day.



She sat on his lap as he zipped about on the machine.

And they had a spin on the dance floor while he was on the electric vehicle.



Gym instructor Andy said: “At first I was gutted on my wedding day as I felt I’d let Lisa down.

“I like dancing all night so it was a bit annoying that I couldn’t get up and dance.

“But I took it in my stride even though my foot was throbbing.”

Social worker Lisa said: “One thing I was thinking before the wedding is, ‘If he’s on crutches we won’t be able to hold hands and walk around together’.

“But when he was in his chair we could. That was an absolute godsend.”

Guests loved Andy’s entrance to Ed Sheeran hit Thinking Out Loud, featuring the lyrics, “When your legs don’t work like they used to before.”



Lisa said: “When we did our entrance song, we were meant to walk down this staircase together but we obviously couldn’t do that.

“I walked down the staircase and Andy used the fire exit out the back. I came in to Raye song Where is My Husband!”

Andy broke his left shin, calf bone and ankle falling down train station stairs in Leeds.



The ankle ended up pointing in the wrong direction.

The dad of two needed surgery to pin the bones together.

After he revealed his wedding was in a week, the hospital found a cancellation and rushed his op through.



But he was still left needing to use crutches and a medical boot.

The couple from Hull, who had their big day in nearby Driffield, had to cancel their honeymoon to Italy while he recovers.

They now plan to head to Bali in September.

News.title: How 100s of teens are descending on Brighton to booze & brawl as social media ‘meet-ups’ turn violent for TikTok likes
News.content:
IT’S the trendy seaside town favoured by DJ Fatboy Slim and Housing Secretary Angela Rayner.

But Brighton has been named the teenage boozing capital of Britain, with the highest number of underage drinkers ending up in hospital there.



Residents say the famous esplanade becomes “lawless” on sunny weekends as social media-organised “meet-ups” turn violent.

Youths have been seen taking drugs and necking vodka before fights — intended to win TikTok likes — break out in front of baying spectators, as well as terrified holidaymakers and locals.



Brighton sailing club committee member Angus Malcolm has seen youngsters urinating in the streets and lighting fires next to his boats.

Angus, 51, said: “They turn up en masse, 200 or 300 of them.



“They will pick an area at the last minute, such as the beach, then descend on it.

“There will always be boozing and fighting and drugs.

“The first bank holiday when there was lots of sun, this was not a nice place to be.

“There was loads of aggro, lots of fights and groups of people. It was bad all weekend but certainly in the evening and someone was stabbed.



“That weekend it felt lawless. There is a bit more of a police presence now.”

Recent figures show that the number of alcohol-related under-18 hospital admissions in Brighton and Hove are 170 per cent higher than the national average.

Across almost every UK region, under-18 girls now account for the highest proportion of alcohol-specific hospital admissions.

And 15-year-old girls in England now report higher rates of monthly drinking than boys of the same age.

Mother-of-two Alex Costlin has been shocked at the number of underage girls in skimpy outfits she has spotted boozing in Brighton.



Speaking outside the seaside shop where she works, she said: “It’s quite scary really because they are so fragile and innocent and they all dress the same. They are almost naked.

“I’m not judging but they get so drunk. It’s no wonder they end up in hospital and it’s very sad to see because they are destroying their health.

“They take drugs too. Sometimes they come into the shop asking me for help with their laughing gas balloons. I say no.



“There are riots all the time, fights and everything.”

The riots Alex describes are the result of unofficial parties organised on the internet.

Promoters make claims like “free entry”, provide sound systems and promise that weed and nitrous oxide balloons will be available for sale.

The trade in drugs is no doubt the motive for planning such occasions.

Youngsters are encouraged to bring their own alcohol and volunteers in Brighton complain there has been an explosion in BuzzBallz litter during the summer months.



BuzzBallz are powerful cocktail-like drinks high in alcohol that have become popular with teenagers.

Around 300 tons of rubbish was collected on Brighton beach last year, with campaigners saying the majority was single-use plastics.

The Leave No Trace group found 3,600 crisp packets, lolly wrappers or sandwich containers, 800 aluminium drink cans and 740 plastic bottles in just five beach cleans.

Marcos Montoya, 40, runs an ice cream store close to Brighton pier and he is calling for greater police presence to combat the yobs.

He said: “There were fights as soon as summer started. A big crowd surrounded about four people aged 15 or 16 who were fighting. They were young kids.



“They were making live TikToks and streams and they were doing it for likes. I don’t know how they are managing to buy the alcohol — they always ask for ID here.

“Some of them are so drunk they need help walking.”

Labour MP Angela Rayner — who was slammed for failing to pay the correct stamp duty on the purchase of her flat in Hove — is promising to build more council houses to help seaside towns like Brighton.

But events supervisor Emily McMillan says more needs to be done to improve hospitals in the area.

Emily, 23, said: “A&E in Brighton is an absolute nightmare and it’s clogged with teenagers. I went in for a head injury before and I was kept waiting around for 12 hours.



“There were so many people and some of the teenagers looked like they were under the influence.”

Mother-of-five Jane Griffin, 65, helps run her family clothing store on the seafront.

She feels that teenage boozing is something residents have to put up with, especially as the city is so hedonistic.

Jane said: “I think it’s a shame that Brighton is labelled with that because teenage drinking is widespread. It is a rite of passage.

“They go through a stage of experimenting with drink and drugs, but most come out the other side and I’ve got five successful children. They’re thriving.



“Of course I worried about them, but I think there’s a lot of doom and gloom around teenage years and everyone grows up.

Councillor Bella Sankey, leader of Brighton & Hove City Council, said: “We know people are worried about young people drinking and gathering in large groups, and we are addressing these concerns.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Brighton & Hove is a busy place for visitors, so we’re working closely with police, health services and youth teams to help keep young people safe, carry out checks across all venues, and offer support early.

“Our aim is to stop harm before it happens by giving young people better choices, clear advice and the right help when they need it.”

News.title: Rare reptile which washed up in Anglesey flown back to Gulf of Mexico in epic 5,000-mile trip after two years in rehab
News.content:
A RARE turtle that washed up on our shores is on a 5,000-mile trip home after a two-year rehab.

Rhossi, a critically-endangered Kemp’s ridley sea turtle, was smeared in sex lubricant KY jelly and Vaseline to stop him drying out on the flight.



He safely arrived in Houston, US, after ten hours in the hold — and next Tuesday will be released into the Gulf of Mexico.

Rhossi was “cold-stunned” — ­battling hypothermia — and close to death when found by a dog and its owner in December 2023.



Barely 25cm long and weighing less than 1kg, the tiny turtle was taken from Llydan Beach, near Rhosneigr, to Anglesey Sea Zoo. He has since grown to 21kg (3st, 4lbs) ahead of his trip home.

The zoo’s owner Frankie Hobro said: “We’ve had to slather Rhossi in KY jelly and vaseline to try and stop him from dehydrating — which is always quite an amusing one going to buy that at the chemist!



“But this is the moment we’ve been working towards every single day for more than two years, so it’s incredibly emotional.

“Rhossi arrived with us fighting for life, and now we’re preparing to watch him make the journey home where he belongs.”



So far, Rhossi’s journey has seen him travel via helicopter from Anglesey to Heathrow then by cargo flight to Houston. He will be put in a large tank provided by Houston Zoo then taken south to be released into the warm waters near Texas’s Padre Island.

Frankie added: “We’re doing loads of tests on him now. Blood tests and all the medical stuff like his weight and strength, to make sure he’s good to have a satellite tracker fitted, which we’re hoping will go really smoothly.

“This will take a couple of days to turn around before we head to Padre Island, where we know there is a really healthy breeding population of Kemp’s ridley sea turtles that are at the tail end of their breeding season.



“They’ve managed to re-establish the species there, and we are pretty sure that’s where Rhossi’s originated from as a hatchling.

“It’s wonderful as we’re having all these people there for the release — everyone that has been involved in his transfer from the US. He’s a big lad so I’ll need someone to help me carry him into the sea!”

Rhossi is the fourth cold-stunned sea turtle rescued and rehabilitated by Anglesey Sea Zoo over the past decade, representing three different endangered species. Each turtle was first discovered by a dog.



Conservationists have said juvenile turtles are occasionally carried across the Atlantic by currents before becoming cold-stunned in northern European waters in winter.

The only two remaining nesting beaches for Kemp’s ridley sea ­turtles are in Mexico and Texas.

News.title: Heartbroken family demand Burnham stop drunk hit-and-run driver’s early release after learning he will benefit from plan
News.content:
FAMILY of a student killed by a drunk hit-and-run driver are directly appealing to the PM to stop his early release.

Abigail Eggleston, 22, was struck by Liam Bowes, who had downed pints and shots at a party before getting behind the wheel.



Cowardly Bowes left Durham University law student Abigail for dead before speeding off and torching his car in a bid to destroy evidence.

He got 12 years for death by dangerous driving.



But now just five months after he was sentenced and less than a year after ­losing their daughter, her devastated parents have been told he will get early release.

Abigail’s mother Mandy, 57, told The Sun the news hit her “like a sledgehammer”.

The family marked what would have been her 23rd birthday on Saturday before the Probation Service letter arrived on Monday.

It told them instead of serving two-thirds, which would have been eight years, he will now spend just six years in jail in a scheme to ease prison overcrowding

They urged No10 to ensure Bowes stays in jail, like the PM has vowed on PC Andrew Harper’s killers.

Mandy said: “My husband has severe MS. He’s traumatised by the loss of Abi and now he’s got the extra stress.”



Abigail’s dad Andy, 52, said: “The leniency of his sentence made us very angry. He may not even serve eight years. He killed our daughter.”

Durham Chief Constable Rachel Bacon said she was “deeply disappointed” Bowes could be released early.

The Ministry of Justice said it was “fast-tracking a plan to keep more of the most dangerous offenders behind bars”.

News.title: What time is the Clacton by-election result? When to expect the winner announcement and full list of candidates
News.content:
CLACTON voters will soon discover who will be their next MP after a record-breaking by-election.

Polling stations opened at 7am, but the 34-candidate ballot means the count could run later than usual.



What time is the Clacton by-election result?

There is no guaranteed declaration time, but the result is expected before breakfast on Friday.

Reports say the winner should be known in the early hours, while the complicated count could push the announcement back to around 5am.



Once voting ends, ballot boxes from 51 polling stations must reach the count centre.

Officials verify that the number of papers matches the polling-station records before counting all votes.



That job may take longer than normal because Clacton’s ballot paper is almost a metre long.

Acting Returning Officer Ian Davidson said its record size created practical problems, including how staff would spread the sheets out while allowing candidates’ representatives to watch.

He explained: “Administratively, it’s about how we fit this ballot into the envelopes for postal voters, and – when the voters receive their postal votes – how they get it into an envelope and get it back to us because it is that long.

“We also have an issue for the counters, how we’re going to lay it out, how we’re going to ensure that those who are watching can see while at the same time managing these metre long ballot papers.



No exit poll is planned, so voters should not expect a 10pm projection.

When do polls close in Clacton?

Voting runs from 7am until 10pm tonight.

The contest uses first past the post, so each elector chooses one candidate and the person with the most votes becomes MP – they don’t need to secure more than 50% of the vote.

The by-election was triggered when Nigel Farage resigned as Clacton’s MP on July 8, 2026.

Farage took 21,225 votes at the 2024 general election, finishing 8,405 ahead of Conservative runner-up Giles Watling.

News.title: Who is Count Binface and what is his real name? Meet the Clacton by-election candidate
News.content:
CLACTON has gone to the polls for a by-election that features a record-breaking 34 candidates on the ballot paper.

Nigel Farage has an unusual list of opponents in the vote, which was triggered by the Reform UK leader’s resignation from the seat in July – and Count Binface is one of the most recognisable.



What is Count Binface’s real name?

While the character claims to be a Recyclon from the planet Sigma IX and a fan of the classic TV show Lovejoy, the man sweating inside the suit is very much a human from Earth.



His real name is Jonathan David Harvey, a 50-something British comedian, satirical writer, and producer.

He has comedy pedigree under his belt, having worked on TV hits like The Thick of It and Have I Got News For You.

But when election season calls, Jon ditches the writer’s desk, straps on a giant metal bin, and transforms into a joke candidate – part of a long line of figures who have poked fun at the electoral process.

Labour, the Conservatives, the Liberal Democrats, and the Greens all refused to stand in the by-election – leaving the “intergalactic space warrior” in the unlikely position as Farage’s closest challenger.

After it emerged that the major parties were refusing to stand, Binface declared himself a “unity candidate”, and said, “Leave him to me!”

What are Binface’s most memorable election moments?

This is far from Binface’s first time at a vote, and the “space warrior” is a seasoned election veteran who loves winding up political heavyweights.



Before he became Count Binface, Harvey stood against Theresa May in Maidenhead during the 2017 general election under his previous alter-ego, Lord Buckethead.

The iconic image of a giant, bucket-headed alien standing next to a stone-faced Prime Minister went viral globally.

Following a copyright dispute over the Buckethead name, Binface was born.

He famously challenged Boris Johnson in 2019 and went toe-to-toe with Rishi Sunak in 2024.

He has also targeted City Hall, running for Mayor of London twice.



While he has never actually come close to moving into Number 10, his unusual manifesto promises – like capping the price of croissants – have won him an army of loyal fans.

News.title: Shock moment ammunition factory explodes as huge blast sends mushroom cloud into sky but firefighters can’t battle blaze
News.content:
THIS is the moment an ammunition factory exploded sending a massive mushroom cloud into the sky, as emergency crews struggling to contain the blaze.

The violent explosion rocked the major arms factory – which supplies weapons and munitions to Ukraine – near Rome, Italy, on Thursday.



Dramatic footage captures the towering mushroom cloud which was visible for miles.

The deafening boom ripped through the area around 4pm, prompting terrified locals to raise the alarm.



Firefighters rushed to the scene near Colleferro – 40km from Italy’s capital – where “complex operations” began.

Several fire brigade teams were deployed to the site but were not immediately able to enter the facility due to the severity of the blaze, local media report.



Videos shared on social media showed a fire at the factory followed by a massive explosion.

Employees were forced to shelter in secure areas at the facility, according to AGI news agency



There are currently no reports of casualties or injuries.

Officials say the blaze likely originated from the powder-pressing department.

In a post to Facebook, Colleferro Mayor Giulio Calamita said the incident caused “a huge scare”.



The alarm was raised shortly after 4:00 PM, when the supersonic bang was heard from a distance.

He said: “The fright is great, but right now it is essential to keep calm and, above all, to avoid spreading untrue information, such as that relating to the 2007 accident which is once again circulating.”

His post referenced a major explosion at the same plant in October 2007 which killed one worker and left 13 others injured.

The plant is owned by European defence group KNDS and manufactures medium and large-calibre ammunition.

The munition is typically used for naval and land defence and is relied upon by Ukraine’s forces.



The cause of the blaze is unknown.

Investigations are underway to reconstruct the events of the explosion and determine what caused the roar.

Police and emergency services remain on scene.

News.title: UK sees hottest day of the year as 38.1C recorded in Kew Gardens
News.content:
The UK has experienced its hottest day of the year and fifth hottest day on record, as a heatwave that gripped much of the country peaked at 38.1C on Thursday, the Met Office said.

Kew Gardens in west London recorded England's top temperature, provisionally surpassing the 38C recorded in Lingwood, Norfolk on 26 June.

The latest spell of extreme heat marks the UK's fifth heatwave this year, with the Met Office warning this summer is on course to be the UK's hottest since records began.

An amber heat health alert, warning of significant detrimental impacts to health and social care services is in place across the whole of England until 21:00 BST on Friday.

News.title: Son of 102-year-old says father died after being 'pushed off stage'
News.content:
Robert said: "He just asked them to turn the music down."

He said his father turned around to come back down off the stage when he was pushed, and that resulted in a broken hip.

"[That's] the most upsetting part. He wasn't going to live forever but it's not a nice way, obviously in pain," he said.

"We want to see justice, of course.

"They must have known he was an old man. It makes you wonder what the world is coming to.

"It has obviously made it difficult. It would've been nice if he'd gone quietly in his sleep.

"He was in hospital, suffering, for a week-and-a-half. It's not nice.

"I feel sad - even though he could be difficult because of his age and dementia, still, you get used to him being around," he said.

Robert, a retired civil engineer, said his father used to visit the Crow's Nest.

"What happened is not nice. The pub has changed a lot over the years. It has become a youngsters' pub," he said.

Robert said he grew up in the home in the the Llanyrafon neighbourhood where his father had lived since 1960.

He said his dad had a career as a design draughtsman and had lived alone since his wife died 40 years ago.

"Me and my brother would visit our father regularly, and clean the house and buy him food.

"His eyesight had deteriorated and he had been diagnosed with dementia two or three years ago."

Robert said: "He's well-known around here, although a lot of his generation are gone," he added.

He said his father would visit the pub two or three times a week, where he would drink beers, and described how he became a familiar face to some locals.

"I suppose he became a pub character," he added.

News.title: The key signs you may have damaged your eyes by looking at the eclipse
News.content:
Eye experts are warning people to be on the alert for any signs their vision has been damaged by looking at the sun during Wednesday's eclipse.

The symptoms can include blurred vision, a central blind or dark spot and increased sensitivity to light.

After the previous total eclipse of the sun that was visible in the UK in 1999, around 70 people were left with damaged sight.

Many of them had spent less than a minute looking at the spectacle, without realising they were harming their eyes.

The danger comes because staring at an eclipse without protection can damage the retina, which sits at the back of the eye, and particularly those cells responsible for sharp central vision.

The sun is incredibly bright, even when partially obscured by the moon.

Normally if we stare at it, we wince and quickly look away.

But when it is darker, during an eclipse, that instinct may not kick in, even while our eyes are being damaged.

The bright light and ultraviolet radiation given off by the sun can lead to a condition known as "solar retinopathy".

And because the retina has no pain receptors, it's hard for people to notice the damage as it happens, so symptoms may only appear several hours later.

Leading up to the eclipse itself, experts were warning only genuine specially-designed solar eclipse glasses should be used, and that ordinary sunglasses or other devices were not enough to prevent potential damage.

News.title: Honeytrap thieves jailed for killing men they had drugged
News.content:
A couple who drugged men seeking sexual services in order to steal from them have been jailed for killing two men and poisoning others.

Adina Mihai and Madalin Dumitru admitted the manslaughter of Gary Mouat, 37, from Oxfordshire, and Malcolm King, 80, from Gloucestershire, in 2025 and 2024 respectively.

On the first day of their trial in June, the pair also each admitted two further counts of administering poison to surviving victims.

Mihai, 31, and Dumitru, 30, were both sentenced to 17 years in prison at Oxford Crown Court.

Mihai, who posed as a sex worker, and her partner Dumitru, arranged to meet men paying for services she had advertised online at their homes.

The court heard four had their alcoholic drinks spiked with the powerful sedative gamma-butyrolactone (GBL) so the pair could steal from them.

Two men died as a result, while two others - who cannot be named due to reporting restrictions - survived.

News.title: Voting under way in Clacton by-election
News.content:
Voting is under way in the Clacton by-election as a record number of candidates vie to become its next MP.

Fifty-one polling stations in the Essex resort, which includes the towns of Jaywick, Frinton and Walton-on-the-Naze, opened at 07:00 BST and will shut at 22:00.

An electorate of 79,785 registered voters have the chance to vote for one of 34 candidates - the most ever to stand in a British election.

Voters will need to show a form of acceptable ID - such as a driving licence or passport - to be able to cast their ballot.

They will receive the longest ballot paper in British electoral history at 90cm - about 3ft long - to choose their candidate and cast their vote.

There are 12 political parties and 20 independents standing.

The constituency also has rural villages including St Osyth, Weeley and Great Bentley.

Polling stations will remain open to anyone registered to vote until 22:00, with the count taking place overnight.

News.title: Bonnie Tyler's classic hit spiked in streams during solar eclipse
News.content:
Born Gaynor Hopkins in a council house in Neath, Tyler grew up with a love for music before she was discovered by talent scout Roger Bell in a Swansea club.

Tyler released her first single, Lost in France in 1977, but it was the release of Total Eclipse of the Heart five years later which changed her life.

The ballad spent two weeks at UK number one and four weeks in the US.

The iconic love song's music video surpassed 1.2 billion views on YouTube and has had over a billion streams on Spotify.

Spotify previously said it had paid out more than $1.4 million for streams of Tyler's catalogue in 2025.

The music platform said Total Eclipse of the Heart was one of a few "celestial" songs that saw a streaming spike in the UK on 12 August.

According to Spotify, the biggest increases in UK streams during the eclipse were:

Evolfo, Moon Eclipsed the Sun (+12,817%)

Chris Staples, Dark Side of the Moon (+2,805%)

Pink Floyd, Eclipse (+594%)

Delta Goodrem, Eclipse (+104%)

Bonnie Tyler, Total Eclipse of the Heart (+94%)

Bill Withers, Ain't No Sunshine (+17%)

Shannon Carragher, senior editor at Spotify, said: "It is always fascinating to see how major cultural events instantly reflect in what the UK is listening to.

"Cultural phenomena like the solar eclipse naturally bring people together and we instinctively look for the perfect soundtrack to share that moment."

Ahead of the solar eclipse, Tyler's McVitie's Jaffa Cakes TV advert also resurfaced - it was originally broadcast in 2023 when there was a partial lunar eclipse.

The nostalgic advert came after research revealed almost half (49%) of Brits did not understand how eclipses occurred.

In the video, Tyler uses a Jaffa Cake as a prop to describe the different types of eclipse.

She said: "There are three types of eclipse. You've got the lunar eclipse, the solar eclipse, and then there's the total eclipse of the heart.

"When the earth is situated between the moon and the sun it creates a shadow, and when it looks like someone has just taken a bite out of the moon. That's a partial lunar eclipse."

The grammy-nominated star had a string of other hits, including Holding out for a Hero and also represented the UK at the Eurovision Song Contest in 2013.

She was named in the Queen's last Birthday Honours list in 2022 and was awarded an MBE for her services to music by Prince William the following year.

Tyler died "unexpectedly" on 8 July, aged 75, at a Portugal hospital, "as a result of the illness that she was being treated for", her family said in a statement released on the star's official website, external.

At the time, tributes poured in from a host of friends and stars including Catherine Zeta-Jones, Bryan Adams and Rod Stewart.

Tyler's funeral service will take place on 17 August at 12:00 BST at St Mary's Church in Swansea.

It has since been confirmed that her coffin will be brought to her Mumbles home on 15 August at 15:30 BST.

People are invited to "pay their respects" by lining Newton Road at 15:15 BST.

News.title: How to get a good night's sleep during hot weather
News.content:
Hot weather can make you feel tired and lethargic during the day.

That is because you are using more energy to regulate your internal temperature.

But if your sleep is disturbed at night, try to avoid napping during the day.

When it is hot, feeling sleepy can be precious - save it for bedtime.

News.title: Dad to stand trial accused of murdering daughter Minnie Merriman
News.content:
The father of a nine-year-old girl who died after being found seriously injured at an industrial estate in Arbroath is to stand trial accused of her murder.

Prosecutors allege Christopher Rice, from Wakefield, West Yorkshire, killed Minnie Merriman, who died in Dundee's Ninewells Hospital on 3 August.

The 35-year-old, who was remanded in custody, made no plea during a second appearance in private via videolink at Forfar Sheriff Court. He was fully committed for trial.

Minnie's family previously paid tribute to their "beloved, absolutely incredible, beautiful and brave Minnie Moo".

Emergency services were called to the Elliot Industrial Estate in Arbroath shortly after midnight on 3 August following reports that a child had been found injured.

Minnie was taken to Ninewells Hospital alongside four other people, but later died as a result of her injuries.

Police Scotland said they were not looking for anyone else in connection with Minnie's death and the other members of the family - who were camping in the area - are being supported by specialist officers.

News.title: Second attempted murder arrest after cycle path attack
News.content:
A second suspect has been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder after a man was attacked on the Bristol to Bath Railway Path.

The victim, aged in his 30s, was taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries believed to have been caused by a "bladed weapon" following the incident near Bitton at about 20:00 BST on Tuesday.

One teenager was arrested on the night of the attack and a second was arrested on Wednesday afternoon.

Both have been released on conditional bail while enquiries continue.

Insp Barny Mabbett, from Avon and Somerset Police, said: "Uniformed officers are conducting patrols along the railway path to provide reassurance because we recognise an incident like this does inevitably causes concern.

"Our investigation into what happened is ongoing, but we are also working with other organisations around making sure the railway path is a safe place for people to enjoy and use both in the short-term and long-term."

News.title: Leicester City put up for sale for more than £200m
News.content:
Leicester City are looking to sell the club for more than Â£200m, with its Thai owners King Power ready to leave after 16 years.

The Foxes have had an eight-page sales booklet produced by a leading US investment bank to help offload the one-time Premier League title winners.

Citigroup lists the Foxes, its women's team, and other major assets - including the 32,000-seat King Power Stadium and its Seagrave training facility which was opened in 2020 and is valued at Â£121m - as well as OH Leuven, Leicester's Belgian sister club, as up for sale in a brochure titled 'Project Lineup'.

The document, seen by BBC Sport, values the club's physical assets at more than Â£200m, though no specific sum has been attributed to the sale of its struggling teams.

The brochure speaks of "a rare opportunity to acquire a club with an excellent track record of winning promotions to higher divisions".

Leicester's successes, including the 5,000-1 Premier League title win of 2016 and the FA Cup triumph five years later, are well promoted in the brochure, while their place in League One, after back-to-back relegations from the top flight and the Championship, fail to get a mention.

The club's turnover, which Citigroup forecast to be more than Â£97m for the 2026 financial year are also part of the pitch, but the years of financial losses and the club's debts - which, as outlined in its 2025 accounts, include Â£103.6m in bank loans - are omitted.

In the years that the club yo-yoed between the Premier League and Championship, with two relegations from the top flight in three years between 2023 and 2025, the club lost more than Â£180m.

News.title: Bishop appears in court over child rape charges
News.content:
A 70-year-old bishop has appeared in court for the first time accused of two counts of rape against a female under the age of 16.

David Oakley, the Bishop of Northampton, was charged in June following an investigation by Staffordshire Police.

He appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court via videolink from his lawyer's office.

Oakley was not asked to enter a plea during the hearing as Chief Magistrate Paul Goldspring sent the case to the Old Bailey.

Oakley was released on bail, with conditions not to contact the alleged victim, or her family, ahead of a plea hearing on 10 September.

The incidents allegedly took place in Staffordshire between February 2000 and February 2001, when Oakley was in his mid-40s working as a Catholic priest.

Oakley was born in Stourbridge, West Midlands, and ordained as a priest in 1980 before becoming Bishop of Northampton in 2020.

Oakley retains the title of Bishop but has withdrawn from public ministry.

The Catholic Diocese of Northampton - which covers Northamptonshire, Bedfordshire and Buckinghamshire â said in a previous statement that it recognised the case was "very distressing for all concerned".

News.title: Human bones found in south-east London garden
News.content:
Human bones found in the garden of a bungalow in south-east London are being examined by the Met Police.

Officers were called to Aperfield Road in Biggin Hill at about 15:30 BST last Friday, the force said.

The bones were sent for specialist examination which confirmed they were human. They are now undergoing further tests to establish their age and identity, police added.

The area around the home was cordoned off for six days, according to The Sun, external, with one resident telling the newspaper the property was being renovated.

"The builders discovered something on Friday and of course they completely had to stop work," they added.

A Metropolitan Police spokesperson added: "The crime scene is now closed and an investigation remains ongoing to establish the full circumstances."

News.title: Ski Sunday host Chemmy Alcott suffers collapsed lung after jumping into lake
News.content:
Ski Sunday presenter Chemmy Alcott says she suffered a collapsed lung after jumping into a lake while on holiday in France.

The 44-year-old former GB Olympic skier posted a clip on Instagram, external that showed her jumping off a five metre platform into Lake Annecy, in the French Alps, before landing badly and ending up in hospital.

"Most people badly time a front flip off a five-metre platform and get winded," she said in the clip.

"I apparently don't do things by halves. Collapsed lung, chest drain and a very expensive lesson in rotation."

Alcott explained that she initially went back to jump again after her difficult landing, out of "embarassment" and "just so I wasn't making a big deal out of it".

But she soon realised she "couldn't breathe properly and should probably go and get it checked out".

She later shared images of herself in hospital with tubes and wires sticking out of her body.

In the caption to the main clip - titled "this didn't end well" - she wrote: "Well... that escalated quickly. Turns out five metres is quite a long way to discover you've got the rotation wrong.

"One badly timed front flip. One very hard landing. One collapsed lung. One chest drain. And a few more hospital overnights than were on the holiday itinerary...

"I absolutely loved Annecyâ¦ but I'm not entirely sure it loved me back."

A collapsed lung - medically known as a pneumothorax - occurs when air becomes trapped in the space between the lung and the chest wall, according the NHS.

News.title: UK economy grows but experts warn of challenging months ahead
News.content:
Summer sun and sports fixtures helped the UK economy grow between April and June, according to official data, but some economists warned the outlook for the rest of the year was weaker.

The economy expanded by 0.4%, in line with market expectations but below a 0.6% increase in the first three months of this year.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said growth had "remained relatively robust", with the UK ahead of other G7 countries for growth this year so far.

Experts questioned whether this resilience would be maintained, however, given growth was fuelled by some temporary factors and energy prices could remain volatile if the Middle East conflict continues.

The British economy is now 1.2% bigger than a year ago, the ONS said, despite fears that the Iran war, which started at the end of February, and politically uncertainty around Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as prime minister would hold back growth.

Between April and June, sectors including computer programming, advertising and the pharmaceutical industry lifted growth. That was offset by falls in power generation and sewerage.

The ONS said some businesses reported that "good weather and sporting events may have had a positive effect" in June, boosting month-on-month growth to 0.3%.

The men's football World Cup, which kicked off mid-June, increased customers at hospitality venues showing the matches.

June also saw several of summer's heatwaves. However, May's growth was revised down from 0.1% to zero growth.

News.title: Harvey Nichols bought by owner of Sports Direct
News.content:
Luxury department store Harvey Nichols has been bought by the owner of Sports Direct, which warned a "significant restructuring" was needed to ensure the 200-year-old business remains sustainable.

Mike Ashley's Frasers Group will take control of the Harvey Nichols stores, including its flagship in Knightsbridge, as well as the international franchise.

The department store was immortalised in BBC sitcom Absolutely Fabulous, but had faced challenges in recent years. The firm had appointed administrators in June.

Michael Murray, Frasers' chief executive and Ashley's son-in-law, called the store a "British institution with significant potential" but added "clear meaningful change is needed".

"The turnaround will require tough choices and we are prepared to make those decisions, even if that means a smaller business in the near term, to create a stronger and more sustainable Harvey Nichols for the long-term," he said.

Harvey Nichols carries more than 800 premium and luxury brands and has over 1,000 employees. Its other stores are located in Manchester, Birmingham, Bristol, Leeds and Edinburgh.

Frasers Group will also acquire the online business, and shops will continue to operate under their existing licensing.

Earlier this week, Harvey Nichols warned in its latest accounts that it would need to "cease trading" within a year if it failed to secure new investment.

It had faced "sustained trading and operational challenges" recently and Frasers Group said it will need to conduct a review of the store's portfolio, structure and cost base.

A recent auction for the store saw Frasers battle retail rival Next to take control of the firm.

Harvey Nichols was bought in 1991 by Hong Kong-based businessman Sir Dickson Poon but he put the group up for sale earlier this year.

Ashley Callingbull, Miss Universe Canada 2024, has paused this year’s pageant to address an instance of cultural appropriation involving two contestants.

While hosting the August 8 event, Callingbull, 36, who became the first Indigenous woman to win the crown in 2024, interrupted director Sonny Borrelli just as he was about to announce the top 20 contestants.

“So with Miss Universe Canada, me being the first Indigenous First Nations Miss Universe Canada, that was such a huge honor,” Callingbull, a Plains Cree woman, said in a clip shared on social media. “One of the biggest dreams of my life was coming here and fulfilling that.

“But sometimes there are mistakes that are made. During this week, I wanted to acknowledge this,” she continued. “During the national competition, the costume competition, there was cultural appropriation that was done towards Indigenous peoples. And I saw this right away. I wasn’t there. I just saw it on video.”

Ahead of the Miss Canada Final, the contestants went through preliminary rounds, including a national costume competition held August 4, which saw contestants Karisa Haverkamp and Jasleen Kaily take the stage in elaborate Indigenous costumes.

open image in gallery Karisa Haverkamp (left) and Jasleen Kaily (right) sparked controversy for their costumes during the 2026 Miss Canada Universe pageant ( Miss Universe Canada/YouTube )

open image in gallery Ashley Callingbull became the first Indigenous First Nations Miss Universe Canada in 2024 ( Getty )

Haverkamp modeled a strapless, patterned dress and an intricate, feathered headdress, traditionally worn by Indigenous leaders, while Kaily came out in fur-covered, knee-high mukluks, boots traditionally crafted by Indigenous people, and a matching fur-covered skin-tight dress.

Callingbull said that she quickly reached out to Borrelli and the Miss Universe Canada team, who “immediately listened.”

“They heard exactly what we need to do to change,” she recalled. “I think we’re living in a time, it’s 2026, we should know better, but most importantly, a part of reconciliation is that we educate and learn and understand and move on from these things in a good way.”

She then offered Borrelli the chance to publicly apologize to the Indigenous community.

“On behalf of all of us at Miss Universe Canada, it was not our intent to offend anybody and if we did, we take full responsibility, we will learn from it,” said Borrelli, announcing that Callingbull will be their new cultural liaison moving forward.

Both Haverkamp and Kaily have apologized for their actions, with the former writing last week in an Instagram post: “I acknowledge and recognize that my outfit for the national costume caused hurt and offense to people in the Indigenous community.

open image in gallery Callingbull has been named the cultural liaison for Miss Universe Canada ( Getty Images )

“I am proud of my own great-grandmother and her resilience and how much she was there for my dad and desired to share that with Canada and the world,” Haverkamp said. “I appreciate what I have learned from this experience and continue my commitment to stand up and speak for all women who have lost their voice because of violence, trauma and oppression.”

Meanwhile, Kaily added in a since-expired Instagram Story: “My intention was never to disrespect or misrepresent Indigenous culture.” She only wanted to “recognize and celebrate one of the First Peoples of Canada.”

“The best thing to do is represent Indigenous people because they have been in Canada the longest and it’s their land at the end of the day,” she later explained to the CBC, admitting that she had difficulty interpreting the guidelines for the national costume competition. “They [Miss Universe Canada] didn’t really have any guidelines on appropriation or anything that we can or cannot do. I don’t want to bash Miss Universe Canada because they were very supportive with everything.”

News.title: Lewes train derailment leaves multiple people seriously injured in ‘major incident’
News.content:
A Southern train travelling from London Victoria to Eastbourne derailed near Lewes in East Sussex on Thursday afternoon, causing three carriages to flip onto their side with approximately 150 passengers on board.

Emergency services and the British Transport Police declared a major incident, confirming that two people sustained serious injuries and nine others suffered minor injuries, with some requiring hospitalisation.

All passengers have now been safely evacuated from the train, with those not requiring hospital treatment being supported by multi-agency emergency services at a local community centre.

Witnesses described the terrifying moment the train derailed over ten seconds, whilst local residents responded alongside emergency crews to help shocked and bruised passengers reaching the welfare hub.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander expressed deep concern following the derailment, as the British Transport Police and the Rail Accident Investigation Branch launched an investigation to establish the exact cause of the crash.

At least 11 people were injured, two of them seriously, when a train was derailed in East Sussex.

Police declared a major incident after three carriages derailed and toppled onto their sides, leaving a number of people trapped inside in scorching temperatures.

The accident, at 3.44pm on Thursday, involved a Southern Railway train travelling from London Victoria to Eastbourne with around 150 people on board. The carriages derailed near Lewes station.

open image in gallery British Transport Police and rail workers at the scene in East Sussex ( AFP/Getty )

A passenger in one of the carriages said the experience was “completely terrifying”.

“There was a banging. Everything just went topsy-turvy,” said 56-year-old Yana Ludwig, from the United States.

“It seemed like a really long time but it probably was 10 seconds of that before the carriage actually fell on the side.”

She described being propped up over the top of another passenger, and added: “I’m pretty banged up.”

Another passenger told how the carriage “jumped vertically upwards” as it derailed.

open image in gallery Buckled tracks after the derailment ( BBC )

“We felt the train speeding up and starting to rock, and at that point we knew something was very strange, and then our carriage actually jumped vertically upwards, and we could tell there was a derailment,” he told the BBC.

Another passenger said he saw people who were injured.

“There were a number of people in ambulances that had had bad head injuries, and there was visible signs of blood on their heads and, you know, down their clothing,” he said.

Ambulance crews, air ambulances, critical care paramedics, fire crews and police all rushed to the scene.

The people who were trapped were later rescued, British Transport Police said.

open image in gallery Emergency services worked from an adjacent field ( PA Media )

Ms Ludwig estimated it was 20 minutes before the emergency services arrived, adding it seemed like a difficult place for them to reach.

She said everyone on the train was checking their fellow passengers were OK, adding: “These moments everybody kind of pulls together.”

The Rail Accident Investigation Branch sent inspectors to investigate what happened.

But photographs appeared to show the tracks had bent, possibly buckled.

Railway engineer Gareth Dennis told The Independent: “The damage here is as likely to be caused by the train as it derailed down the embankment, so very difficult to confirm a buckle with the available evidence.”

Residents of homes near the scene took chairs to a community hub for casualties to sit on.

One resident, Oriana Evans, who with her son helped casualties to the community centre at Lewes, said some of them seemed in shock and told her they were alright but “really bruised”.

open image in gallery Rail and emergency workers helped free people who had initially been trapped on board ( AFP/Getty )

“They were in the carriages that rolled over,” she said.

Some of the casualties were on holiday, Ms Evans said.

Transport secretary Heidi Alexander said she was deeply concerned and was “working quickly with the rail industry and local partners to assist passengers”.

Eastbourne MP Josh Babarinde, who said one constituent had suffered rib injuries, wrote on social media: “Once this immediate emergency is over, there are some serious questions that must be answered about how this happened, how this situation will be mitigated against from happening again, and how those on board will be compensated for what they have suffered.”

British Transport Police said it was believed that two patients suffered serious injuries and a further nine had less serious injuries.

“Patients have been assessed and treated at the scene, with some transported to local hospitals,” the force added.

South East Coast Ambulance Service said a number of passengers who did not need hospital treatment were being cared for at a local community centre.

“This remains a complex and ongoing multi-agency response,” a spokesperson said.

Most trains between Brighton, Lewes and Eastbourne or Seaford were cancelled.

The chief prosecutor in Fairfax County, Virginia, is reviewing footage of an ICE agent pointing a gun at a woman after she shouted profanities at the officers for conducting immigration enforcement.

The Fairfax County Commonwealth’s Attorney’s Office said it was looking into Monday’s encounter between Carolina Molina, a licensed personal counselor, and the ICE agents who cornered her in Falls Church, about 10 miles southwest of Washington, D.C.

“We have heard from community members who are concerned about this situation. We are aware of the incident and are reviewing it,” Laura Birnbaum, the public information officer for the Fairfax County Commonwealth’s Attorney, told The Independent.

Molina, who works with immigration lawyers to conduct psychological evaluations, says she was dropping business cards off at lawyers’ offices when she saw agents making arrests and yelled at them out her car window: “You’re a hoe, you f***ed up.”

Dashcam and cellphone video show ICE vehicles pulling up in front of and behind Molina’s vehicle, before a masked agent approached her driver’s-side window with a gun drawn.

open image in gallery The chief prosecutor in Fairfax County, Virginia, is reviewing footage of an explosive encounter between ICE and a woman who was yelling profanities at the agents ( tinyandstrongthings/Instagram )

The agent shouted at Molina, “Are you following us?” to which she replied, “No, I’m not.”

“You need to stop following us,” the agent said in the video. “This is your warning.”

He added: “You almost ran us over.”

Molina replied: “I didn’t almost run you over. You’re so full of s***.”

“Stop playing. Alright? You’re not being funny. I will arrest you; keep it up,” the agent yelled back.

Molina has denied following or threatening the agents. She said she drove in a circle around the parking lot before turning around because she didn’t want ICE agents following her into the immigration lawyer’s office in case an immigrant was inside.

“I think my life was in danger at that point,” Molina said Tuesday during a news conference alongside local immigrant-rights groups. “I think they should be investigated, and if their body cam was on, then put it out there.”

open image in gallery ICE agents in Virginia confronted a woman who shouted insulting profanities at them with a firearm and accused her of trying to run them over – which she says never happened ( tinyandstrongthings/Instagram )

Molina said that she told agents she was a U.S. citizen and that she had dashcam footage of the incident. The agents eventually let her leave without detaining her.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said that ICE was conducting “targeted immigration enforcement” against undocumented immigrants with criminal charges of hit-and-run as well as drug trafficking.”

The spokesperson said that an “anti-ICE agitator” was driving circles around ICE officers and tried to harm them by “weaponizing” her vehicle.

“Fearing for their safety, ICE officers conducted a vehicle stop of the driver,” the spokesperson added.

The agency said Molina could face criminal prosecution. She was not arrested and has not been charged following the encounter.

While the Commonwealth’s Attorney’s Office said it is reviewing the incident, it declined to provide any other information.

An enduring conspiracy theory has resurfaced on social media after a 7.4 magnitude earthquake hit western Colombia on Monday, with users blaming a research program in Alaska for the disaster.

Posts falsely claim that the earthquake, which has killed at least 270 people and left widespread damage, was caused by the High-frequency Active Auroral Research Program, or HAARP, which studies the properties and behavior of the upper atmosphere.

But the earthquake was caused by natural movements in the Earth's crust. Experts say it had nothing to do with human activities.

Here's a closer look at the facts.

CLAIM: HAARP caused the 7.4 magnitude earthquake in western Colombia on Monday.

THE FACTS: This is false. The U.S. Geological Survey says that the Colombia earthquake was caused primarily by “strike-slip faulting” — when two sections of Earth’s crust move horizontally past each other. The epicenter of the earthquake is within the country's Pacific region, which lies along the “Ring of Fire,” a line of seismic faults encircling the Pacific Ocean where most of the world's earthquakes occur.

“No human endeavor caused this earthquake,” said Suzan Van der Lee, a seismologist and professor at Northwestern University. “The Colombia earthquake occurred in a region with many natural earthquakes.”

She said there are cases where human activity in shallow parts of the Earth's crust such as gas extraction or waste water injection has caused small- to moderate-magnitude earthquakes. But the earthquake in Colombia occurred at a depth of 110 kilometers — at least 10 times deeper than any caused by humans, Van der Lee noted.

The University of Alaska Fairbanks has operated HAARP since 2015. It was previously run by the U.S. military, which still owns the land where the program is located.

HAARP has been the subject of conspiracy theories since the military started building it in the early 1990s. In addition to allegations that it can cause earthquakes, believers have falsely claimed that it is a mind-control device and that it can control the weather.

Researchers at HAARP study the physical processes occurring in the highest parts of Earth's atmosphere — the thermosphere and ionosphere — by using high-frequency radio transmitters to heat small regions and observing the effects.

The program uses many scientific instruments, but the one that is often at the heart of conspiracy theories is its Ionospheric Research Instrument (IRI), the world's most powerful high-frequency radio transmitter.

“I can confidently state that there is ZERO physical basis for radio-frequency transmissions having any effects on the occurrence of earthquakes,” said Dean Whitman, a geophysicist at Florida International University, who called hypotheses about HAARP's supposed impact “ridiculous.”

He pointed to a number of reasons the claims are not valid. One, the energy released by the Colombia earthquake was “much larger than that released by even the largest hydrogen bombs” and “millions of times larger than the energy produced by the HAARP array.” Two, HAARP's equipment is pointed upward, not downward toward where earthquakes occur. And three, the radio transmitters it uses produce electromagnetic waves that would not be able to cause earthquakes because they “involve a completely different set of physics."

The search for those buried in the rubble of the Colombia earthquake is ongoing. Tons of aid from regional partners began to roll into the country on Wednesday.

Detroit carmakers plan to caution the Trump administration that proposed updates to a North American trade deal could cost companies billions of dollars and hurt their ability to compete with foreign rivals.

American car producers are still struggling to absorb a wide range of levies imposed last year, including duties on steel, aluminum, parts, and vehicles imported from Mexico and Canada, while competitors from Japan, South Korea, and Europe face lighter tariff burdens.

U.S. auto executives now worry that proposals floated ahead of talks with Mexican trade officials next month could raise operational costs even further.

open image in gallery Detroit carmakers plan to caution the Trump administration that proposed updates to a North American trade deal could cost companies billions of dollars ( Getty Images )

A key point of friction is a U.S. demand that vehicles contain at least 50% U.S.-made content to qualify for lower tariffs. That requirement, alongside a plan to raise overall North American content beyond the current 75% level, would add at least $2 billion in annual expenses for each Detroit automaker, according to estimates from two companies.

Those expenses would come atop the substantial costs manufacturers have already incurred from various trade duties in place since last year.

The U.S. Trade Representative's office did not respond to a request for comment. However, administration officials have maintained that tariffs aim to spur domestic factory investment and job growth.

General Motors expects gross tariff-related costs between $2.5 billion and $3.5 billion this year, potentially representing over 20% of its operating profit, while Ford Motor pegs its net tariff hit at about $1 billion this year.

Ford’s latest onshoring

In an apparent signal to the White House of its commitment to make more cars domestically, Ford said on Wednesday it would move production of Lincoln models for the U.S. market to American factories from China, citing the Trump administration’s tariffs as a driving factor.

Ford CEO Jim Farley told Reuters the company might have been unprepared early on for the administration’s commitment to increasing U.S. auto production. But Ford – which already builds a larger percentage of its U.S.-sold vehicles domestically than its Detroit rivals – got the message, he said.

“It dawned on us very quickly, ‘Hey, look, we need to make some changes here,’” he said.

U.S. Commerce Secretary ​Howard Lutnick, in a joint interview, said he is hopeful more automakers will follow the lead of Ford and GM by moving factory work to the U.S.

“We worked together to get it right,” Lutnick added.

U.S. and Mexican officials are planning a fourth round of trade talks next month. Canadian trade officials have been meeting with their U.S. counterparts this week in an effort to avert another round of tariffs on Canada set to take effect next week.

Asian automakers’ advantages rankle

The American Automotive Policy Council, which represents Ford, GM and Jeep-maker Stellantis, referred Reuters to a June 30 statement saying that U.S. automakers are at a disadvantage to Japanese, South Korean and European automakers that export into the U.S. and face a flat 15% tariff.

GM CEO Mary Barra said on a July earnings call that the company is focused on “making sure that the U.S. automakers are going to be able to compete and win when we look at what the tariff rates are for Europeans, the Japanese and the Koreans.”

One U.S. auto executive said Trump more quickly forged deals with Korea and Japan because those governments were able to advocate on behalf of their automakers as part of broader trade agreements focused on national security, whereas the U.S. car companies didn’t have the same leverage.

“We don’t have a president or a prime minister who can call up Trump on our behalf,” the executive said.

Jennifer Safavian, president of Autos Drive America, a trade group for foreign automakers in the U.S. including Toyota and Hyundai, said the U.S.-Mexico-Canada trade talks are critical for all automakers.

"Our American and North American-made vehicles use significant amounts of U.S. content and international automakers are also being harmed by the current trade environment with Mexico and Canada," Safavian said in a statement.

U.S. automakers currently face a duty of about 25% on imports from Mexico and Canada, but vehicles with heavier amounts of U.S.-made content get lower tariff bills.

GM told Reuters that vehicles that have significant U.S. and North American content “should receive better treatment than vehicles that do not,” and added that the automaker is encouraged by the administration’s progress on negotiations.

Stellantis said it is encouraged by the talks and is working with the three governments "to ensure that we can build and sell affordable vehicles across the region."

A safety recall involving roughly 213,500 "Goody King" magnetic toy sets was announced in the U.S. after reports that defective parts caused severe injuries, requiring surgery for at least two young children.

The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission warned that the product's building blocks are prone to cracking or splitting open, leaving small internal magnets loose and creating a critical ingestion hazard for children.

If swallowed, these high-powered components can attract each other or other metal and become lodged in the digestive system. The CPSC warned this can potentially cause "perforations, twisting, and/or blockage of the intestines, blood poisoning and death."

open image in gallery Distributor Yi Suen Commerce has received at least 27 separate reports of the cubes fracturing, alongside the two confirmed cases where children ingested the loose magnets and required surgery to remove them ( U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission )

Distributor Yi Suen Commerce, a Hong Kong-based firm, has received at least 27 separate reports of the cubes fracturing, alongside the two confirmed cases where children ingested the loose magnets and required surgery to remove them.

The recall affects Goody King-branded Magnetic Building Cubes are in sets ranging from 45 to 300 pieces. The cubes contain small, strong magnets that connect the pieces, allowing users to build three-dimensional structures and designs.

The recalled magnetic cubes were sold in sets under 18 different style names, including Cute Zob, Dark Castle, Dinosaur, Farm, Firefighter, Forest, Galaxy, Game, Grassland Forest, Magic, Mineral Adventure, Sky Grass, Solid Blocks, Transparent Solid Blocks, Travel Game, Unicorn, Volcano Forest and Woods.

The model numbers for the recalled cubes can be found on the back of the product packaging.

Consumers in possession of the now-recalled magnetic toys are urged to stop using them immediately and contact Yi Suen Commerce for a full refund. More information on the affected model numbers and the recall can be found both on the CPSC's notice and Goody King's recall website.

In an online FAQ, Goody King noted that it will send prepaid shipping labels to customers who successfully register for the recall — and that refunds will be issued after the company physically receives the returned products. Receipts are not required.

The recalled toys were sold online through Amazon between January 2024 and July 2026 — under a variety of themes to build 3D designs like forests, dinosaurs and unicorns. They were priced between $17 and $50.

News.title: ‘More pain’ to come after economic slowdown
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. The economy grew at a slower pace in the second quarter of the year, official figures show, under pressure from the Iran war.

The UK’s gross domestic product (GDP) expanded by 0.4pc between April and June, down from 0.6pc in the first three months of the year, according to the Office for National Statistics.

The figures underline the challenge that the conflict poses for Andy Burnham, who has pledged to deliver “growth in every postcode”.

The Prime Minister has already been warned that the economy will slow further next year if Donald Trump continues his war in the Middle East.

Treasury officials have predicted UK growth of just 0.3pc in 2027 if the Strait of Hormuz stays blocked for the rest of this year.

That is far lower than the 1.6pc predicted by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) in March, based on assumptions made before the start of the war. Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) Iran war threatens to cripple growth, Treasury warns Burnham | Officials predict economic expansion of just 0.3pc in 2027 if Strait of Hormuz stays blocked

2) Britain facing £54bn bill for North Sea shutdown | Costs soar amid shortage of specialised ships needed to clear up abandoned oil rigs

3) Ban on zero-hours contracts to cost companies up to £3bn | Businesses face huge bill to offer workers guaranteed hours under Employment Rights Act

4) Nvidia’s AI push has echoes of Enron, says Big Short investor | Michael Burry claims chip giant is engaging in ‘circular’ financing

5) Shadow bank founder battles to stave off bankruptcy threat | Paresh Raja launches legal claim to prevent administrators from chasing him for repayment

What happened overnight

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng rose 0.3pc to 3,967.28, while the Shanghai Composite index added 0.5pc to 3,967.65.

In Australia, the S&P/ASX 200 slipped 0.4pc to 9,155.80.

Data from the US on Wednesday showed consumer prices had risen in line with analysts’ expectations in July.

Wall Street stocks were boosted on Wednesday by gains made by tech companies CoreWeave and Super Micro Computer, both of which closed up by more than 19pc.

The Nasdaq Composite ended the session up 0.5pc, with the S&P 500 up nearly 0.3pc. The Dow Jones Industrial Average finished the session marginally down.

Oil prices were little changed as investors weighed the deadlock in talks between the US and Iran over the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, was broadly flat at nearly $89 a barrel.

News.title: H5N1 sparks a very Australian epidemic
News.content:
H5N1 bird flu has reached Australia’s shores and is threatening to infect some of the country’s most unique wildlife.

Australasia is the last continent to be hit by the highly infectious avian influenza H5N1, a new strain of which has been circulating worldwide since 2020.

Since recording its first case in June, more than 200 wild seabirds in Australia have been infected, with fears that the highly infectious flu could quickly ‘jump’ to other species.

While H5N1 has infected animals from foxes to sea lions in other parts of the world in recent years, the epidemic now threatens some of Australia’s most iconic wildlife – many of which are found nowhere else on earth.

An Australian government assessment of more than 2,000 native species warned that nearly one in five faces a high risk from the deadly H5N1 bird flu, with hundreds of unique birds and mammals vulnerable to severe population reductions or even extinction.

Those animals include iconic species like the Tasmanian devils, quolls, and dingoes.

Other aquatic mammals, including the platypus, which is only found in Australia, are at risk of infection through contact with bird droppings in shared wetlands and coastal environments.

News.title: Selfie-seekers bring Man Utd vs Leeds match to premature end
News.content:
Aren’t friendlies supposed to be non-events? Manchester United against Leeds United in Dublin always had the capacity to be lively, but try explaining the half hour that Bruno Fernandes experienced in one breath. It would be impossible.

There was only one player the vast majority of the crowd wanted to see in the grandiosely named Boyle Sports Cup and, in chronological order from his 60th minute introduction, he received a standing ovation, hit the bar, had a goal disallowed, missed a penalty in a shoot-out and lifted a trophy.

Most remarkably – and, certainly, worryingly – of all, he was central to the game being ended early as five young boys, one after the other, breached security and ran to him in the middle of pitch, all of them successfully posing for photos with the Portuguese.

You could say it was harmless fun but it should not have happened and the flummoxed faces that were pulled on the Manchester United bench, as an army in high-visibility jackets stood and watched it all unfold, suggested they took a dim view.

News.title: Brian Madjo, 17, electrifies Villa despite Super Cup defeat by PSG
News.content:
His team played with all the resilience and bravery that has become a trademark, epitomised by the powerful Madjo and another teenager in midfielder George Hemmings.

Emery said: “Brian has scored goals for us in pre-season and has shown his capacity to work in our idea. I am so happy because the young players were involved in our work and not playing last season.

“Of course there is still work to do but they showed they can play with us. They have responded fantastically and will then feel the confidence. With a loss you can never be happy but overall I am proud of all the players and everything we’ve done. Some changes will be needed but we’re confident.”

This was a fine Villa performance to silence the doom merchants who have been fearing a troubled season. After the painful sales of Morgan Rogers, Youri Tielemans and Lucas Digne, Villa are clearly a team in transition. They are operating under restrictions to comply with Uefa’s financial rules and there is still the possibility of another important player leaving before the transfer deadline day.

England centre-back Ezri Konsa remains a priority target for Premier League champions Arsenal, and was absent here. Konsa, Emiliano Martínez and Ollie Watkins were all granted extended leave after their participation in the World Cup, which has done little to ease the fears of supporters over more departures. The trio will return to training this weekend.

While some outsiders are predicting a difficult season for Villa, do not bother telling Emery. He has turned putting noses out of joint into an art form since sweeping into Villa Park and with him around anything feels possible.

The Basque remains optimistic about the future and those hopes will only have been underlined by the performance of Madjo. He bullied PSG centre-back Willian Pacho for much of the evening and even managed to steal the limelight from PSG’s magician Khvicha Kvaratskhelia.

News.content:
When it comes to sending a child or grandchild off to university, it can be tempting to fill their room with every conceivable gadget.

So to help, we asked the Telegraph Recommended Community for their best gift recommendations and their suggestions ranged from desk lamps to cookery books and supermarket gift cards.

Here are the essentials worth buying.

Kitchen basics

From cupboard essentials to electrical appliances and cookbooks, most readers say they’d gift kitchen equipment.

Thinking back to his university days, reader TJ, 43, from London, says “the main essentials are around kitchen items and good long lasting food”.

News.title: Ebola outbreak ‘doubling every 20 days’, warns UN chief
News.content:
Congo’s runaway Ebola outbreak is doubling in size every 20 days, according to the United Nations humanitarian chief, putting it on track to soon be the largest ever seen.

Three months after the outbreak was officially declared, the case load is expanding exponentially and many believe the true toll is far higher than recorded.

If cases continue to double at the same rate, the flare-up in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) will surpass the record West African outbreak sometime around the end of September.

Modelling by one health analytics firm already predicts there is a more than 90 per cent chance that the DRC will become the largest on record.

The two-year West African outbreak grew to more than 28,600 cases and 11,325 deaths across Sierra Leone, Liberia and Guinea from late 2013 to 2016.

This year’s outbreak centred on the DRC province of Ituri has already seen 4,449 cases and 2,061 deaths in only a few months.

News.title: Madagascar forced to divide and share mpox vaccine as epidemic takes off
News.content:
Authorities in Madagascar are being forced to split single vaccines into fifths to try to protect as many people as possible during an ongoing mpox outbreak.

The method, known as “fractional dosing”, is authorised by the World Health Organization (WHO) in emergencies when there are critical vaccine shortages, but is not routinely recommended and carries a level of risk.

Madagascar, the African island with a population of roughly 33 million people, is currently battling its largest-ever outbreak of the virus formerly known as monkeypox, with at least 4,000 cases recorded so far.

Another one million people are thought to be at risk of contracting clade 1b mpox, a fast-spreading strain of the virus that emerged from the Democratic Republic of the Congo in late 2023.

High risk groups include sex workers, young children, and people living with HIV/Aids. Medical workers are also at risk.

“Public health authorities in Madagascar have been given too few doses to protect the at-risk population; they were initially given 30,000 doses in May, and a subsequent 30,000 have just arrived at the end of July,” said Akhil Bansal, a doctor of internal medicine working on the mpox response in Madagascar and a policy fellow at the Centre for Global Development.

“However, we need to vaccinate more than one million people, so we have been “fractionally dosing”, or splitting vaccines, into fifths, to stretch the supply as far as we can.

“This is a somewhat established approach for vaccines, but even then, the number of doses we have is insufficient,” said Dr Bansal.

Sports.title: Pep Guardiola copycats have been ruining the EFL slams veteran boss Tony Mowbray
Sports.content:
PEP GUARDIOLA copycats have been ruining EFL football.

That is the damning verdict from veteran boss Tony Mowbray as Blackburn travel to Wolves tonight for the Championship curtain-raiser.



And Mowbray, 62, insists a generation of bosses have been brainwashed into over-complicating the game with total-football tactics their players cannot pull off.

The Rovers boss told SunSport: “Pep Guardiola changed the landscape of football.



“People say it almost spoilt the game because everybody wants to play like Pep — but we can’t all play like him.

“In 2012, he had a formidable team at Barcelona with Xavi and Iniesta, a generation full of talent playing a false nine.

“A generation of coaches have come through inspired by him, inverting full-backs and playing overloads in different areas.

“And yet every week in lower leagues we see teams giving pathetic goals away by the goalie trying to play a little triangle in his box.

“At teams lower down, it’s much more difficult. It’s easier to press than to be the team with the ball.

“We can’t all play like Pep — you need a fusion of football and pragmatism.”



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

Mowbray believes the era of blind possession copycats is finally shifting into a far more practical, diverse age of football.

Mowbray said: “I think it’s riveting. Guardiola’s left now, and I think the game will resort back — not back to the 80s where everybody just has a striker and a little guy fast over the top.

“But I think it will become more diverse. More teams will be playing off the front and beating the press.

“It will become more pragmatic as well. I think there’s going to be a really special, good era of football.

“I love the game, all aspects of it. I can see the benefits of having a big centre-forward who can bring it in or flick it on, playing over the top of all these pressing teams who understand where the pressing lines are.



“When teams commit so many men to a press to win the ball high up, if you play over it, you’re two passes away and you can score. I think that’s really thought-provoking.

“That’s why I love the job of being a coach — analysing the teams we’re going to play and seeing whether we are going to kick every goal kick long today, or build from the back with four or five men and play through their lines. I like the idea of a team who can do both. A fusion of football.”

That obsession with trendy coaching metrics and extra tactical staff almost made Mowbray fall out of love with the game.

In early 2024, his world was turned upside down when forced to step down from Birmingham following a bowel cancer diagnosis.

And after undergoing surgery and treatment, Mowbray admits modern football’s push toward technical directors interfering with squad selection made him question returning.



He said: “I started thinking I wasn’t enjoying where football was going.

“I remember once trying to sign a very young Gerard Pique for Hibs on loan from Manchester United.

“I was at a petrol station, looked at my phone that was ringing and it said Alex Ferguson. I didn’t know whether to keep filling my car or take the call.

“I stopped and answered. He couldn’t let me have Pique but told me, ‘I’d advise you to have total control. The only way to succeed is to have control so players know who the boss is.’



“When I was at West Brom against Sir Alex, he’d come in for a drink and talk about control. That’s gone now.

“There are too many layers. Do I want to get told by a technical director who to pick or why players ran too hard? It’s about trust.”

That search for respect drew Mowbray back to Ewood Park following his recovery.

Following a short interim spell at West Brom last season, a homecoming at Blackburn gave him what Sir Alex insisted on… freedom to manage.

Mowbray said: “The job has become harder for coaches. I’ve always felt the manager needs to manage and pick the team.



“I found integrity and honesty in this ownership model. They look me in the eye and let me get on with it. The respect is there.

“There are different layers from when I was here before, but I don’t want total control. I want to do it together.”

Mowbray points to Blackburn’s academy products as proof that passing quality and direct power must coexist.



Crystal Palace and England midfielder Adam Wharton came through the ranks during Mowbray’s last spell between 2017 and 2022.

He said: “Adam was only 14 or 15 — but he’d train with the first team because he was so special with the ball.

“Jon Dahl Tomasson, who followed me, gave him his debut and Adam allowed the team to play an amazing passing game.

“I love seeing that, but I see the benefits of a big centre-forward who can bring it in or flick it on, playing over pressing teams.

“It’s a fusion of football. You have to figure it out.”



Despite his wariness of all the layers of analysts and technical staff in football, do not brand Mowbray a dinosaur.

He said: “I like data pointing us to the right players.

“There might be a winger in Belgium’s second division putting in the most crosses and I’d never know until data points at him.

“Then your wisdom correlates whether he can step up to Championship level and if he has the right personality to fit your group. Ultimately, data cannot tell you that.”

Mowbray admits his time off while fighting illness left him climbing the walls at home.



And with his children flying the nest for university, the family hit a major turning point.

Mowbray revealed: “I was driving everyone mad at home! Walking the dog was the highlight of my day.

“My kids are older now. One is 19 and flying off to college in America. We’re at a crossroads as a family because everyone’s flying the nest.



“How relieved is my wife Amber that I got back to work? She’s happy. She knows football is my driving force.

“She’s made so many sacrifices and deserves a medal.”

Back at Ewood Park, the thrill of managing still burns.

Mowbray said: “Seven months at home with the health pressure, I had dark moods.

“People asked if I looked at retirement — but my fire still burns. Why do I love it? Because you’re dealing with 30 individuals every day.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Some feel they’re the best player in town, asking, ‘Why am I not playing?’ Others are quiet and shy, yet they’re the best technicians, and you try to bring personality out of them.

“It’s an amazing job. You need trust and empathy. Computers are great, but you need a human touch.”
