The discussions covered judicial reform, media freedom, the treatment of people in detention, the rights of religious minorities, gender equality and the fight against corruption.

The EU also raised concerns about individuals who had been arrested or barred from leaving the country for exercising their fundamental rights.

Human rights issues also featured in sectoral dialogues on public administration, justice and social policy.

However, despite the continued channels of engagement, the EU says that “progress on structural reforms remains limited”.

Media freedom and fundamental rights

Media freedom and freedom of expression remained among the areas closely monitored by the EU.

The report notes that throughout the year, the EU closely monitored developments concerning digital rights, freedom of expression and media freedom.

EU-funded programmes supported independent media, human rights monitoring, legal assistance, gender equality and children’s rights.

The EU continued to support civil society organisations and human rights defenders working under restrictive conditions.

Azerbaijan on international platforms

The EU continued to raise human rights concerns in Azerbaijan through international organisations.

At the UN, during the 80th session of the General Assembly’s Third Committee, the EU raised issues concerning the space for civil society, judicial independence and media freedom.

Cooperation with the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights also continued, including preparations for Azerbaijan’s next Universal Periodic Review, scheduled for 2026–2027.

Within the Council of Europe, the EU supported mechanisms for implementing ECHR judgments and engaged with the Venice Commission and the Commissioner for Human Rights.

At the OSCE, the EU and its member states took part in discussions on media freedom and electoral standards, including restrictions affecting the work of the Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights.

European Union annual report

World.title: ‘Even if nuclear power plant is shut down, Armenia will not face serious problems’: Reaction to Aliyev’s remarks
World.content:
Yerevan reacts to Aliyev’s AzTV interview

“Every nuclear power plant has an operating lifespan. Neither the Armenian government nor the Azerbaijani government, nor the government of any other country in the world, determines that lifespan,” Armenian ruling-party MP Arman Yeghoyan said in response to the Azerbaijani president’s remarks.

In an interview with AzTV, Ilham Aliyev said the Metsamor Nuclear Power Plant was “outdated” and posed a potential threat to the entire region. He said “sooner or later it must be shut down”, after which “Armenia will face a full-scale energy crisis”.

At the same time, the Azerbaijani president said an energy corridor running through Armenia to Nakhchivan, then to Turkey and Europe, would “allow Armenia’s energy system to withstand a crisis”.

MP Arman Yeghoyan responded that “Aliyev has not made any revelation”. The maximum permitted operating period of the nuclear power plant expires in 2036, a fact that has long been known.

“And we have already announced that we are considering building a new nuclear power plant and are negotiating with several international partners,” the MP said.

Political analyst Samvel Meliksetyan believes Azerbaijan is trying to portray itself as a “generous country ready to help Armenia solve its problems”, despite the long-running conflict.

He noted that this was not the first such case. Baku had previously said that Azerbaijan could serve as a reliable partner for supplying energy resources to Armenia. Meliksetyan, however, said Armenia currently has a surplus of electricity. He stressed that even if the nuclear power plant shuts down, the country will not face serious problems.

“The claim that Armenia’s energy system will face a crisis after the Metsamor Nuclear Power Plant closes is not true,” the political analyst told JAMnews.

He said Armenia does not currently need additional sources of electricity. He noted that the project for a new nuclear power plant remains under discussion and that Armenia has opportunities to expand solar power.

In addition, the fifth unit of the Hrazdan Thermal Power Plant has roughly the same generating capacity as the nuclear plant. The only problem is that the nuclear power plant produces cheaper electricity.

Aliyev again refers to TRIPP as the “Zangezur Corridor”

During his visit to Nakhchivan, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev gave an interview to state broadcaster AzTV. Alongside the issue of the nuclear power plant’s closure, Aliyev discussed the 2020 Second Karabakh War. He called the trilateral statement of 9 November, which ended the fighting, “an act of Armenia’s capitulation”. He added that “there is no need to look for any humiliating or offensive meaning in this term; it is simply a reality”.

He then turned to the issue of transport links between mainland Azerbaijan and Nakhchivan. He stressed that this route had remained one of Baku’s strategic goals for many years.

“On 9 November, trilateral negotiations took place with the mediation of the Russian president. I insisted categorically that the statement we were about to sign must include a corridor linking mainland Azerbaijan with the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic. The Armenian side did not want to agree to this. But it did not have many alternatives. If the war had continued, we would of course have suffered losses as well, but Armenia’s losses would have been much greater. Its troops were, so to speak, surrounded, and their destruction had effectively become a possibility,” the president said.

Point 9 of the November [statement], which the leaders of Armenia, Azerbaijan and Russia signed, does not refer only to a road linking Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan. It states: “All economic and transport links in the region shall be unblocked.” Moreover, the document does not contain the term “corridor”.

Aliyev went on to say that Armenia had delayed implementation of the relevant provision of the 9 November statement and had taken no practical steps to create the “Zangezur Corridor”.

According to him, Russia, the third signatory to the statement, either could not ensure its implementation or had other reasons for not doing so.

“Until August last year, this issue remained frozen. The situation changed when the United States became involved, around spring 2025. The implementation of the project known as TRIPP then began successfully,” Aliyev said, linking the Trump Route transit project to the idea of the “Zangezur Corridor”.

For several years, Baku had demanded that Armenia provide a “Zangezur Corridor” to connect Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan. The Armenian authorities repeatedly said they were ready to unblock all transport links, but refused to provide a “corridor”. The issue stemmed from the fact that Azerbaijan used the term “corridor” to refer to an extraterritorial route. Armenia, meanwhile, refused to give up sovereign control over its own territory.

On 8 August 2025, the sides reached an agreement in Washington, with the mediation of the US president, under which Armenia would provide a route while retaining its sovereign rights. The transit project therefore received the name “Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity” (TRIPP).

Aliyev also said that, as part of TRIPP, Azerbaijan had already prepared a project to build power transmission lines from mainland Azerbaijan to Nakhchivan through Armenian territory:

“As a result of our specialists’ survey of Armenian territory, we identified the points where the supporting pylons should be installed.”

The Azerbaijani president expressed hope that “Armenia will not delay this process”, saying it would also benefit the country.

“There is no infrastructure by that name in Armenia” — MP

Arman Yeghoyan, an MP from Armenia’s ruling Civil Contract party, said that documents signed by Armenia and Azerbaijan, including the peace agreement initialled in Washington, do not contain the term “Zangezur Corridor”.

“At the level of political narratives, you can say many things. But we are saying that there is no such concept or infrastructure with such a name or term on Armenian territory.”

The MP urged people to remember that Armenia is implementing the TRIPP project. The leaders of Armenia, Azerbaijan and the United States signed the declaration launching the project in Washington on 8 August 2025.

Comment

According to political analyst Samvel Meliksetyan, when the Azerbaijani side explains what it means by the “Zangezur Corridor”, it refers to the railway from Horadiz to Nakhchivan and then on to Turkey. He also noted that Aliyev used the name TRIPP in his interview.

The analyst said the meaning attached to the term “Zangezur Corridor” in 2022–2023 differs from what it means today. In his assessment, the project no longer involves an extraterritorial corridor:

“From a legal standpoint, TRIPP cannot become an extraterritorial corridor. But from a propaganda standpoint, Azerbaijan uses and will continue to use the term ‘Zangezur Corridor’, with some modifications.”

Meliksetyan stressed that the “Trump Route” project would proceed according to principles agreed with US mediation.

Commenting on Aliyev’s statement about building power transmission lines through Armenian territory, the political analyst said the sides were assessing the most suitable routes. He said the involvement of Azerbaijani specialists should not be interpreted as “acting on their own”.

“All the work is being carried out within the TRIPP framework. An electricity link will run through Armenian territory and connect the two parts of Azerbaijan. Azerbaijani specialists can only discuss where the link will enter Armenia from Azerbaijani territory and where it will re-enter Azerbaijan,” the expert explained.

Summing up his impressions of Aliyev’s interview, Meliksetyan said the Azerbaijani president had spoken in his characteristic style, seeking to highlight his “political achievements”.

The analyst said it was no coincidence that Aliyev focused on Nakhchivan’s economic and energy development, as well as its transport prospects. The president said Azerbaijan would finance the railway restoration itself, but also expressed interest in attracting international investors.

“Although Azerbaijan has repeatedly said that it has no financial problems, they certainly exist. Baku is trying to attract new investment to Nakhchivan through TRIPP to restore this section of the railway,” Meliksetyan said.

Yerevan reacts to Aliyev’s AzTV interview

World.title: Severe petrol shortages hit Abkhazia amid Russia fuel crisis following Ukrainian attacks — VIDEO
World.content:
Fuel shortages in Abkhazia

Severe fuel shortages continue in Abkhazia in the middle of the tourist season. All petroleum products are supplied exclusively from Russia, leaving one clear explanation: fuel shortages in Russia caused by Ukrainian drone attacks on oil and gas facilities.

The Abkhaz authorities are holding emergency talks with Moscow and say progress has been made. Reports say Russia has already arranged for 1,600 tonnes of AI-92 petrol to be sent to Abkhazia, with the first shipment expected to arrive in the coming days.

For now, petrol is available only at Rosneft and Podorozhnik filling stations.

Meanwhile, reports say petrol was supplied from territory controlled by Tbilisi

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze confirmed this:

“Amid the severe fuel shortage, a shipment was made to Abkhazia, but it was not supplied by the state, it was supplied by private businesses. If we continue to have the opportunity to ease the situation for the people living there, both Georgians and Abkhaz, we will continue to do so,” Kobakhidze said.

The Abkhaz news agency Apsnypress asked the Abkhaz government for comment following Kobakhidze’s statement and received the following response:

“Due to the circumstances caused by external factors, there is not enough motor fuel to meet Abkhazia’s needs. The authorities therefore decided to allow fuel supplies from alternative sources. Fuel market participants managed to arrange a shipment of petrol from Georgian territory. As is well known, Abkhazia also supplied fuel to Georgia from its territory in the post-war 1990s.”

Kobakhidze’s statement drew criticism from the opposition in Tbilisi. Opposition politicians said the fuel supplies to Abkhazia “could in fact mean supplies to Russian military bases”.

Economist and opposition politician Roman Gotsiridze said: “It is possible that the fuel could also have been transported to Russian territory. The company that made these deliveries will not escape sanctions.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Fuel shortages in Abkhazia

World.title: Georgian PM confirms “fuel was supplied to occupied Abkhazia from Tbilisi-controlled territory”
World.content:
Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze confirmed that petrol had been supplied from Tbilisi-controlled territory amid a severe fuel shortage in occupied Abkhazia. A journalist asked Kobakhidze about the issue.

Occupied Abkhazia has recently faced a severe fuel shortage, leading to significant restrictions on supplies of petrol and other petroleum products.

“We did not introduce this; it was introduced by private businesses,” Kobakhidze said at a briefing. He added that such measures were being taken in line with Georgia’s existing legislation, including the Law on Occupied Territories.

He said the Georgian government was ready to help ease the situation for people living in occupied Abkhazia where possible.

“If we can ease the situation, including for the population living in Abkhazia, we will do so, but we will act within the framework of the Law on Occupied Territories,” Kobakhidze said.

Kobakhidze also referred to the government’s “A Step to a Better Future” programme. According to him, it provides support for people living in the occupied territories, including the Abkhaz population.

Comment

Opposition Coalition for Change leader Nika Gvaramia reacted to Kobakhidze’s statement and called on the government to provide further clarification.

Gvaramia noted that Georgia’s Law on Occupied Territories generally prohibits direct unauthorised economic activity in Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region, although it provides certain exceptions, including for activities carried out for humanitarian purposes.

Gvaramia suggested that the fuel supplies in this case could have been intended for Russia’s “war machine”.

Nika Gvaramia: “We are dealing with an action that was presumably authorised by the government in advance. However, the public has not been told the grounds for such authorisation, or when and why it was issued.

“Given that:

— the Russian military machine is facing a severe fuel shortage, while Russian military bases are located in occupied Abkhazia;

— the Ivanishvili regime has repeatedly and deliberately stressed the need for cooperation with Russia;

— taking into account Georgia’s security and territorial integrity interests, as well as Western sanctions imposed on Russia, fuel supplies to territory controlled by Russia cannot be justified on legitimate humanitarian or socio-economic grounds,

“it becomes clear that the Ivanishvili regime has effectively acknowledged that, with its authorisation — and, in essence, by the regime itself — an action is being carried out that runs counter to Georgia’s sovereign interests. It:

violates Georgia’s Constitution;

violates Western sanctions imposed on Russia;

is aimed at assisting the Russian military machine by supplying strategically important products.”

Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

World.title: Tasmanian parliament to probe transparency of Rushy Lagoon sale
World.content:
The sale of Tasmania's largest farm to a UK investment firm will be probed by a state parliamentary committee.

Rushy Lagoon, a 21,745-hectare property in the state's north-east was sold to Gresham House after the sale was vetted by the Foreign Investment Review Board and approved by federal Treasurer Jim Chalmers last month.

Gresham House plans to plant about 12 million radiata pine seedlings across 9,000 hectares of the farm over the next five years.

It is also considering cropping and leasing out parts of the farm for grazing, tourism and mountain biking.

There has been community outcry about the sale, mainly over the pine plantation plans.

Gresham House plans to plant about 12 million radiata pine seedlings across the farm over the next five years. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

Advocacy body TasFarmers described Mr Chalmers' decision as a "betrayal of Tasmanian agriculture".

The Tasmanian government has been vocal in its opposition to the sale and proposed the parliamentary inquiry.

Primary Industries Minister Gavin Pearce told parliament yesterday that significant questions remained, including whether federal government policies were "inadvertently favouring carbon credit outcomes over ongoing fibre and food production".

He said the inquiry was "not about relegating a decision".

"It's about transparency, it's about accountability, it's about ensuring that Tasmania's interests are properly considered in the future," he said.

Gavin Pearce says the inquiry is about ensuring transparency and accountability over the sale. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

With four independent MPs David O'Byrne, George Razay, Craig Garland and Carlo Di Falco voting with the government to establish the inquiry, it had enough support to pass.

Pine, cattle and tourism for Rushy Lagoon The buyer of Tasmania's largest farm says in addition to the pine plantation it has planned for the property, it's also considering cropping and leasing out parts of the farm for grazing, tourism and mountain biking.

Mr O'Byrne told parliament every inquiry had a level of politics about it, but he said if done well the inquiry could be important for the community affected by the sale.

"At the end of the day no-one can doubt that there is significant community concern and we have a responsibility as legislators, as parliamentarians, as representatives of our community to work through a process to inform our community," he said.

Mr O'Byrne also said farming communities "across the country" were looking at the Rushy Lagoon sale.

Neither Labor nor the Greens supported the motion for the inquiry.

Shane Broad says the inquiry is a "witch hunt" which "won't change a thing". (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

Labor's resources spokesperson Shane Broad said the inquiry was "a complete farce".

"The property [sale] settled on Friday, they can't change the outcome," Mr Broad said.

" Regardless of what people think of the sale, the witch hunt committee the Liberals want to set up will have no power to call federal officials and won't change a thing. "

Greens primary industries spokesperson Tabatha Badger said while she acknowledged there was significant concern about the sale, and the Greens also had questions, a federal parliamentary inquiry would be more appropriate.

World.title: One of Australia's longest-serving editors dies aged 96
World.content:
One of Australia's longest serving journalists and editors has died aged 96, after nearly eight decades of contribution to a local newspaper in Victoria's north-west.

Robin Letts had worked at The Buloke Times at Donald since 1947, and had been editor since 1987.

The family newspaper was started by the Letts family in 1875 and had been passed through generations until it was sold late last year.

For over half of the newspaper's history, Letts had been involved with the paper.

On Thursday The Buloke Times announced Letts had died on Wednesday evening.

"We said goodbye to our beloved editor — the man who always found the words when we couldn't," the post read.

"We'll miss him more than we can express.

" Our hearts are broken. "

'An incredible man'

Before starting at the paper in 1947, he had a short stint in the navy aiming to become a sailor, but life on the ocean was not for Letts and he returned to work with his father, Goff Letts.

He became editor after the death of his father in the 1980s.

A young Robin Letts pictured with his father and then editor Goff Letts circa 1985. (Supplied)

Former Buloke Times journalist Shane O'Shea worked with Letts for over half a century.

"I started as a hand and machine compositor and he's been a mentor, friend to me," O'Shea recalled.

"He started off as my boss and later become a business partner and just an incredible man and his contribution to Donald over the years through his writing, through his interest in every group was phenomenal.

"He's left a legacy that will be impossible to emulate, but it'll last forever."

O'Shea said there were no "gutter tactics" in whatever Letts wrote and everything was always honest, factual and from the heart.

Robin Letts (left) with his son, David, and a picture of their ancestor Godfrey Morgan, who founded the newspaper in 1875. (ABC Landline: Tim Lee)

In 2003, Letts was awarded the Medal of the Order of Australia for his service to the Donald community and for his commitment to the publication of the local newspaper.

Last year, the newspaper celebrated its 150-year milestone.

The newspaper surpassed the Fairfax family as the longest continuous family newspaper dynasty in Australia.

Earlier this year, Letts had a fall at work and was unable to fulfil his role as editor, but he retained the title and was committed to the paper until his death.

Letts was still working six days a week until his fall.

"Everyone respected him, everyone was his friend and he just about knew everyone in town and if you wanted help, Robin was there to give it through the newspaper," O'Shea said.

"I think the newspaper is held in high esteem because it represents the community and Robin was the main face of the newspaper."

'A passionate community man'

Buloke Shire Council mayor Graeme Milne said Letts was a gentleman and would help anyone.

"He was a passionate community man, very much involved in anything to do with Donald and the wider community. He had a real interest in people and a great passion to tell their stories," Cr Milne said.

He said Letts would leave a real legacy in the community and across regional Victoria.

"His family was everything, his work was everything and then it was his community and his love for sport and travel," Cr Milne said.

The Buloke Times has been published in Donald since 1875. (ABC Landline: Tim Lee)

ABC Landline senior reporter Tim Lee interviewed Mr Letts and his son, David Letts, last year for the 150-year milestone of the newspaper.

Lee recalled Letts as a "consummate newspaper man".

"He lives and breathed that job and did it from the time he was 17 until 96," he said.

"He almost wrote his last newspaper editorial from his hospital bed, as his late father did."

Lee said Letts had come from an amazing pedigree stemming all the way back to his grandfather.

According to Lee, Letts's great grandfather came to Australia to report on the Goldfields with a letter of introduction from Charles Dickens.

Rural Press Club of Victoria president Kellie Lazzaro said many were reflecting on Letts's remarkable and enduring legacy.

"More than 70 years at the one paper must be a record-breaking innings for any editor and journalist in regional Australia," Lazzaro said.

Earlier this year the press club presented Letts with a Lifetime Achievement Award for his service to the media industry and to the Donald community.

"I'm just so grateful that our industry broadly was able to recognise Robin in that way, and I know that he was incredibly humbled to receive the award," she said.

"It's not easy being a journalist in a small town, there is nowhere to hide.

"The tributes that are coming through today for Robin Letts show that he has been able to work as a journalist and maintain the respect and admiration of his community whilst doing things like holding people to account, attending sporting events and keeping busy."

World.title: Long careers increase risk of brain damage, but is informed consent enough?
World.content:
The secret document that Geelong defender Jake Kolodjashnij signed to release his club from any legal risk over future concussions has opened an enormous can of worms.

That is aside from the ethical considerations, the conflict of interest faced by the AFL chairman, Craig Drummond, who was Geelong president at the time, and the Cats' response to why they did not lodge the document with the AFL.

What the incident does shine a light on is the logical extension of sanctioning high-collision sports.

Because the truth is, by allowing people to play contact sport, particularly at the elite level, they are exposed to a life of potential brain injuries and chronic pain.

Neurophysiologist and concussion researcher Alan Pearce from Swinburne University found the longer professional athletes participated in certain contact sports, at any level, the greater their chance of some form of brain trauma.

His findings sparked a realisation involving multiple swear words.

"I say 'holy f***" a lot," he told ABC Sport.

"As I progressed with the increasing of the numbers, I began to realise that there is a spectrum of damage that players were getting.

"This is something that's going to happen to everyone who plays this sport for a long period of time."

Professor Alan Pearce is a leading researcher on concussion in sport. (Four Corners: Ryan Sheridan)

For some it was micro damage that would not affect a person's quality of life, but for others it was more serious.

"So, how do we accept a certain amount of damage that is not going to significantly affect the rest of their life or even cut their life short?" Professor Pearce asked.

He and his colleagues published the work earlier this year in the Journal of Clinical Neurophysiology, studying 113 retired male professional Australian rules, rugby league and rugby union players, aged between 28 and 68.

They found that it was the length of a player's total career, not the length of their professional career, nor the number of concussions they suffered, that was the problem.

Consider someone starting Aussie rules as a 10-year-old, getting drafted when they are 18, but then continuing to play long after they retire from the professional game.

Professor Pearce had some test subjects who had played at various levels for 35 years.

The damage was not necessarily caused by major concussions; it was the constant sub-concussive knocks that were the problem.

What does this mean for professional contact sports?

When someone signs a professional contract to play Aussie Rules, or another collision sport, they are potentially signing up to future brain damage.

That is not to mention any number of other risks: An ACL injury, the likelihood of a knee or hip replacement at an early age, the possibility of chronic pain or injuries that restrict a person's lifestyle and career.

There is a risk of sustaining many different types of serious injuries when playing professionally. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Jason McCawley)

This is the price they pay, but is it worth the cost?

"It's like this unspoken acceptance of professional sport," Professor Pearce said.

"It goes beyond healthy living; in some ways professional sport is extreme sport."

Which raises a difficult question the AFL and other codes are facing: How do you run a sport where there is an implicit risk of brain damage for participants?

Acknowledgement of risk

Which brings us back to the document that Kolodjashnij signed and that Geelong did not think necessary to run by the AFL.

It has now been reported the document was titled "Voluntary Assumption of Risk" and stated: "You take upon yourself the physical and legal risk of loss, damage or injury of any kind arising directly or indirectly as a result of concussion sustained by you following your decision."

There may be a myriad of problems with what happened, but the concept of an acknowledgement of risk is not so far-fetched.

Kolodjashnij signed the concussion waiver with the Cats in 2024. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Anyone undertaking surgery signs a consent form. It does not absolve a surgeon of gross negligence or malpractice — you cannot break the law or contract your way out of legislation.

But consent effectively protects surgeons from foreseeable events that may occur in surgery, like an infection.

The idea is that people go into the surgery fully aware of the potential risks.

Have we reached a point, given what we know about the dangers of concussion in collision sports, that players may need to sign a consent form when they take up a professional sports contract?

Professor Pearce thinks so; not to absolve clubs and the AFL of responsibility, but for ethical reasons.

"So that everyone knows everything up front," he said.

"It's also about risks of ACL and other injuries. I don't know if young players understand the psychological stress that they're going to be under."

The AFL's concussion protocol says players must be sidelined for at least 12 days before returning. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

At present, there is nothing in the AFL standard players' contract or the players' collective bargaining agreement that spells out the potential risks of the game.

"You could argue that the whole premise of the AFL educating the playing group on concussion probably covers that," a spokesperson for the AFL Players Association told the ABC.

Professor Pearce said the expectation is that the AFL should do all it can to minimise the chances of players getting concussed and for clubs to play their part.

He cited monitoring loads through the use of smart mouthguards, placing limits on kids playing football and limiting contact training.

The latter was a recommendation of the Victorian State Coroner, John Cain, from his findings into the death of the former AFL player Shane Tuck in 2023.

The AFL responded in 2024, saying it was implementing that recommendation, although it is still yet to come into place after a long period of collecting training data.

It is understood the AFL is considering limiting contact training from next year.

The bigger picture

Consent would not stop players from suing the AFL or clubs if they have acted negligently.

That is an allegation that will play out in the Supreme Court of Victoria next year, when a class action led by the former Geelong player Max Rooke will hear arguments that he was left with brain damage because of the actions of the AFL and his club.

Rooke has been joined by around 120 former players who are suing the AFL and 11 clubs.

Loading...

This is the bigger picture of the risk facing the entire AFL, and all other collision sports for that matter.

In a writ lodged with the court, Rooke claimed he suffered between 20 and 30 concussions while playing for Geelong, resulting in "life-altering injuries".

This week Margalit Lawyers, acting for the players, signed up two more former players to the class action.

The writ argues the AFL and the clubs failed in their duty of care to enforce rules and protocols around concussion to ensure the players' safety and to avoid exposing them to risk.

"We say that the precautions that we allege should be taken in our statement of claim should have been in place a lot earlier based on medical evidence," special counsel with Margalit Lawyers, Daniel Schram, said.

While Schram believes the AFL should continue to educate players and keep them up to speed with the newest evidence around concussion, he doesn't believe a consent form is the way to go.

Neither does the University of Melbourne Law Professor, Jack Anderson.

"We do know that there is a risk there and the players do agree to that to a certain extent," he said.

"It's an implied consent."

But he said the risk shouldn't be placed on the players.

"The risk should lie with the AFL to make the game as safe as it possibly can."

World.title: Swans AFLW head coach looking to turn his young age to advantage
World.content:
One of the best pieces of coaching advice Sydney Swans AFLW head coach Colin O'Riordan ever received was to never forget what it feels like to be a player.

Luckily for O'Riordan, who is 30, those days are not far behind him.

"Sometimes you feel like, coming in as a young person, you just want to get that respect with the group really quickly, but there is a daunting element where you know … I'm not that much older than some of the girls," he told ABC Sport on the eve of the AFLW season.

"Some of them are probably older than me."

Defender Tanya Kennedy is 33, and the list has a number of players in their late 20s.

"So it's just gaining that respect. And hopefully I have got that respect," O'Riordan said.

"What I probably have in my favour is I'm not long finished playing, so you understand what it feels like to be a player … It's a bloody tough sport to play."

O'Riordan played 34 games for Sydney between 2016 and 2022 before chronic hip injuries forced his retirement.

He remained in the Swans' ranks as head coach of the under-18 male academy and then AFLW assistant coach before being appointed the top job in December last year.

He is the first Irish senior coach in AFL/AFLW history.

Colin ORiordan retired from playing in 2022. (Getty: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

He said part of holding onto the feeling of being a player was understanding the pressure of game day.

"It's a hard game. In W, you're asking the players to run eight, nine kilometres at very high speed, sprint-running, and make decisions under pressure in front of crowds, [in] front of people watching on TV," O'Riordan said.

"It's a pretty hard thing to do and yes, we train for it and yes, we get paid. I get that. But at the same time, they are still people, and that's what you hope people see."

Colin O'Riordan during a match simulation at Tramway Oval. (Getty: Matt King/AFL Photos)

He wants to take "a relationship-based approach" to coaching.

"I want to know who's running out for me, who's playing for me, and actually what makes them tick is huge for me," he said.

"In the W side, I feel like it's if you don't connect like that with the girls, it's very hard to ask them to do something for you if they're kind of looking at you, going, 'Well, you don't really care about us.' So having that caring element is huge for me."

O'Riordan has had to adjust to emotionally approaching the game, which he says can be up and down.

"Very much you ride the roller coaster of footy," he said, speaking of players, coaches and fans.

"Football is an emotional game. It's a game basically built on passion, and fans are passionate, and that's why you love the game.

"But also, as a coach, sometimes you got to — not sometimes, probably more often than not — you got to remove that emotional side from the passionate side.

"I think that's when you start making blurred decisions. Yes, it's emotional. Yes, it's a passionate game, but you just have to really know where that line is, which is a constant battle for anyone coaching the team."

Colin O'Riordan with Swans teammates Zippy Fish, Chloe Molloy and Paris McCarthy. (Getty: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos)

The first game of the Swans' upcoming season is against three-time premiership side Adelaide on Sunday, August 16.

While it will be O'Riordan's official debut as AFLW coach for premiership points, the Irish import coached the Ireland side against Australia earlier this month for the historic representative game.

O'Riordan took over from Scott Gowans, who had mixed results in the Swans' early years.

The club entered the competition as an expansion side in 2022 and made an impressive semifinal run the following year, but failed to reach the top eight in the following two seasons.

Last year the Swans finished ninth on the ladder.

"It's a new chapter, it's a new beginning, and I'm just really excited to see where we can get, to be honest … politician's answer," O'Riordan laughed.

Colin O'Riordan says knowing the hard work has been done during the week helps to ease the nerves on game day. (Getty: Matt King/AFL Photos)

He admits he is nervous, but those nerves are a good thing.

"I think that's human nature," he said.

"I mean, you care, and yes, while you can be nervous, the second game day comes, I get a lot of solace in the fact that I've done the work during the week.

"And if we've done the work, game day is our chance to really excel in what we plan for the whole week. So yes, there's nerves, but there's also an excitement that today's the event … in my head, that should override the nerves to say, 'No, I've done the work.'"

Plus, he added, on game day "you don't have time to think too much" about emotions.

World.title: Hospital missed critical signs before young dad's death, review finds
World.content:
There were no free beds or even an empty treatment bay in the emergency department on the night youth worker Amenatave "Mena" Tuibua walked into Mackay Base Hospital with a sharp pain in his chest.

The public hospital was at capacity on the night of May 26, 2025. Patients waiting for beds were stuck in the emergency department and others were ramped in ambulances.

Mr Tuibua, 41, sat in the emergency department waiting room with no cardiac monitoring for three hours before he was sent home.

Resina Tuibua visited family in Fiji with her mum Shey and dad Mena in 2025. (Supplied: Shey Tuibua)

He left unaware doctors had failed to correctly read his ECG, which showed an abnormal heart rhythm, and had failed to follow guidelines for assessing cardiac pain.

Later it was judged "highly probable" that medical staff had looked at another patient's blood test result instead of his and therefore missed a tell-tale sign of heart damage.

The father of four was leading a youth camp on Whitsunday Island three weeks later when he collapsed in front of students. He was unable to be revived.

Shey Tuibua says she had a "sinking feeling" when her phone rang on June 19, 2025. (ABC Tropical North: Bryn Wakefield)

Mr Tuibua's wife, Shey Tuibua, was at rugby training with their son in Mackay when she was told her husband had a heart attack.

"He died the day before our 17th anniversary," she said.

"The helicopters flew in and just couldn't get him, couldn't save him.

" The moment your life goes from being awesome to a living nightmare. "

Falling through 'the cracks'

An internal review ordered by Mackay Hospital and Health Service (MHHS) found Mr Tuibua was not treated as a high-risk patient despite his history of high blood pressure and a family history of cardiac problems.

The root cause analysis (RCA) probe into his treatment said several clinical findings "fell through the cracks on a very busy evening".

It said "highly suspicious" changes to his heart's electrical activity were missed and that it was "highly probable" a clinician looked at another patient's blood test results instead of Mr Tuibua's.

Mackay Base Hospital's emergency department has been under increasing pressure. (ABC Tropical North: Daniel Battley)

A critical blood test for troponin, a marker that shows damage to heart muscle, was not reviewed until the next morning, long after Mr Tuibua went home.

A doctor, who had not treated Mr Tuibua, observed the elevated troponin level result but did not raise this with a senior doctor.

The review also found chest pain guidelines, which would have informed the doctors' treatment plan, were not adequately followed.

Additionally, a "statement of attendance" to take to a GP for follow-up care was not issued.

Reviewers found no hospital documentation to suggest Mena was pain-free at any point prior to discharge. (ABC Tropical North: Bryn Wakefield)

"It cannot be discounted that excessive clinical workload, clinician fatigue and environmental challenges have impacted clinical assessment, timely investigations, and contributed to the risk for human error," the reviewers said.

Ms Tuibua said the analysis raised questions about how often mistakes were happening in Mackay's health service.

"We deserve a safe and well-run [emergency department] in this town and, right now, I feel like it's not," she said.

"My kids have gone through hell and back. The young people he worked with … they're all having to grieve because of human error."

Shey Tuibua says Mena held the family together and was "fully involved" in their four kids' lives. (ABC Tropical North: Bryn Wakefield)

Bed shortage contributes to 'poor patient outcomes'

The RCA document says the overcrowded hospital may have contributed to other deaths and patient harm.

"Multiple Severity Assessment Code (SAC1) incident reviews have identified access block to right treatment in the right place at the right time as a contributor to a poor outcome," it said.

Queensland Health's website defines SAC1 incidents as those that include death or likely permanent harm that are not reasonably expected as an outcome of health care.

MHHS did not respond to the ABC's questions about how many avoidable deaths and permanent-harm outcomes had been caused by bed shortages.

Sean Birgan was appointed chief executive of MHHS in February. (ABC Tropical North: Bryn Wakefield)

In a statement, chief executive Sean Birgan said hospital representatives had met with Mr Tuibua's family to offer a "sincere apology".

He said the health service was continuing to offer support, but was unable to make further comments due to patient confidentiality.

However, the MHHS said it had seen an 11 per cent increase in urgent presentations to its ED from July 2025 to May 2026, and that 80 per cent of patients were seen within recommended time frames.

It said the review of Mr Tuibua's case had resulted in improvements to several procedures.

MHHS says a master plan for the Mackay Base Hospital expansion will soon be made public. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

In a statement, the Queensland Coroners Court confirmed it had reopened an investigation into Mr Tuibua's death.

It said the Far Northern Coroner was awaiting "information from a Queensland statutory body".

Pressure across Queensland

Health Consumers Queensland's Keith Tracey-Patte said he was worried more mistakes were occurring because of growing pressure on the health system.

"What we're seeing here in Mackay, like we are seeing across the rest of the state, is real pressure that's put on the staff and the patients in a really complex environment," he said.

" It's really hard to grow the workforce to make sure you've got enough people available with the right skills to deliver the care that people need. "

Keith Tracey-Patte says the state's medical workers are "highly skilled" but more investment is needed to build the healthcare workforce. (ABC News)

The planned 128-bed expansion of Mackay Base Hospital has not started despite initial promises to have the work complete by late 2026.

The expansion was announced in 2022 but an independent review revealed the project was underfunded and that a new master plan was needed to ensure it met the needs of the community.

On Tuesday, the Queensland government unveiled the new plans for the hospital upgrade, with the completion of 128 beds and a new clinical services building set down for 2030.

Viliame Tuibua says losing his dad left him in a "void", but he's doing his best to stay active. (ABC Tropical North: Bryn Wakefield)

'Mena' remembered

Viliame Tuibua, 13, said the loss of his dad had "ruined him", but he and his sister, Resina, had relied on their Christian faith and community support over the past year.

"It felt like I was just in this unescapable void," he said.

"I'm getting there … I've been playing a lot of touch [footy] and going to new places. It's given me a spark of happiness."

Mr Tuibua's family remembers him as an "extraordinary" member of the community and a "kind and caring" father.

Shey Tuibua volunteered to help coach students for the Mena Cup. (ABC Tropical North: Bryn Wakefield)

This year, Mackay State High School announced plans to honour his youth work through the Mena Cup, a rugby carnival to be played each year on the anniversary of his death.

Resina, 14, said she would always remember her dad's generosity.

"I just know he was such a good person that I just, in any situation, I think, 'What would dad do?'" she said.

World.title: Travel giant double-billed hotel rooms in refugee accommodation scandal
World.content:
An Australian travel giant embroiled in a $100 million overcharging scandal for refugee accommodation was invoicing a government for more rooms than a hotel actually had, the ABC can reveal.

Brisbane-based Corporate Travel Management, a former share-market darling valued at $2 billion, was also double-billing the UK government during the refugee program or charging for exclusive use of hotels when no exclusivity existed.

The overcharging was detailed in a presentation to Corporate Travel, revealed today by the ABC, which also shows the then PwC auditors in 2023 urged some directors to disclose details linked to the overcharging.

The matter remained unknown to investors until this year, stunning analysts about why nothing was divulged earlier.

Corporate Travel was founded in 1994 by Jamie Pherous, and its share price rose so giddily he became a rich lister who hired Jimmy Barnes to sing at his 50th birthday party on Hamilton Island.

Jamie Pherous at Corporate Travel's all stars winner tour in Spain in June 2025. (Supplied)

The company arranges business trips globally and clients have ranged from Australian parliamentarians to big enterprises such as Wesfarmers.

Corporate Travel also ran UK government accommodation programs for people fleeing countries from Ukraine to Afghanistan, at one stage controversially housing refugees on a floating barge. The overbilling scandal emerged in the accommodation work.

People board the Bibby Stockholm accommodation barge at Portland Port in Dorset in August 2023. (AP: James Manning/PA )

In 2021, Corporate Travel was contracted to rapidly find 1.4 million nights of accommodation across about 60 UK hotels.

But controls, the company later said, were problematic including some government requests coming verbally.

Corporate Travel by late 2022 quietly found a gap of almost 50 million British pounds ($96 million) between how much it had billed the UK government for accommodation, and how much the travel company was then paying to the hotels.

Do you know more? Contact Liam Walsh on encrypted email or Signal. Please note end-to-end encryption is only possible with your own encrypted email system like Protonmail or Signal account.

The gap became a flashpoint in drafting and auditing Corporate Travel's accounts in August 2023.

The then auditors gave a 40-plus page presentation with almost six pages flagging UK issues to the board's audit and risk committee, who included company chairman Ewen Crouch.

Headlines included referring to accounting to UK government arrangements as a "significant" risk.

Corporate Travel has refused to publicly detail how any overcharging occurred while maintaining no evidence of intentional overbilling was uncovered.

The presentation details legal advice was sought and what internal investigations found.

Problem billing went into five "buckets". One bucket included Corporate Travel incorrectly sending bills, such as twice in the same month, or for more rooms than the actual number of rooms in a hotel.

Some were technical, including Corporate Travel having billed the UK government for exclusively securing all a hotel, when the hotel might only charge the company for a lesser amount of rooms used even in an exclusive deal.

Other hotel deals were not exclusive, despite Corporate Travel billing the government as such. Corporate Travel also charged for services when there was no evidence of a formal hotel contract being in place and no hotel invoice received for the relevant period.

A promotional video for Corporate Travel Management. (Corporate Travel Management)

Corporate Travel supposedly reached a secret agreement — later alleged to be fake — with the UK government: the company could keep 22 million British pounds and refund the remaining 28 million British pounds.

That refund would supposedly be via measures such as providing services in lieu of actual cash repayments.

The auditors wrote a UK Home Office official, whom the ABC has identified as a department procurement veteran, was named as signing that deal.

"Management has represented to us that (the official) has the appropriate and required authority in order to commit the Home Office to these financial and contractual arrangements," they noted.

An Australian travel CEO crash-landed this week Australian travel mogul Jamie Pherous foundered on the rocks of an accounting scandal in the UK.

A key auditor dispute lay in explaining to investors the supposed 28 million British pounds refund deal.

The company had planned on listing the amount among hundreds of millions of dollars in "client payables" liabilities. Management would add "wording in the financial statements to broaden" that term's definition.

But the auditors did "not agree" as client payables were usually what was paid to suppliers such as hotels or airlines. It was "more appropriate" to list the liability in a different area with "an explanatory note included given the different nature and materiality of this amount".

No such note is in the final accounts, which the auditors signed.

Still, changes occurred: the final accounts' definition of "client payables" altered from the previous year to include amounts "where clients did not use the travel services and products, or where services were not rendered".

The auditors also questioned classifying as "transactional revenue" the 22.1 million British pounds that Corporate Travel could supposedly keep.

They supplied the committee with regulatory disclosure guidelines and said a draft operational review had only limited information about the UK issue's "material impact" on revenue and earnings in Europe, meaning investors might think plump margins there could continue.

The subsequent published directors' review does contain caveats such as warning European margins were "unlikely to be sustained". The accounts also explained UK accommodation work had grown, while "transactional revenue" was widened to include margins on accommodation.

Then managing director Mr Pherous was not on the committee and left the company on good terms this February. He has not answered ABC queries.

Corporate Travel Management founder Jamie Pherous at the AFL grand final in 2025. (Facebook: Corporate Travel Management)

He trumpeted Corporate Travel's UK work upon publishing the 2023 results.

"We've built up, I guess, three things, a lot of expertise, very good software and process around this, because it's very complicated work," he told analysts. "We've built up a lot of controls as well to make sure it's effective and efficient."

The supposed 50 million British pounds overbilling deal from 2023 only emerged this April, when Corporate Travel blamed former UK executive Michael Healy as responsible for handling the client and the signed government-deal letters.

It admitted the letters "may not, in fact, be authentic" and the UK government "has no record" of them.

Market analysts complained about why nothing earlier had been divulged.

"Unbeknownst to the market, issues were identified by (Corporate Travel) in late 2022 with a refund of 28 million British pounds agreed to with customers in July 2023," RBC Capital Markets analyst Wei-Weng Chen told clients.

The amount represented almost one-third of company cash and underlying earnings, which "should meet most materiality thresholds for disclosure", he wrote.

The ABC put questions and presentation details to Corporate Travel and PwC. Both declined to comment.

Corporate Travel Management's client list has included the federal government. (Supplied)

Peter Carey, a Deakin University auditing expert, said, in general, auditors and companies could have "constant argy-bargy" about disclosures.

He said auditors might acquiesce on initial recommendations for reasons ranging from concluding an issue was ultimately not material, to being afraid of "upsetting the client".

He added auditors could contact third parties, such as banks, to verify items related to accounts, rather than rely on management's word. They may be obligated to make such contact for items of material value, to show reasonable care, Professor Carey said.

Corporate Travel's problems have ballooned; it may now undo up to 128 million British pounds in revenue after probing contracts between 2019 and 2026, and $15 million in Australia-New Zealand related to rebates.

The company, 14-time winner of Australia's travel management company award, is endeavouring to file delayed accounts to avoid removal from the share market.

It even this week won a 28 million pound UK government contract, helping Afghans, who worked with British forces, resettle.

World.title: Farmers 'very nervous', poultry show cancelled as bird flu reaches Tasmania
World.content:
For the past 25 years, Matthew Gunningham has been farming in the green pastures of Tasmania's north-west.

But confirmation the deadly H5N1 strain of bird flu had reached the state's shores put his family-run farm on high alert.

"I feel very nervous about it," Mr Gunningham said.

" This is a business that we've poured our hearts and souls into. "

Matthew Gunningham fears for his flock, which numbers in the thousands. (ABC News: Sandy Powell)

An infected brown skua, a migratory seabird from the sub-Antarctic region, was found at Rocky Cape, just 15 kilometres from his farm at Shakespeare Hills.

So far, it is the only case in Tasmania, with no sign of any local spread of the virus.

What bird flu looks like A bird's unusual and disturbing behaviour catches the eye of passers-by. On the ground it flaps its wings, turns in circles and then somersaults.

But Mr Gunningham fears for his flock of more than 4,000 laying hens if an outbreak eventually occurs.

"Let's say we [were] found to be infected, and we were directed to cull the entire flock, that would cut off the income from this enterprise entirely," he said.

"And we'd have to start back from scratch again, which would be very, very difficult — very difficult financially.

" And certainly very, very difficult emotionally. "

To report sick or dead birds or other animals Call the ​ Emergency Animal Disease Hotline 1800 675 888 ( 24 hours)

Emergency Animal Disease Hotline 24 hours) Use the online bird flu reporting form

Do not touch sick or dead birds or other animals. To report sick or dead wildlife (other than birds), please visit the wildlife health in Tasmania webpage.

The virus has caused devastation to wildlife and poultry farms around the world.

In anticipation of its arrival, Mr Gunningham drafted a biosecurity plan for his farm more than a year ago.

He activated it once cases started to rise interstate in recent weeks.

The plan includes restrictions on visitors entering the farm's paddocks and moving the mobile chicken coops closer together.

Guardian dogs are also being used to keep wild birds away. (ABC News: Sandy Powell)

But on a free-range farm, there's only so much that can be done.

" So really from here, it's just being really vigilant and watching and waiting and hoping that we don't succumb. "

Major poultry event called off

Exhibitors were expected to bring thousands of birds to the Hobart event, which has been cancelled. (ABC News: Jonny McNee)

The detection of bird flu has prompted the Royal Agricultural Society of Tasmania to cancel one of its upcoming events

The Royal Hobart Poultry and Pigeon Show, scheduled for August 22, was expected to feature more than 1,000 birds.

But the event will no longer go ahead.

"The risks to our exhibitors, their prized birds and the broader animal population are considered too high under the current circumstances," RAST chief executive Scott Gadd said.

"We are extremely disappointed to have to make this decision.

"This was shaping up to be the biggest Royal Hobart Poultry and Pigeon Show we have held in many years, with entries from Tasmania's north-west coast for the first time in many years."

Serious and amateur poultry enthusiasts have been affected by the news. (ABC News)

Mr Gadd said competitors had spent countless hours preparing and caring for their birds, but a precautionary approach was needed.

"Given the current detection of avian influenza in the state and the movement of birds that would be required for the event, we believe cancellation is the responsible decision," he said.

" Our priority must be to minimise the potential for disease transmission and protect the health and welfare of the birds involved, as well as the broader Tasmanian poultry and animal industries. "

Mark Robertson with some of his cherished birds. (ABC News: Jonny McNee)

Speaking to the Tasmanian Country Hour prior to the cancellation, heritage bird breeder Mark Robertson said he was concerned about the future impact of bird flu.

"It's [a] concern for the hobby," Mr Robertson said.

"What would happen if, for the next four years, we don't have poultry shows?

"I'm probably one of the younger poultry exhibitors getting around.

"[But] what happens to that older generation who've been exhibiting their whole life, have a break — do they come back?

"We've seen things like that happen with COVID."

Wildlife sanctuary bracing for impact

George, the cockatoo, with Raphael, the musk lorikeet, at Bonorong sanctuary. (ABC News: Jake Grant)

The Bonorong Wildlife Sanctuary near Hobart has been preparing for the arrival of bird flu for the past three years.

"It's devastating to hear that it's finally here," chief executive Matt Clement said.

" But we are well prepared and we are working closely with other agencies and government to mount an effective response. "

The sanctuary is dedicated to the rescue, rehabilitation and preservation of native animals.

One of the biggest unknowns is how the virus will affect the endangered Tasmanian devil. (ABC News: David Robertson)

Mr Clement said a range of biosecurity protocols were in place to reduce the risk of the virus spreading to the facility, including a zoning system to limit movement between different areas.

"So one way of us preventing the spread of infection is to really control the movement of people and equipment, and for that matter, other animals that come and go as the day goes on.

"So that compartmentalisation of our operations has been really important.

"And the moment we received notice [on Thursday] that there'd been a detection in the north-west of Tassie, we immediately implemented our zoning protocols."

Tasmania's wombats are also potentially at risk from the disease. (Supplied: Beatrice Thurston-Regan)

While Mr Clement is confident about the protection measures in place for resident animals at the sanctuary, he is concerned about how the potential spread of the virus could affect Bonorong's animal rescue service.

"We receive around 20,000 calls for assistance every year, and I am absolutely focused on keeping that service running despite the background risk associated with this terrible disease."

He said volunteer rescuers were aware of the need to follow government guidelines, including avoiding contact with sick wildlife and referring suspicious cases to the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline.

World.title: Voting underway in Farage by-election battle with bin-wearing comedian
World.content:
Voting is underway in a by-election in the British constituency of Clacton where Reform UK leader Nigel Farage is hoping to regain his parliamentary seat.

Mr Farage, who had been facing scrutiny over a 5 million pound ($9 million) donation made to him from a Thailand-based crypto billionaire, dramatically quit as an MP last month and declared he would contest the by-election.

He said he would let voters judge him in a "people versus the establishment" contest.

None of the UK's other major parties decided to field candidates for the poll, deriding Mr Farage's move as a stunt, leaving the former banker to face a mix of independent candidates including a comedian known as Count Binface.

Count Binface has emerged as the key rival to Nigel Farage in the by-election. (AP: Kirsty Wigglesworth)

Polls are set to close at 10pm Thursday, UK time, with the results expected to be announced some time on Friday morning.

Unlike Australian elections, British election results are only publicly declared once all the votes are counted, and there is no preferencing, meaning the first-placed candidate only needs to have one more vote than every other candidate to be elected MP.

While Mr Farage is widely expected to win the race, his likely victory is not set to satisfy questions about the millions of pounds in donations that he has received.

Donation investigation to restart if Farage wins

Mr Farage triggered the vote last month when he resigned as an MP in the hope that it would put to bed questions about his finances and result in a resounding victory over his main political rivals from the Labour and Conservative parties.

What to know about Britain's strangest by-election Nigel Farage is the clear favourite, but Count Binface is attracting serious support in a by-election featuring a record 34 candidates, including an Australian software engineer and three "Loonies".

The UK Parliament's standards watchdog is investigating the 5 million pound undeclared donation made by 2024 from cryptocurrency billionaire Christopher Harborne.

Mr Farage has insisted he did not need to declare the money because it was a personal gift he used to fund his security and came before he was elected.

When he stood down on July 7 he described an investigation into the undeclared donation as an "establishment hit job" and a media-driven "witch hunt".

Newly-elected politicians must declare gifts worth more than 300 pounds received in the previous year if they are related to political activities.

His decision to stand down put a pause to the parliamentary investigation, but if he wins the by-election it is set to start again. This could result in a second by-election.

Key candidate vows to 'nationalise Adele'

The election is a novelty with a record 34 candidates, including Howling Laud Hope of The Official Monster Raving Loony Party and Marcus White from the Everyone is God Party.

They have pounded the streets of Clacton over the past few weeks as they seek to win the support of around 80,000 voters.

Despite 34 candidates contesting in Clacton, voters will not find candidates for Labour nor the Conservatives on their ballot papers. (Supplied: Trendring District Council)

Given the numbers standing, Clacton residents have had to contend with a one-metre-long ballot paper.

Besides Mr Farage, polling has suggested Count Binface, a political satirist posing as a comic space alien, was on track to secure the second highest number of votes.

His policies include "nationalising Adele", building a single affordable home, and relocating the hand dryer within the bathroom of a west London pub.

He has been a regular candidate in high-profile elections before, having previously stood against then-prime ministers Boris Johnson and Rishi Sunak.

He has previously said his candidacies are aimed at promoting the beauties of Britain's centuries-old democracy where even the most high-profile politicians are above no-one, including someone from his fictional native planet of Sigma IX.

ABC/wires

World.title: ‘We just went over’: Passenger train from London derails, flips
World.content:
Breaking WorldEuropeTrains ‘We just went over’: Passenger train from London derails, flips David Crowe August 14, 2026 — 5:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Passengers were thrown from their seats and dragged along the floor when a train derailed on a major line south of London, trapping some in carriages that were tipped to their sides. Many passengers climbed out of the carriages and walked to safety from the wreckage of the train after it left the tracks during its journey from Victoria Station in London to the seaside town of Eastbourne. Flipped carriages of the derailed train near the town of Lewes, in southern England, on Thursday. AFP But two passengers were seriously injured and another nine were also hurt, the British Transport Police declared after paramedics assessed patients at the scene before taking them to hospital. One passenger told the BBC he was on the train when he felt it was “sliding” over the tracks.



“We just went over and we were dragging along the floor,” said Charlie Hobden, 31, from Lewes, a town close to the scene of the accident. “We tried to open the doors and then we saw people standing on top of the train and so we managed to get out on our own. Others waited and got on ladders to get out. London Victoria station. Getty Images “Then the emergency serves helped us out and got we got assessed.” Hobden did not have any injuries and returned home. The incident involved a Southern train travelling from London Victoria to Eastbourne, with no report of any collision with any other train or vehicle.



“We’ve declared a major incident and a significant emergency service response is ongoing at the scene, but all passengers on the train have now been safely evacuated from the service,” said Assistant Chief Constable Ian Drummond-Smith of the British Transport Police. “Our thoughts are of course with everyone affected, and I’d like to reassure the public that we’re supporting the Rail Accident Investigation Branch to establish exactly what’s happened.” Photographs from the scene showed three carriages were lying on their side in a field alongside the railway line, while several other carriages were still on the tracks. The South East Coast Ambulance Service said there were about 150 people on board the train. “SECAmb are continuing to respond to a major incident following a train derailment near Lewes Railway Station this afternoon,” the ambulance service said at about 6pm (3am on Friday, AEST).



“Ambulance crews, specialist responders and colleagues from partner emergency services remain at the scene.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Secret funding cuts put Premier Ben Carroll’s integrity pledge under fire
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsVictoriaVictorian Parliament Secret funding cuts put Premier Ben Carroll’s integrity pledge under fire Chip Le Grand August 14, 2026 — 5:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One of Victoria’s essential integrity agencies is being decimated by secret budget cuts, prompting transparency experts to call for new Premier Ben Carroll to intervene and protect people’s access to information held by government. The Office of the Victorian Information Commissioner (OVIC), the agency that administers freedom of information and privacy laws, is being forced to reduce its expenditure by nearly 10 per cent, which will result in one in 10 staff being shown the door. Premier Ben Carroll is set to reshuffle his cabinet in coming days. Eamon Gallagher The cut is part of a broader funding squeeze across the Department of Justice, which, according to the state government’s most recently published financial statements, must spend $194 million less this financial year than it did last year to meet budget. The hidden cuts to OVIC, confirmed by unpublished budget figures provided to this masthead, challenge Carroll’s promise upon taking the Labor leadership that within his government “integrity is non-negotiable”.



It is expected to aggravate an already large backlog of freedom of information complaints and lead to a further blowout in waiting times. The agency last year cleared 873 of the 1135 freedom of information complaints it received, but as of June 30, 2026, still had 570 complaints on its books. The average time to finalise a complaint is now 129 days – up nearly a month since 2023-24. The agency’s budget for this financial year is $7.7 million – a 9.3 per cent cut from what it spent in 2025-26 and down 24 per cent since 2022-23. Over four years, OVIC’s headcount has shrunk from 55 people to 42, despite the number of FOI complaints they handle nearly doubling. “You cannot make integrity non-negotiable while leaving the watchdogs that safeguard it vulnerable to government budget decisions,” said Professor Gabrielle Appleby, research director for the Centre for Public Integrity.



“The test of an integrity agenda is not in promises – it is whether governments are prepared to properly resource institutions capable of holding them to account.” Related Article Victorian Parliament Private medical and police record searches would be free under FOI shake-up While all integrity agencies in Victoria have pushed for greater funding and for their budgets to be set by parliament rather than the government of the day, OVIC is particularly vulnerable to any funding squeeze. Unlike IBAC, the Ombudsman and the Auditor-General, standalone agencies that report directly to Special Minister of State Ingrid Stitt, OVIC is housed within the Department of Justice and its budget is overseen by the departmental secretary. The parliament’s integrity and oversight committee (IOC), in a report tabled on Thursday, renewed its call for this to change and for OVIC to be funded in the same way as other integrity agencies.



“The committee remains concerned that eroding OVIC’s funding over time will affect OVIC’s ability to fulfil its legislated remit and perform at an optimal level,” the report warned. “The committee considers it imperative that OVIC is adequately funded to perform its functions, and to maintain up‑to‑date service delivery for the Victorian community.” Victorian Information Commissioner Sean Morrison. YouTube/Victoria Law Foundation Victorian Information Commissioner Sean Morrison backed the proposed change. “As one of Victoria’s key integrity agencies, OVIC supports the recent integrity and oversight committee’s recommendation that the Office of the Victorian Information Commissioner is funded through parliament’s appropriation, similar to the funding arrangements for the Independent Broad‑based Anti‑corruption Commission, Integrity Oversight Victoria and the Victorian Ombudsman,” Morrison said.



OVIC’s own figures, provided to this masthead, show that at the same time its funding is being reduced, its case load is surging. The number of freedom of information complaints received by the agency in 2025-26 jumped by 35 per cent from the previous financial year. The agency has also recorded a significant increase in privacy complaints. IOC chair Tim Read, a Greens MP, said he had been made aware that OVIC was “struggling to function” within its budget. “It is vital that OVIC be funded as the integrity agency that it is, and that it is not subject to cuts that interfere with its ability to administer the Freedom of Information Act, which is important for transparency in this state,” he said. Related Article Opinion

Political leadership The 2300-year-old advice and the AFL coach whose wise words helped shape Ben Carroll’s rise Chip Le Grand State political editor Shadow attorney-general James Newbury said the OVIC funding cut exposed as empty Carroll’s first day pledge to make integrity a cornerstone of his government.



“He promised he had integrity but continues Labor’s campaign of undermining our key integrity agencies, like the Office of the Victorian Information Commissioner,” Newbury said. “The tightening of the screws of the office responsible for ensuring transparent government only proves the Carroll government is just the same as Andrews and Allan before him.” Stitt did not respond to questions on the funding cut. “Integrity is not negotiable in Victoria, and OVIC is pivotal in upholding this standard,” a government spokesperson said.



“We expect all public sector bodies, including integrity agencies, to manage their budgets and ensure public money is spent efficiently and effectively.” Changes made last year to Victoria’s Financial Management Act created a statutory expectation on all government departments and agencies to operate within budget. This has put additional pressure on the state’s cash-strapped integrity agencies. IBAC chief executive Alison Byrne and Ombudsman Marlo Baragwanath told this masthead earlier this year their current budget allocations would not cover their operating costs and force them to shelve some investigations. State government agencies receive more than 48,000 requests for information annually, which can include Victorians’ medical, police or TAC records, with less than 80 per cent of decisions made on time. Part of OVIC’s scope includes handling complaints about rejected or redacted applications.



Transparency International Australia chief executive Clancy Moore said the funding cuts to OVIC would reduce government accountability and weaken the health of democratic institutions. “When an integrity agency faces funding cuts, it can silence those that are meant to speak out,” Moore said. “New Premier Ben Carroll has made integrity his number-one priority. His government should make the agency an independent statutory authority like IBAC and remove it from under the control of the department.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Luigi Mangione is tipped to plead guilty to stalking. What does that mean for his murder trial?
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaCrime Luigi Mangione is tipped to plead guilty to stalking. What does that mean for his murder trial? Michael Koziol August 14, 2026 — 5:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Luigi Mangione, the American man accused of killing healthcare chief executive Brian Thompson, is expected to plead guilty to federal stalking charges, creating legal uncertainty about his upcoming state-level murder trial. His anticipated plea opens the door to his lawyers attempting to get his state trial dismissed on double jeopardy grounds, legal experts say, with New York law particularly grey on the matter. Luigi Mangione during a pre-trial hearing for the New York state murder charges on Tuesday,. Steven Hirsch/Pool New York Post via AP How did we get here? Mangione, who is now 28, was arrested on December 9, 2024, in connection with the fatal shooting of Thompson on a midtown Manhattan street several days earlier.



The brazen crime shocked the world, but also generated sympathy for Mangione from parts of the community amid broader controversy over access to American healthcare. For some people, he became something of a pin-up or political prisoner. In court, he has faced two separate tracks of charges – murder charges levelled by New York state and stalking charges (resulting in death) levelled by the federal government. Other federal charges have been dropped. He pleaded not guilty to the state charges. What has happened now? A special hearing has been scheduled on Friday (US time) at the request of both the prosecution and defence, where Mangione is widely tipped to plead guilty to the federal charges. Karen Friedman Agnifilo, attorney for Luigi Mangione, arrives for this week’s pre-trial hearing. Bloomberg



Many US media outlets reported he would do so, citing sources familiar with the matter, while a former federal prosecutor in New York, Berit Berger, agreed it was “very likely” based on the sequence of events. “You would typically have one of those [hearings] if he was going to plead guilty,” she told this masthead. “That doesn’t necessarily mean it will happen tomorrow.” Mangione could also change his mind at any time. Loading Why it matters Such a plea could have a significant impact on his state-level murder trial, for which jury selection is due to begin within weeks.



Berger said she expected Mangione’s legal team would try to have the state murder charges dismissed on the basis of double jeopardy – the principle that someone can’t be tried for the same crime twice. “It’s actually a pretty interesting legal question,” she said. In the US, the state and federal prosecutors can both bring charges in relation to a crime, if applicable. Berger says that for the most part, they co-operate and don’t double up, unless the federal government believes it has a significant interest in the matter, or that a federal sentence would be substantially longer. Members of the public, including a woman wearing a "Free Luigi" shirt, enter a courtroom before Luigi Mangione is escorted in. AP In most cases, she said, pleading guilty to the federal stalking charges would not invoke double jeopardy on the state murder charges, as the court would consider the harms to be significantly different. Why it’s complicated



But “New York’s a little different than other states”, Berger said, owing to some quirks in the law. “My guess is this will not preclude the New York case from going forward, but it’s a little bit more complicated.” One of the reasons for that complexity is the case of Paul Manafort, Donald Trump’s former campaign chairman, who in 2019 was charged with mortgage fraud by the Manhattan district attorney. Luigi Mangione, pictured in September 2025. Jury selection for his state murder trial is due to begin next month. AP Manafort had already been convicted federally, and a judge ultimately dismissed the state case due to double jeopardy. The lawyer who argued the case for Manafort was Todd Blanche, who just last week was confirmed as Trump’s attorney-general, in charge of the Department of Justice. What happens next?



Either way, Berger – who now lectures at Columbia Law School – said there was no prospect Mangione would escape a long jail sentence. The federal charges are two counts of stalking resulting in death, which carry a maximum sentence of life in prison. Related Article Updated

Crime BBQ fork and pizza cutter: the bizarre plot to break Luigi Mangione out of jail A judge sentencing him on federal charges would know the context of the state matter, even if it is abandoned. “There’s not going to be a deal where he gets out of jail earlier,” Berger said. “I don’t think this is a chance for him to evade accountability.” Mangione’s lawyers did not immediately respond to a request for comment. At an unrelated news conference in Washington, Jamie McDonald, the US attorney for the Southern District of New York, declined to elaborate on what would happen. “There’s a [court] conference scheduled for 11am on Friday. That’s all we can say at this time,” he said. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Between death and new love, Phoebe Bridgers’ new album is a ferocious gut punch
World.content:
CultureMusicReview Between death and new love, Phoebe Bridgers’ new album is a ferocious gut punch Jules LeFevre , Tom W Clarke , Ben Madden and Ify Obiegbu August 14, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Lost Weekend by Phoebe Bridgers contains widescreen, beautiful melancholy and threads of optimism.
