World.title: ‘We just went over’: Passenger train from London derails, flips
World.content:
Breaking WorldEuropeTrains ‘We just went over’: Passenger train from London derails, flips David Crowe August 14, 2026 — 5:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Passengers were thrown from their seats and dragged along the floor when a train derailed on a major line south of London, trapping some in carriages that were tipped to their sides. Many passengers climbed out of the carriages and walked to safety from the wreckage of the train after it left the tracks during its journey from Victoria Station in London to the seaside town of Eastbourne. Flipped carriages of the derailed train near the town of Lewes, in southern England, on Thursday. AFP But two passengers were seriously injured and another nine were also hurt, the British Transport Police declared after paramedics assessed patients at the scene before taking them to hospital. One passenger told the BBC he was on the train when he felt it was “sliding” over the tracks.



“We just went over and we were dragging along the floor,” said Charlie Hobden, 31, from Lewes, a town close to the scene of the accident. “We tried to open the doors and then we saw people standing on top of the train and so we managed to get out on our own. Others waited and got on ladders to get out. London Victoria station. Getty Images “Then the emergency serves helped us out and got we got assessed.” Hobden did not have any injuries and returned home. The incident involved a Southern train travelling from London Victoria to Eastbourne, with no report of any collision with any other train or vehicle.



“We’ve declared a major incident and a significant emergency service response is ongoing at the scene, but all passengers on the train have now been safely evacuated from the service,” said Assistant Chief Constable Ian Drummond-Smith of the British Transport Police. “Our thoughts are of course with everyone affected, and I’d like to reassure the public that we’re supporting the Rail Accident Investigation Branch to establish exactly what’s happened.” Photographs from the scene showed three carriages were lying on their side in a field alongside the railway line, while several other carriages were still on the tracks. The South East Coast Ambulance Service said there were about 150 people on board the train. “SECAmb are continuing to respond to a major incident following a train derailment near Lewes Railway Station this afternoon,” the ambulance service said at about 6pm (3am on Friday, AEST).



“Ambulance crews, specialist responders and colleagues from partner emergency services remain at the scene.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Secret funding cuts put Premier Ben Carroll’s integrity pledge under fire
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsVictoriaVictorian Parliament Secret funding cuts put Premier Ben Carroll’s integrity pledge under fire Chip Le Grand August 14, 2026 — 5:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One of Victoria’s essential integrity agencies is being decimated by secret budget cuts, prompting transparency experts to call for new Premier Ben Carroll to intervene and protect people’s access to information held by government. The Office of the Victorian Information Commissioner (OVIC), the agency that administers freedom of information and privacy laws, is being forced to reduce its expenditure by nearly 10 per cent, which will result in one in 10 staff being shown the door. Premier Ben Carroll is set to reshuffle his cabinet in coming days. Eamon Gallagher The cut is part of a broader funding squeeze across the Department of Justice, which, according to the state government’s most recently published financial statements, must spend $194 million less this financial year than it did last year to meet budget. The hidden cuts to OVIC, confirmed by unpublished budget figures provided to this masthead, challenge Carroll’s promise upon taking the Labor leadership that within his government “integrity is non-negotiable”.



It is expected to aggravate an already large backlog of freedom of information complaints and lead to a further blowout in waiting times. The agency last year cleared 873 of the 1135 freedom of information complaints it received, but as of June 30, 2026, still had 570 complaints on its books. The average time to finalise a complaint is now 129 days – up nearly a month since 2023-24. The agency’s budget for this financial year is $7.7 million – a 9.3 per cent cut from what it spent in 2025-26 and down 24 per cent since 2022-23. Over four years, OVIC’s headcount has shrunk from 55 people to 42, despite the number of FOI complaints they handle nearly doubling. “You cannot make integrity non-negotiable while leaving the watchdogs that safeguard it vulnerable to government budget decisions,” said Professor Gabrielle Appleby, research director for the Centre for Public Integrity.



“The test of an integrity agenda is not in promises – it is whether governments are prepared to properly resource institutions capable of holding them to account.” Related Article Victorian Parliament Private medical and police record searches would be free under FOI shake-up While all integrity agencies in Victoria have pushed for greater funding and for their budgets to be set by parliament rather than the government of the day, OVIC is particularly vulnerable to any funding squeeze. Unlike IBAC, the Ombudsman and the Auditor-General, standalone agencies that report directly to Special Minister of State Ingrid Stitt, OVIC is housed within the Department of Justice and its budget is overseen by the departmental secretary. The parliament’s integrity and oversight committee (IOC), in a report tabled on Thursday, renewed its call for this to change and for OVIC to be funded in the same way as other integrity agencies.



“The committee remains concerned that eroding OVIC’s funding over time will affect OVIC’s ability to fulfil its legislated remit and perform at an optimal level,” the report warned. “The committee considers it imperative that OVIC is adequately funded to perform its functions, and to maintain up‑to‑date service delivery for the Victorian community.” Victorian Information Commissioner Sean Morrison. YouTube/Victoria Law Foundation Victorian Information Commissioner Sean Morrison backed the proposed change. “As one of Victoria’s key integrity agencies, OVIC supports the recent integrity and oversight committee’s recommendation that the Office of the Victorian Information Commissioner is funded through parliament’s appropriation, similar to the funding arrangements for the Independent Broad‑based Anti‑corruption Commission, Integrity Oversight Victoria and the Victorian Ombudsman,” Morrison said.



OVIC’s own figures, provided to this masthead, show that at the same time its funding is being reduced, its case load is surging. The number of freedom of information complaints received by the agency in 2025-26 jumped by 35 per cent from the previous financial year. The agency has also recorded a significant increase in privacy complaints. IOC chair Tim Read, a Greens MP, said he had been made aware that OVIC was “struggling to function” within its budget. “It is vital that OVIC be funded as the integrity agency that it is, and that it is not subject to cuts that interfere with its ability to administer the Freedom of Information Act, which is important for transparency in this state,” he said. Related Article Opinion

Political leadership The 2300-year-old advice and the AFL coach whose wise words helped shape Ben Carroll’s rise Chip Le Grand State political editor Shadow attorney-general James Newbury said the OVIC funding cut exposed as empty Carroll’s first day pledge to make integrity a cornerstone of his government.



“He promised he had integrity but continues Labor’s campaign of undermining our key integrity agencies, like the Office of the Victorian Information Commissioner,” Newbury said. “The tightening of the screws of the office responsible for ensuring transparent government only proves the Carroll government is just the same as Andrews and Allan before him.” Stitt did not respond to questions on the funding cut. “Integrity is not negotiable in Victoria, and OVIC is pivotal in upholding this standard,” a government spokesperson said.



“We expect all public sector bodies, including integrity agencies, to manage their budgets and ensure public money is spent efficiently and effectively.” Changes made last year to Victoria’s Financial Management Act created a statutory expectation on all government departments and agencies to operate within budget. This has put additional pressure on the state’s cash-strapped integrity agencies. IBAC chief executive Alison Byrne and Ombudsman Marlo Baragwanath told this masthead earlier this year their current budget allocations would not cover their operating costs and force them to shelve some investigations. State government agencies receive more than 48,000 requests for information annually, which can include Victorians’ medical, police or TAC records, with less than 80 per cent of decisions made on time. Part of OVIC’s scope includes handling complaints about rejected or redacted applications.



Transparency International Australia chief executive Clancy Moore said the funding cuts to OVIC would reduce government accountability and weaken the health of democratic institutions. “When an integrity agency faces funding cuts, it can silence those that are meant to speak out,” Moore said. “New Premier Ben Carroll has made integrity his number-one priority. His government should make the agency an independent statutory authority like IBAC and remove it from under the control of the department.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Luigi Mangione is tipped to plead guilty to stalking. What does that mean for his murder trial?
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaCrime Luigi Mangione is tipped to plead guilty to stalking. What does that mean for his murder trial? Michael Koziol August 14, 2026 — 5:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Luigi Mangione, the American man accused of killing healthcare chief executive Brian Thompson, is expected to plead guilty to federal stalking charges, creating legal uncertainty about his upcoming state-level murder trial. His anticipated plea opens the door to his lawyers attempting to get his state trial dismissed on double jeopardy grounds, legal experts say, with New York law particularly grey on the matter. Luigi Mangione during a pre-trial hearing for the New York state murder charges on Tuesday,. Steven Hirsch/Pool New York Post via AP How did we get here? Mangione, who is now 28, was arrested on December 9, 2024, in connection with the fatal shooting of Thompson on a midtown Manhattan street several days earlier.



The brazen crime shocked the world, but also generated sympathy for Mangione from parts of the community amid broader controversy over access to American healthcare. For some people, he became something of a pin-up or political prisoner. In court, he has faced two separate tracks of charges – murder charges levelled by New York state and stalking charges (resulting in death) levelled by the federal government. Other federal charges have been dropped. He pleaded not guilty to the state charges. What has happened now? A special hearing has been scheduled on Friday (US time) at the request of both the prosecution and defence, where Mangione is widely tipped to plead guilty to the federal charges. Karen Friedman Agnifilo, attorney for Luigi Mangione, arrives for this week’s pre-trial hearing. Bloomberg



Many US media outlets reported he would do so, citing sources familiar with the matter, while a former federal prosecutor in New York, Berit Berger, agreed it was “very likely” based on the sequence of events. “You would typically have one of those [hearings] if he was going to plead guilty,” she told this masthead. “That doesn’t necessarily mean it will happen tomorrow.” Mangione could also change his mind at any time. Loading Why it matters Such a plea could have a significant impact on his state-level murder trial, for which jury selection is due to begin within weeks.



Berger said she expected Mangione’s legal team would try to have the state murder charges dismissed on the basis of double jeopardy – the principle that someone can’t be tried for the same crime twice. “It’s actually a pretty interesting legal question,” she said. In the US, the state and federal prosecutors can both bring charges in relation to a crime, if applicable. Berger says that for the most part, they co-operate and don’t double up, unless the federal government believes it has a significant interest in the matter, or that a federal sentence would be substantially longer. Members of the public, including a woman wearing a "Free Luigi" shirt, enter a courtroom before Luigi Mangione is escorted in. AP In most cases, she said, pleading guilty to the federal stalking charges would not invoke double jeopardy on the state murder charges, as the court would consider the harms to be significantly different. Why it’s complicated



But “New York’s a little different than other states”, Berger said, owing to some quirks in the law. “My guess is this will not preclude the New York case from going forward, but it’s a little bit more complicated.” One of the reasons for that complexity is the case of Paul Manafort, Donald Trump’s former campaign chairman, who in 2019 was charged with mortgage fraud by the Manhattan district attorney. Luigi Mangione, pictured in September 2025. Jury selection for his state murder trial is due to begin next month. AP Manafort had already been convicted federally, and a judge ultimately dismissed the state case due to double jeopardy. The lawyer who argued the case for Manafort was Todd Blanche, who just last week was confirmed as Trump’s attorney-general, in charge of the Department of Justice. What happens next?



Either way, Berger – who now lectures at Columbia Law School – said there was no prospect Mangione would escape a long jail sentence. The federal charges are two counts of stalking resulting in death, which carry a maximum sentence of life in prison. Related Article Updated

Crime BBQ fork and pizza cutter: the bizarre plot to break Luigi Mangione out of jail A judge sentencing him on federal charges would know the context of the state matter, even if it is abandoned. “There’s not going to be a deal where he gets out of jail earlier,” Berger said. “I don’t think this is a chance for him to evade accountability.” Mangione’s lawyers did not immediately respond to a request for comment. At an unrelated news conference in Washington, Jamie McDonald, the US attorney for the Southern District of New York, declined to elaborate on what would happen. “There’s a [court] conference scheduled for 11am on Friday. That’s all we can say at this time,” he said. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Between death and new love, Phoebe Bridgers’ new album is a ferocious gut punch
World.content:
CultureMusicReview Between death and new love, Phoebe Bridgers’ new album is a ferocious gut punch Jules LeFevre , Tom W Clarke , Ben Madden and Ify Obiegbu August 14, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Lost Weekend by Phoebe Bridgers contains widescreen, beautiful melancholy and threads of optimism. Olof Grind Phoebe Bridgers, Lost Weekend ★★★★ On the opening track of Phoebe Bridgers’ Lost Weekend, we are wrenched from our body. In The Outside, Bridgers’ voice, icy and obfuscated by a harsh vocoder effect, lays out the funereal scene: we’re crying in a suit and tie, watching someone be carried away, throwing a fist through drywall. The next verse takes us elsewhere: Bridgers held aloft while crowd-surfing at a gig, buoyant above the bodies, fist raised in the air. The contrasting, parallel scenes both dissolve in the same way, with the vocoder fading and Bridgers’ high, clear voice suddenly lifted by soft piano and guitar, swallowed up. We’re not in these moments, we’re floating above. Disconnected, unmoored.



It’s a fitting introduction for Lost Weekend, in which the Californian indie songwriter attempts to find her way through waves of grief and newfound love. It arrives a full six years after her second record, 2020’s vivid and sensitive Punisher. She certainly wasn’t idle in between, touring extensively for Punisher which included a stint on Taylor Swift’s Eras Tour. She also joined up with her Boygenius supergroup mates Lucy Dacus and Julien Baker to make the Grammy-winning album, The Record. Plenty more touring followed, and plenty of life happened as well. Her father, with whom she had a strained relationship, died in 2023, and her high-profile engagement to Irish actor Paul Mescal came to an end. On her first solo release since 2020’s revered Punisher, the 31-year-old generational talent unleashes her hyperspecific songwriting to devastating effect. Olof Grind All of this finds its way onto Lost Weekend, which is one of the finest representations of the mess of grief that you’ll find. Bridgers’ signature hyperspecific, visual songwriting is unleashed with ferocious power across its 16 tracks. There are some gut-punch moments: “I found her bleeding over the sink/But when you said sorry, you were looking at me,” she sings on Still Standing, about her father. Later, when a voicemail from him asking for a call drifts into frame in Never Going Back!, it cuts like a knife. The gradual dismantling of a relationship is traced on The Governor’s Waltz (which also may contain a sideswipe at Mescal’s new partner, singer Gracie Abrams: “And she can pretend to be me/Since she took my place and bed on that stage/I have not lost anything”).



There’s plenty of widescreen, beautiful melancholy, but Bridgers is also careful to follow threads of optimism to give you a reprieve. The tracks Bobby and Liberty Tree are rushing alt-country turns in which Bridgers finds new love: “You were made in the image of God/But you look like your mum,” she sings on Liberty Tree. As we heard on The Outside, much of Lost Weekend (produced with a team including Jack Antonoff, Alex G, Tony Berg and Ethan Gruska) is filtered through a feeling of dislocation and suspension. Bridgers has always been a fan of setting fire to songs and having them collapse around her – see Punisher‘s spectacular closer I Know the End. Lost Weekend is a masterful example of form following feeling: Bridgers’ voice is often smothered by effects, the instrumentation bursts through and changes in strange and eerie moments. The track Kill Me (perhaps featuring the guttural vocals of Geese’s Cameron Winter?) ends so abruptly that I checked (more than once) that the stream hadn’t malfunctioned. The title track sputters with harsh breathing before cracking open with lashes of strings and guitars. It renders the brighter moments more impactful, like the clear bluegrass of Haunted. Appropriately, the final song on the record, Lost Weekend (Reprise), in which Bridgers says goodbye to her father and addresses her new lover, is bluntly cut off halfway through a bar. A final throw into the abyss. Jules LeFevre



Reality Awaits by The Strokes is occasionally profound, sometimes cringe. The Strokes, Reality Awaits ★★★ At Coachella in April, The Strokes made headlines after playing a politically charged video montage of military strikes in Iran and Gaza, as frontman Julian Casablancas chanted, “What side are you standing on?” Anyone expecting their new album to build upon this protest may be disappointed. After all, this is a band whose first single back in 2001 was the controversial New York City Cops. But Reality Awaits lacks that urgency – The Strokes aren’t in a hurry at all, shambling through a broken world with weary bones and a strange affection for AutoTune.



Reality Awaits is often inscrutable, deeply nostalgic, occasionally profound, and sometimes cringe in a way that only the most charismatic voice of 21st century rock can pull off (no one else is talking about Josh Groban and John Legend in 2026, or still saying “YOLO”). Album opener Psycho Shit is a sinister slow build (one of four five-plus minute songs on the album), and our first taste of the off-kilter warbling that permeates the record. The Fruits of Conquest is close to a powerful moment of protest, a thundering guitar riff and reverberating chant of “I’m a leech”. Falling Out of Love is transportive, shimmering in Casablancas’ delicate falsetto. Lonely in the Future is a return to their garage-rock roots following the cheesy ’80s-dipped new wave of 2020’s The New Abnormal. And Going to Babble On is the most dynamic and fun The Strokes have sounded in years. Elsewhere, the album meanders with little to say – Dine N Dash and Liar’s Remorse sound like droning latter-era Arctic Monkeys offcuts, and Tyrants of the Mellow Moon is an odyssey that wanders too far into the abyss and forgets to take us with it. Tom W Clarke



Jonny Chopps, Catalyst On Catalyst, Jonny Chopps further establishes himself as a leader among our new generation of rappers. ★★★ Since emerging onto the Australian rap scene in early 2025, Sydney MC Jonny Chopps has gone supernova. Co-signed by the likes of The Kid Laroi and Ninajirachi, the dexterous artist has outworked many of his peers, crafting a sound that draws from sub-genres like rage, trap, pluggnb and more – while maintaining a distinctly Australian flair. It’s a particular source of pride for him, too. On his 10-track mixtape Catalyst, which quickly follows the release of his Free Will EP in February, Jonny further establishes himself as a leader of Australia’s new generation of rappers.



Running with the ideas first expressed on Free Will, Catalyst does a far better job of conveying his artistic vision. It may not be an exercise in cohesiveness, with tracks like the hyperactive Garbage slotting in alongside the melodic Typa Guy, but when he truly finds his pocket, like on closer Motorola, he raps like a man possessed. There are brief moments where his lyricism holds him back, but this feels more like an area for growth than an Achilles heel. In a scene where many artists can often appear overly lackadaisical, Catalyst offers a vision of what’s possible when an Australian rapper leans all the way in. Ben Madden Yasmina Sadiki, Made for the past ★★★



With her debut EP Made for the Past, Eora artist Yasmina Sadiki doesn’t arrive searching for an identity; she arrives defining one. Across eight tracks, Sadiki refines the improvisational spirit that has long made her live performances so compelling into a body of work that feels deliberate, cohesive and deeply personal. Sydney artist Yasmina Sadiki emerges fully formed on Made for the past. Rather than chasing immediacy, the record trusts careful songwriting, intuitive musicianship and spacious production to create an emotional arc that reveals itself more fully with every listen. The understated piano of opener Wounds establishes Sadiki’s preference for restraint over spectacle, while the lush harmonies and layered backing vocals of Give It To Me showcase the richness of the sonic world she has built. Craving is the record’s defining moment. Built around a slow-burning crescendo, it unfolds with remarkable patience as Sadiki stretches the title refrain with effortless control, shimmering guitars gathering around her voice which remains the song’s unwavering centre.

World.title: Almost 20 years on, Peking Duk have made their debut album. Why now?
World.content:
As AI slop takes over the local dance charts, Reuben Styles and Adam Hyde are still doing it the right way.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Adam Hyde closes his eyes and pictures the Australia he loves, he’s not really thinking about a beach. “There’s an ashtray with heaps of cigs in it,” he explains. “There’s a beer that’s almost done but it’s really hot. There’s a shitty speaker somewhere and there’s all these characters, from all walks of life, and they all seem to get along.” Hyde’s Peking Duk bandmate Reuben Styles nods across the table from him. “We want to write a love letter to all the caravan resorts out there,” Styles continues. “The places that are such beautiful parts of your childhood that you took a little bit for granted. You think of a trailer park in the American sense. It sounds trashy as, but we call them caravan resorts. It’s paradise.” Styles takes a sip of his Coke. “Shout out to the beach caravan resorts of Jervis Bay,” he smiles, forever a Canberran. The cigs aren’t exactly overflowing in the Imperial Hotel in Paddington, where Hyde and Styles are sitting in the middle of a vast, empty front bar on a Monday afternoon. We’re sitting here because nearly 20 years after becoming best friends in a Canberra skate park and forming one of Australia’s most popular dance acts, Peking Duk are finally releasing their debut album, Paradise. The first and most obvious question to ask is, why now? “I think it’s more of a why not,” Styles answers. “We’ve done about 16 years now of Duk just doing singles. Whenever you feel like things are getting a little bit repetitive in any sense, shaking it up and trying something totally new just makes the whole thing f---ing exciting again.” “I think the era that we came up in, we were just making beats for clubs,” Hyde adds. “There was no calling for an album necessarily. It was like, ‘just make the track, put out the track’. And then we kind of found ourselves … not trapped – that’s very dramatic – but we found ourselves stuck in this rhythm. And once these songs found some skerricks of success, we were kind of like, ‘Okay, well, we should keep that going’. We were bound to the structure of drop a single, do a tour. It became a bit of a machine that we created ourselves.”



That machine gifted them great success. A scan over their CV reveals multiple ARIA award wins and nominations for bounding festival-fillers like 2014’s High and 2016’s Stranger; a fistful of Hottest 100 placements; sold-out tour after sold-out tour. Their brand of spiralling, supercharged EDM, born from the scrappy clubs in Canberra (shout out Block 33, say the pair) and the heyday of Sydney’s Kings Cross, helped define Australian dance in the 2010s. For year after year, the duo would drop one or two big-hitting singles and then crisscross the country in what seemed like endless loops. “Every single you drop then fortifies the prison you’ve made around yourself,” Styles laughs. “When you’re doing just one or two singles a year, you’re really hoping for some type of result from the single. I feel like the second we got into album mode, it just made us completely unthink ‘Is it going to do well or not?’ It just made us think of, ‘Is it sick or not?’. We f---ed off the whole rule book.” Still rolling after all these years: Adam and Reuben from Peking Duk, pictured in May 2014. Brianne Makin “I should add,” Hyde jumps in. “There was a long period of time where there was somebody in our team that made things very hard for us to move forward, in many ways. I don’t want to shit on anyone, but there was somebody that we had to farewell in order to move forward. I think in hindsight, just sitting here now, candidly speaking, it’s like that was a big thing that held us in our own constraints of like, ‘It’s got to be like this. Picture perfect, Peking Duk!’” The duo don’t elaborate about the team member they farewelled, except to add it feels like they now have the keys to their own car back. “We’re stealing our own car and doing burnouts,” Hyde smiles. ‘We were bound to the structure of drop a single, do a tour. It became a bit of a machine that we created ourselves.’ Adam Hyde, Peking Duk Stretching across 14 tracks and featuring an extensive guest list that includes Killer Mike, Matt Corby, Phantogram, Rico Nasty and Kah-Lo, Paradise feels polished and focused. Rather than building a Frankensteinian monster of offcuts from over the years, the duo went into sessions in LA with a clean slate, determined to build something fresh.



The album loosely wraps around the concept of a pirate ship sailing into paradise – where paradise is an empty metaverse of being famous, being seen. Its best tracks, like Forever with Phantogram and Let Go with Matt Corby, take on this dreamy, somewhat melancholy air. After 16 years as Peking Duk, the project is no longer their sole focus: Hyde is now arguably better known around the country as Keli Holiday thanks to the success of 2025 track Dancing2, while Styles has been busy flirting with alt-country as Y.O.G.A. While they’re steadfast that both ventures feed the creative fire rather than extinguishing it, they admit it’s led to some awkward moments with festivals. “Promoters will try and do a cheeky thing, where they’ll book Reuben and then book me and will say ‘Oh you’re both in, we’ve got some decks here!’,” Hyde laughs. “But God bless them, they’ve got a hard job, I guess.” In the week leading up to our chat, the local music industry has been tearing itself apart over the number-one song on the Australian airplay charts. Josh Fawaz’s Madonna cover, Like A Prayer, reportedly used generative AI tools in its construction. Fawaz has since added AI credits to the track. Styles laughs in disbelief. Related Article New music The worst girl in America? More like the best story in pop music “I can’t believe it,” he says. “I landed in Australia three days ago just to find out the number one song played on Australian radio is AI vocals… I wonder what the average person listening to [radio station] KIIS, for example, how they feel about the song or if they’re just like, ‘Oh yeah, don’t mind’? Would you have dinner at a restaurant on your birthday if you knew there was no human cooking your steak?” “To me, it’s like, do you want perfect? If you want perfect, go get it,” Hyde adds. “But music and art and romance, love and hate, it’s so far from perfect. The longing is the most crucial part of the experience. If you lose that, it kills everything. The whole thing … it’s heartbreaking. Even if you were to program a bot to make it more imperfect, then it’s like, what are we doing?!”

World.title: Happy Eurovision (War Is Over): Song contest issues new rules amid conflict
World.content:
Analysis CultureMusicEurovision Happy Eurovision (War Is Over): Song contest issues new rules amid conflict Michael Idato August 14, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

After a year of behind-the-scenes hand-wringing over the withdrawal of Spain, the Netherlands, Ireland, Slovenia and Iceland from the Eurovision Song Contest 2026, the competition’s organisers have moved to steady the ship. The new rule: any country involved in “an armed conflict [or] a sensitive geopolitical situation” will be unable to host the competition. Eurovision’s archaic but much-beloved rules hand the hosting of the contest each year to the previous year’s winner. That quirk has turned a win into a diplomatic coup, and the opportunity for more energised countries to engage in a little geopolitical PR. Loading The new rule is surprisingly loose. It includes this clause: “or any other situation [that] materially affects the security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region”, which means it is open to a wide degree of interpretation. And while observers cannot fail to see how it immediately applies to Israel, one of the most energised countries in the competition and currently enmeshed in a war in Gaza, it might equally apply to Ukraine, which is defending itself against Russia, or indeed Denmark, should America make good on its promise to invade Greenland.



The rule does not stop a war-affected country from pursuing a Eurovision win, though it might serve as a deterrent if it seems a soft diplomatic victory might never eventuate. After all, participating in Eurovision is costly and being denied the prize after winning would be a substantial penalty. But the organising body, the European Broadcasting Union (EBU), had a big problem in 2026, with five countries withdrawing over Israel’s participation. One, Spain, is a so-called “big five” country, the moniker given to the five largest financial contributors to the EBU. Even when people are singing songs like Jaja Ding Dong, money talks. Spain, Ireland, the Netherlands, Slovenia and Iceland boycotted the 2026 song contest over Israel’s participation, while pro-Palestinian protesters marched in Vienna ahead of the grand final. Getty Images In that sense, the question was never whether the EBU would find a way to manage the situation, as it has struggled to do for several years, but that getting those five countries, and the others murmuring about joining them, was an existential necessity. Lose the “U” – the union – and you have no EBU. So, what does it all mean? In effect, should Israel, Ukraine or another war-affected country win the contest, the EBU would commission an independent security assessment of the region, and if deemed unsafe, an alternative hosting country would be found.



Related Article Updated

Eurovision Bulgaria wins Eurovision, Delta Goodrem ‘stoked’ as Australia comes fourth The thing is, all of that happens already. It’s why, for example, Liverpool hosted on behalf of Ukraine in 2023, and why Brighton hosted in 1974 – the year ABBA won – because the previous year’s winner, Luxembourg, declined citing high costs. What’s different now is that instead of letting the winning city negotiate its replacement, the EBU will. And any new host city will not be obligated to host “on behalf” of the city it is replacing. All of this comes as Canada is entering the competition, much as Australia did over a decade ago. But unlike Australia, which must renegotiate each year, Canada – no doubt helped by the fact that French is one of its two national languages – enters as a full EBU member. It helps, too, that Canada has had de facto competitors previously: Canadians Natasha St-Pier and La Zarra, who competed in 2001 and 2023 respectively, both represented France. And one of Canada’s most successful music exports, Celine Dion, competed and won in 1988, representing Switzerland.



What that tells us is that there is substantial evolutionary change taking place within the EBU, and while the Canada decision and the war-zone eligibility rules do not directly impact one another – unless, again, America makes good on another of its threats, to invade Canada – it’s difficult not to see both of them as part of a wider set of changes within the organisation. The inclusion of new countries is seen as both commercially necessary to the enterprise, as it draws in more participation fees and greater exposure to a global TV audience, and as vital to the morale of the competition. Some European countries still grumble about Australia’s inclusion, but few deny Australia’s presence has almost universally been welcomed enthusiastically by both fans and national delegations. Canada will only amplify that. Noam Bettan from Israel during the grand final of this year’s Eurovision Song Contest in Vienna in May. Israel placed second out of 25 countries competing in the final. AP And the tightening of rules is an exercise in smoothing turbulent political waters that were seen as an existential problem. You lose Spain and you lose a fifth of the major players at the table. You lose four more countries this year, you’re negotiating on the backfoot not to lose eight next year. No part of that would be seen by the EBU’s leadership as sustainable. The broad objection: that Israel, using state-funded marketing and targeted online campaigns, was seen as aggressively ramping up international phone voting to secure higher audience scores.



So what happens now? The truth is, very little in real terms. Next year’s competition will be held in Bulgaria – thankfully, a country with no threat of invasion by America, at least at press time – and plans will proceed to deliver that country the cultural crown of post-war Europe’s pop world. Four cities – Burgas, Plovdiv, Sofia and Varna – are bidding to host, with Burgas and Sofia seen as the most likely contenders. Bulgaria will host the next Eurovision Song Contest after winning this year’s event with the song Bangaranga by Dara. Getty Images At press time, only 19 of the usual 40-plus participating countries had signed on for the 2027 competition, though that is quite usual at this point in the calendar. Most participating national broadcasters will announce their participation in the coming months. Some, like Cyprus and Serbia, have signalled yes, but have not yet made formal announcements. Israel’s Kan confirmed last month they would participate. But none of this year’s five striking countries – Spain, the Netherlands, Ireland, Slovenia and Iceland – have signalled their intentions for 2027. And Australian broadcaster SBS has not confirmed its participation either.



Which means the only certain thing is this: Canada is coming to Europe’s musical pot luck next year, though they might just wonder what on earth they have walked into. Find out the next TV, streaming series and movies to add to your must-sees. Get The Watchlist delivered every Thursday.

World.title: My boss said I was ‘emotional’ when I asked for a pay rise. Is that fair?
World.content:
BusinessWorkplaceWork therapy Opinion My boss said I was ‘emotional’ when I asked for a pay rise. Is that fair? Jonathan Rivett Careers contributor August 14, 2026 — 5:15am

August 14, 2026 — 5:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I read your column last week and identified with the question-asker’s situation. Like them, I went through a period of being told during salary reviews that my performance did not warrant a pay increase. At first, this was disappointing but not worrying. The friendly tone of the discussions put my mind at ease and I told myself I just needed to work harder. After the third time, I politely raised the problem of a lack of any pay increase becoming a pay decrease in real terms. When it happened again the next time, I became incensed. I said that if my performance was really so bad, my employer should just say so, and we could have an honest conversation about whether I needed to look for a new job. I was told I was being “emotional” and “unrealistic”. I look back now and wonder if my employer had a genuine reason for doing this or if I was blatantly being ripped off. If your work needed to be critically evaluated, it should have been. John Shakespeare It sounds to me that your employer left you in a kind of career limbo, enacting a professional version of cruel and unusual punishment. Getting warm and upbeat performance reviews that concluded with “... and you’re not getting a pay increase” would have been disorienting for you. The fact that you felt it necessary to state what should have been the bleeding obvious – that your pay was effectively going backwards – tells me that by the third review, the whole thing was bordering on farce. I’m not even slightly surprised that your frustration eventually boiled over.



If their approach was “genuine”, as you put it, it was certainly not judicious. The point you made in the meeting where you couldn’t hide your anger was a strong one. While it’s important that a performance review never descends into malicious condemnation, if your work needed to be critically evaluated, it should have been. Like the reader from last week who was left without answers to fundamental questions, you weren’t given anywhere near enough information. When your boss resorted to labelling your concerns as “emotional” and “unrealistic”, they were stooping to a deep rhetorical low. Unlike the case of the reader from last week, however, I suspect this is not a problem caused by an ultimate decision-maker assuming that the (possibly shallow) determination they had come to was self-evident and so would naturally be accepted by the person affected by it. In that case, I think the boss was over-confident to the point of ignoring the valuable contribution of their employee. In your case, my guess is that you had a manager bereft of conviction. The giveaway for me was the sudden shift from genial pussyfooting to withering condescension.



When your boss resorted to labelling your concerns as “emotional” and “unrealistic” they were stooping to a deep rhetorical low. To my mind, this is a slightly less insulting way of expressing that classic in the genre of belittling evasion, “you’re being hysterical”. Editor's pick Opinion

Productivity It might terrify Gen Z, but the humble phone call is a wonderful thing Tim Duggan Work columnist Apart from being disastrously unprofessional, it strikes me as the ad hominem attack of a person who has nothing to support their main contention. Yes, it can be difficult when a work conversation becomes heated. And, yes, it’s easy to get swept up in such an escalation and say something regrettable. But I’m not convinced that this was just an ill-chosen, spur-of-the-moment retort to your animated demand. If it had been, your manager would likely have later expressed remorse or at least tried to explain what they meant by “unrealistic”. They never did.



With all that in mind, I can’t say for sure that you were being “ripped off”, but I doubt very much whether your manager was acting in good faith. Even still, I don’t necessarily think the blame lies entirely at their feet. I think a plausible explanation for what you experienced started with a new policy prescribed by managers at a higher level than your boss. They had the relatively easy job of telling line and middle managers: “We need to drastically cut labour costs.” If there was no plan or strategy behind the directive, your manager may have been burdened with the invidious responsibility of putting the policy into practice all on their own. They may have found themselves needing to justify your pay freeze even if they didn’t believe it was warranted. And if they actually thought your work was good and/or (as we discussed in last week’s column) that your organisational citizenship was valuable, the weird incongruence between the benevolent tone of the initial meetings and their negative outcomes might be more understandable. Understandable but not defensible. Even if the person you reported to was acting under coercion – placed under intense pressure to make decisions they found impossible to defend – their cutting outburst was unnecessary. And the fact you spent years going backwards financially, but were never explicitly told why, is just absurd.



Send your questions through to Work Therapy by emailing jonathan@theinkbureau.com.au Get workplace news, advice and perspectives to help make your job work for you.

World.title: ASX set to retreat; Wall Street climbs as oil prices drop, inflation eases
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to retreat; Wall Street climbs as oil prices drop, inflation eases Stan Choe August 14, 2026 — 5:12am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The US stock market is ticking toward an all-time high following the latest sign that inflation is getting less bad. Stocks also got a lift from easing oil prices in their latest yo-yo move. The S&P 500 climbed 0.6 per cent and was on track to top its record set last week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 22 points, or less than 0.1 per cent, in mid-afternoon trade, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.7 per cent higher. The Australian sharemarket is set to slide, with futures at 4.52am AEST pointing to a loss of 35 points, or 0.4 per cent, at the open. The ASX lost 0.2 per cent on Thursday. The AUstralian dollar was steady at US70.53¢. Wall Street got more positive inflation news on Thursday. Reuters Wall Street relaxed after a report showed prices at the US wholesale level were 4.7 per cent higher last month than a year earlier. While that’s still very high, it’s not as bad as June’s 5.5 per cent inflation rate at the wholesale level, and it was slightly better than economists expected.



If inflation continues to trend that way, the Federal Reserve could decide to hold off on hikes to interest rates. Higher rates would help keep a lid on inflation, but they do so by intentionally slowing the economy and making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money. Fed officials are split on whether they should have already begun hiking interest rates. But Thursday’s report, following a similar update on inflation at the US consumer level the day before, has traders now betting on just a 37 per cent chance that the Fed will raise rates at its next meeting in September. That’s down from the roughly 50 per cent probability seen two days ago, according to data from CME Group. Related Article Opinion

AI Wall Street is about to sell AI bonds. What could go wrong? Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Any increase by the Fed would be the first in more than three years. It also could anger President Donald Trump, who has been lobbying for lower interest rates. Treasury yields sank in the bond market, which eases pressure on stocks and other investments. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.64 per cent from 4.68 per cent late Wednesday and from 4.72 per cent on Monday, though it’s still well above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran sent oil and gasoline prices surging.



Oil prices eased back on Thursday, helping to limit worries about inflation. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil fell 1.4 per cent to $US87.71. It’s been swinging sharply recently and pinballed between $US72 and $US102 last month as hopes rose and fell that a deal in the war could allow oil tankers to freely exit the Middle East again and deliver crude worldwide. On Wall Street, stocks in the real-estate industry helped lead the way. When interest rates are lower and bonds are paying less in yield, the dividends that many real-estate investment trusts pay look more attractive. Lower mortgage rates could also drive more activity in the housing market. AvalonBay Communities, which owns apartments across the country, rose 2.3 per cent. Builders FirstSource, which sells countertops and other building materials, added 1.7 per cent. Fossil Group rose 4.7 per cent after the seller of watches and jewellery became one of the latest companies to report better results for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Such reports have helped drive Wall Street to its records because stocks tend to track the path of corporate profits over the long term.



They helped offset a drop for Cisco Systems, which fell 8.9 per cent even though the tech giant reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than Wall Street expected. Analysts said investors may be worried about its profit margins going forward, and its stock has been shaky through the summer amid worries that AI-related stocks in general shot too high. Related Article Opinion

NRL 2026 Murdoch left Melbourne Storm to a betting entrepreneur. What a howler Elizabeth Knight Business columnist In stock markets abroad, indexes were mostly lower in Europe and mixed in Asia. South Korea’s Kospi again had one of the world’s biggest moves and jumped 3.6 per cent. Seoul has been home to the world’s sharpest swings for artificial-intelligence stocks because it’s dominated by two tech giants, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.
