World.title: Two investigations launched after police shoot armed man at Sylvia Park
World.content:
Investigations underway following a fatal shooting Morning Report Download MP3 2m

At least two investigations have been launched after an armed man was fatally shot by police at Auckland's Sylvia Park.

That includes a critical incident investigation and an Independent Police Conduct Authority investigation.

On Thursday, police said a man was shot and killed as he approached Sylvia Park Shopping Centre carrying a stolen air rifle.

Superintendent Sunny Patel said police had received information about the theft of an air rifle from Gun City in Penrose around 2pm.

Police vehicles and the Eagle helicopter were dispatched to the area, locating the car near Sylvia Park.

Spikes were successfully deployed but the car continued towards Mount Wellington Highway, still being driven in an erratic manner, Patel said.

Police confronted the man underneath an overpass as he approached the entrance of Sylvia Park, still carrying the air rifle. He was then shot by police.

The scene on Thursday afternoon. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

An eyewitness to the chase, who did not want to be named, said he had never seen so many police cars in one place.

"When they passed me, there would have been about 20 [police cars], and by the time I got to Sylvia Park, there was still more coming from every direction, unmarked cars.

"Minutes had passed and there was still more arriving on scene. There was so many."

He said he was shopping nearby when he saw a white Suzuki Swift "go flying past", followed by dozens of police cars.

"When I saw it I was like something must have gone on beforehand for them to have formed that formation with the convoy and for them to have armed offenders and dogs, they must have known something was up. If it's just a normal police chase there wouldn't be that many cars," he said.

Police confirm investigations

On Thursday night, Patel addressed media at a press conference in Auckland.

There, he confirmed police had stood up the critical incident investigation. He also confirmed the IPCA had been notified and would be carrying out their own investigation.

Answering questions from the media, Patel said it was not known whether the air rifle was loaded, or whether the man had any ammunition.

Patel was not aware of how many times the man was shot, whether there had been any attempt to detain him or whether he had aimed the weapon at anyone.

"That's something that will need to be uncovered when we carry out the full investigation, when we've actually spoken to the police officers involved," he said on Thursday night.

The decision to shoot rested with the officer at the scene, and no clearance was required, he said.

"Our investigation is still at the very early stages of piecing together the events," he said.

Patel could not comment on whether the man had threatened staff at the gun shop, or if staff had attempted to stop the man. The gun theft had been a shoplifting incident and the man had walked in through the front door.

The police investigation would look into what happened at the store, but it was concerning the man was able to steal a weapon, Patel said.

"We just don't know the circumstances of how he became in possession of that firearm.

"Until we've actually figured out the nature of the actual theft and how it occurred, it is of concern."

Deceased was known to police

At the press conference on Thursday night, Patel declined to go into detail about the identity of the man who was killed, as next of kin had not yet been notified.

He did, however, confirm the man was known to police and was on bail.

The man was not being electronically monitored and was not wanted by police prior to the incident.

He would not go into detail about how the man was known to police or what the bail related to.

An eyewitness said he had never seen so many police cars in one place. RNZ / Kim Baker Wilson

Patel said the man was alone, and they were not looking for anyone else in relation to the incident.

Witnesses or anyone with phone or dashcam footage were urged to come forward.

Patel said he was happy with police response times to the incident, and said they were providing support to the officer who fatally shot the man.

"We've put support in place for the officer concerned and that support will be ongoing. No one comes to work and expects this kind of result. Our staff work very, very hard on a daily basis to make sure the community is safe, and this is the last thing that they want to experience."

World.title: No mention of climate change in new curriculum until Year 11
World.content:
Climate change dropped from curriculum until Year 11 Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Children will learn about money management and the origins of Moriori but not about climate change in their first 10 years at school thanks to newly-published curriculums.

The Y0-10 Science and Social Sciences curriculums were published this week and contained less content than draft versions widely-criticised for being over-stuffed with things to learn.

Both curriculums dropped all mention of climate change, despite it being in the earlier drafts, meaning students would not study the topic in any depth until the senior secondary school.

A document summarising submitters' comments said some argued climate change should not be covered in Year 5 Geography because it was too complex and noted that the curriculum it would replace left the topic till Year 11.

University of Waikato education professor Chris Eames said the change was a massive omission and it was no consolation that the topic was included in the draft Y11-13 Geography and Science curriculums.

"Climate change is a subject that people do find a bit challenging in some of the younger years of schooling. However, to leave it out completely up to the age of 14 seems an incredible and bewildering step to take," he said.

"I could imagine there would be students turning up to class when the latest flood has happened in their community, asking questions about how do we stop this from happening, why has this happened and a teacher who has the best of intentions, has perhaps a limited understanding of climate change and how these things have occurred, will be struggling to provide the answers.

"It just does not seem right that the the Ministry of Education can put our young people into this position. They have to address this issue."

Eames said the word "climate" did not appear once in the science curriculum.

"Now, that seems incredible. Climate is a key part of the atmospheric systems that we're operating in... it does beg the question who has made that decision," he said.

Intermediate school science teacher John Marsh told RNZ primary teachers would cover climate change because they could not avoid it when teaching about topics like habitats and the water cycle.

"By and large, New Zealand teachers have a pretty good understanding of what climate change is all about and they will talk about it," he said.

Marsh said the final science curriculum was a big improvement on the draft.

"It's obvious they've listened and there's some local content. They've removed some stuff which I thought was not age appropriate and it looks very clear, very simple and quite a nice way of kind of setting it up," he said.

However, Marsh said the final document was still too light on teaching children the process of science such as interpreting data.

"It's very content-heavy. I suppose that's the nature of science in some ways but it'd be nice to have a a bit more about that process front and centre," he said.

Marsh said the new curriculum would not change his teaching much, but he worried regular primary teachers would struggle if they did not get good training and support.

He said they would be heavily reliant on the science kits the government was funding to support science lessons.

Principals Federation president Jason Miles said the two new curriculums had less in them than the drafts, but there was still more than schools could cover in a 40-week year.

"In science and social sciences we have an hour a week in the primary environment to teach the the curriculum, and there are up to 50 or 60 goals that are listed per year," he said.

He said that could not be done, especially in classrooms that had more than one year group.

"We have 93 percent of our schools across Aotearoa have composite classes, which means there's more than one year level in each class... How the teachers are to teach those goals to two different year levels is very complicated and untenable," he said.

The New Zealand History Teachers Association said in a statement it welcomed changes that had been made to the Social Sciences curriculum, including a reduction in the amount of content that had been in the draft.

"We are also pleased to see significant Aotearoa New Zealand histories explicitly included, such as the New Zealand Wars/Ngā Pakanga o Aotearoa at Year 9," it said.

But the association said there was still too much content and too much prescription of what must be taught.

It also warned that schools had little time to prepare to start teaching the curriculum from next year.

"This is especially important for primary and intermediate teachers teaching complex contexts such as He Whakaputanga and Te Tiriti o Waitangi," it said.

A ministry report on feedback to the Social Sciences draft curriculum said 578 of 637 email submissions concerned the Holocaust, resulting in greater coverage of it within an optional history topic about Nazi Germany.

It said submitters supported the shift to more explicit content, but warned the draft had tried to cover too much.

"Overall, feedback showed support for a clearer and more explicit Social Sciences learning area, particularly the separation into distinct strands, year-level expectations, and the potential for greater consistency across schools. Submitters also valued specific inclusions such as civics, democracy, financial education, volunteering, environmental issues, Moriori history, and Holocaust Education," it said.

"However, feedback also identified substantial concerns that the draft learning area placed too much emphasis on prescribed content and coverage, and not enough on inquiry, skills, critical thinking, local contexts, and student agency. Many questioned whether the volume and complexity of content could be taught well within the available time, especially in primary settings and composite classrooms."

The ministry said in a statement feedback from consultation and subject matter experts showed climate change was best taught in ways that matched students' age and stage of learning.

"While the term climate change may not appear in the curriculum content, the science that underpins it is taught throughout the Science learning area," it said.

World.title: Aged care sector faces $650m funding gap, despite $5b a year in village sales
World.content:
New Zealand's aged residential care sector funding gap increased to an estimated $650 million last year, a new report from Westpac says - and a lack of profitability may be stalling further investment.

The report from Westpac looks at how service providers can tackle the sector's challenges.

Westpac industry economist Paul Clark said more people than ever were entering care, and they were doing so later in life when their care needs were more complex.

There are about 41,500 beds across New Zealand offering rest home, hospital dementia and psychogeriatric care.

Aged residential care sector under funding pressure - report Morning Report Download MP3 6m

"The big challenge is how to fund this care. Aged residential care is funded jointly by government and residents, with a system of add-ons and top-ups for added extras and higher needs care," Clark said.

"That funding has increased steadily over time, although not enough to keep pace with rising costs of delivery, underpinned by ongoing workforce shortages. The net result has been a structural funding gap that has widened from an estimated $170m in 2014 to $650m in 2025."

He said total sector funding had risen to just over $2.7b in 2025, of which $1.2b came from residents. He estimated the sector-wide deficit had increased about 290 percent since 2014 as funding growth diverged from the rising cost of offering care.

At $1.5b, hospital-level care accounted for the biggest share of spending last year, followed by $1.1b for rest home care and $600m for dementia care.

Clark said labour was the sector's largest cost.

Aged Care Association on the aged care funding gap Morning Report Download MP3 7m

There are a range of different providers offering different levels of care, and sometimes a mix of options. He said they were looking to extract efficiencies from their own operations to bring down their costs.

"The gap reflects a persistent mismatch between government funding and the actual cost of care, with labour, clinical, compliance, insurance, and capital costs generally rising faster than funding over the past decade."

He said another issue to consider was the difference in provider models. Retirement villages were a more profitable prospect than rest homes.

Westpac industry economist Paul Clark said more people than ever were entering care. RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

He estimated that retirement village operators offering units and apartments for general living, rather than just care facilities, were making about $5 billion a year from sales of occupation rights agreements.

This was calculated on the basis of about 8000 changing hands for $600,000.

"The report talks about two basic business models.

"One is the standalone model which basically refers just to care. They're more exposed to funding gap issues than some of the really big players which provide a continuum of care, that run aged residential facilities with retirement villages together.

"Those guys are a bit better off because they can use property income to offset losses. That's not to say they want to do that in the future, In fact, my understanding is they would like to see their aged residential care facilities being profitable just by themselves, standing on their own two feet.

"It's actually my understanding that it's resulting in less investment being made in aged residential care. These players are putting less investment in because it's not as profitable as it could be."

World.title: Who is Chris Penk: Instigator, numbers guy, fall guy, or nice guy?
World.content:
Former National Minister Chris Penk's decision not to contest the coming election brings an abrupt end to the political career of a rising star.

In Parliament for nine years, he rose from 63rd on the party's list to being in Cabinet as Minister for Defence, Veterans, Space, the spy agencies, and Building and Construction.

The last update on his MP's Facebook page was hopeful: "Wonderful, uplifting start to the week at the blessing of the new Kindred Family Services space in Kumeu," he said.

But that was stripped away on Wednesday after a failed challenge to Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's leadership.

"Chris Penk launched a leadership challenge this week, which resulted in today's confidence vote. This makes his role untenable and as such I have removed his portfolios," Luxon said.

This was delivered in a statement released by Luxon's office after his 76-second media conference declaring the "full confidence" of his MPs.

Chris Penk, with Prime Minister Christopher Luxon. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Just over three hours later, the office released another statement - this one in Penk's name.

"I have reflected on my political future with my family tonight, and have decided I will not seek re-election as an MP in November," the missive said.

Appearing on Morning Report, political commentator and National supporter Liam Hehir said Penk was a "good, close personal friend" who was popular in the caucus.

"I haven't pumped him for information because I guess I'd rather be a bad pundit than a bad friend," he said.

"What I understand happened .... Chris Penk did front a challenge or front a change, the idea was that it would be a Stanford-Penk ticket ... a prominent liberal Cabinet minister (Erica Stanford) as the leader, and you'd have a solid conservative (Penk) who's quite popular as the deputy."

Hehir said the plan had been to "do it properly" by counting supporters for a spill, then taking that to Luxon and calling for his resignation - a fait accompli - but Luxon calling all his MPs to Wellington for an in-person meeting after the media got wind of the rumours seemed to put a stop to it.

And Penk had been identified as the one doing the counting.

Chris Penk, in his position as Defence Minister. RNZ / Kim Baker Wilson

"Someone has to be the scapegoat or someone has to be punished, and I feel very bitter about the fact that it was Chris Penk - who's a popular and hardworking and very liked minister - but at the end of the day the prime minister did had to do something ... it's just politics," Hehir said.

Former National press secretary Janet Wilson agreed, saying the "botched coup" was a "disaster" for the party - and Penk was "the fall guy".

"I think there were more senior people above him who were part of this whole team who couldn't get their numbers right, basically ... an absolute travesty that he has lost his position. Should he have? Yes, quite possibly. He was named as the numbers man. He was the guy doing the business, but he has lost a stellar career up until now."

From the frigate to the Cabinet

Before politics, Penk had been a military man, having served on the HMNZS Te Kaha in the Navy, served as an aide to Governor-General Silvia Cartwright, then joined Australia's defence force for four years before going to law school and becoming a property lawyer.

First elected in 2017, he picked up the safe blue seat of Helensville from the last National prime minister John Key, retaining a majority of more than 37 percent - down from Key's 52 in 2014 but a good showing for a political newcomer.

He learned politics in opposition, seeing the party's leadership change hands multiple times - from Bill English, to Simon Bridges, Todd Muller, and Judith Collins - in his first term, even being appointed spokesperson for the Courts in 2018.

In 2020's "red wave" election he held onto his electorate but Labour won more party votes and Penk's majority dipped to 9.7 percent as the electorate changed names and boundaries to become Kaipara ki Mahurangi.

Chris Penk heads to Parliament ahead of the caucus meeting where he would soon be stripped on his ministerial portfolios. RNZ / Zach Cornelisen

Later that year, Collins gave Penk the Veterans and, later, the Defence portfolios.

In 2021, he responded to Winston Peters calling National members "sex maniacs" with a social media post saying "Winston Peters is the real s*x maniac because he can f**k a whole country at once".

Collins apologised and ordered him to take the post down, but that didn't stop her giving him the Electoral Reform portfolio in August that year.

After Luxon's ascension to the leadership in November, he was given the shadow Attorney-General role and held onto Courts and Associate Justice - and was elected by the party as senior whip.

At the 2023 election he recovered his electorate margin to 39.6 percent, and was given three ministerial portfolios: Building and Construction, Land Information, and Veterans, along with associate roles in Defence and Immigration.

Since then, he's picked up Small Business and Manufacturing in early 2025, and later the big guns - Defence, Space, and the GCSB and SIS - after Collins' retirement.

But in a strip 450m down the road from Penk's electorate office, most shop owners RNZ spoke to said they had never, or hardly ever, seen him visiting.

One said he had not heard much from Penk at all over the nine years he had been in the role.

"With politicians, once they got what they wanted, they tend to forget the people who voted for them, you know ... since he became a minister he's disappeared. Hardly seen him around here anymore. You know, before I usually see is you driving around, but now no.

"I think he's just going too fast ... jumping too high, too far. I think he's a great guy, but he's try to follow John Key's step, becoming prime minister."

Another said she'd seen him pop up on Facebook and at a couple of openings - but he had never met with her "and we're business owners".

She was disappointed he had decided to stand down, saying it "would have been braver for him to stick around and represent what he stood for".

The main thing she knew him for was he had announced a new high school for the area, which did not have one, in the next three years. It took her six children 45 minutes to bus to their schools on Auckland's North Shore.

"They've shut their zones at Rangitoto College so this high school's way overdue. We've got loads of primary schools, full primary school right up to year eight, but no high school ... and yet they're letting people build thousands of houses."

Another woman - a National voter for more than 50 years from an Air Force family - said Penk was "a really good guy", and after everything that happened this week she was looking at other parties.

"Be nice about him, because Luxton (sic) is evil. Look what he did to Chris Bishop - he did the same thing, he took all his portfolios - Chris Penk is a really good guy, I would like him not to quit politics ... Luxton needs to go.

"He didn't do anything to Erica Stanford, why? Chris Bishop lost portfolios, and Chris Penk's lost all of them, why? He isn't incompetent. He's bloody good."

Another man said he'd "always respected him, and we thought he was quite a good MP, and coming from a military background I think he actually did a pretty good job".

The man who would have been Penk's Labour Party rival at the coming election, Jo Swinburn, told RNZ he was optimistic about winning with Penk gone, but he was disappointed not to be learning the ropes from an experienced Cabinet minister.

Swinburn said he briefly had reported to Penk when he was brought in as Minister for Small Business and Manufacturing, but soon after left to take up a role at the Transport Ministry.

"In addition to people within the Kaipara ki Mahurangi electorate saying to me that Chris was a hard working and nice MP for them, that is also true for MBIE colleagues that worked for him," Swinburn said.

World.title: Buyer sought for unfinished Seascape tower on Auckland waterfront
World.content:
An abandoned tower on Auckland's waterfront could soon find a new owner.

The enormous $300 million Seascape tower has been unfinished since construction stalled in 2024.

But real estate agency Bayleys says it's on track to choose a preferred buyer within the next month.

For neighbour Judy Rawhiti, the 56-storey skeleton blocks what used to be a picturesque seaside view.

"It is ugly, it is absolutely ugly. We used to have a beautiful view across to Devonport. My view now, I'm looking out and I can see the unfinished building and it's all grey and gloomy," she said.

"When the wind blows it sounds like a train's going past because there's a big 'ooooh' sort of ghostly noise, that's probably why they call it the ghost building."

Construction on the ambitious apartment building began in 2017 and was due to be completed in 2021, but disruptions from Covid-19 pushed it into 2024.

Then, a fallout between developer Shundi Customs and contractor China Construction NZ ground the project to a halt.

All that time, Rawhiti had watched the half-finished tower sit exposed to the elements.

"I'd love it to be dismantled," she said.

"If someone else buys it, half of it... Especially up the top, there's no windows in there, so it's exposed to the elements all right. I mean there'll be so much inside that'll need to be replaced."

Seascape was put in the hands of receivers early this year and real estate agency Bayleys had been searching for a buyer.

Managing director Mike Bayley said rumours about the building's weather damage were exaggerated.

"Obviously when structures are exposed to the elements for an extended period of time, there is degradation," he acknowledged.

"I think there's been a lot of speculation in the marketplace around the potential degradation of the building and all I can say is it's not as far reaching as some may have speculated."

The $300 million Seascape tower on Auckland's waterfront has been unfinished since construction stalled in 2024. Judy Rawhiti

He said Bayley's listing had positive attention, and a shortlist of interested buyers had made it through to the second phase of the sale.

Bayley said they had until the 28 August to review the nitty gritty details of the building, including its wear and tear, then make a submission to become the final, preferred buyer.

"It'll then take a couple of weeks for the receivers to assess the depth and content of those offers before engaging with a preferred party or parties," he said.

RNZ / Marika Khabazi

"I think that's a fair assumption, that we will have a party or parties narrowed down [two weeks after the 28th of August]."

Despite wanting the tower gone, Judy Rawhiti said seeing it finished would be the next best thing.

"If someone came in and bought it and were prepared to pay all the extra for wear and tear, I'd be quite happy," she said.

"It'll make me feel better, having a better outlook and I can sort of look to the side... I definitely don't want it to be sitting there as it is now. I don't want it to fall on us."

Deputy mayor Desley Simpson said it was great to see movement on the long-stalled project.

She hoped the project would pick up quickly once a buyer was found.

"From Auckland's perspective we're backing a solution every step of the way and as soon as possible. My take would be, if this is all due at the end of August, I'm hoping for a conclusion pretty smartly after," Simpson said.

World.title: Flights cancelled, delayed as fog restrictions hit Auckland Airport
World.content:
Fog restrictions are in place at Auckland Airport.

By 7.20am, several domestic regional flights had been cancelled as well as some arrivals.

A number departing had been delayed as well as arriving.

Of the main trunk domestic flights, one to Christchurch had been delayed, as had an arrival from Dunedin.

International flights have not been affected by the fog.

World.title: 'I was like a zombie': ADHD diagnosis eases Christchurch woman's years of suffering
World.content:
ADHD diagnosis eases Christchurch woman's years of suffering Morning Report Download MP3 3m

A Christchurch woman who struggled for years with chronic pain and opioid addiction says an ADHD diagnosis and medication changed her life.

Natasha Howell was working in a pharmacy, a job she loved, when a workplace accident kicked off some serious back problems.

Natasha Howell Supplied / Natasha Howell

After repeated hospital admissions for the pain, she had surgery, an L5/S1 spinal fusion - an operation to join the fifth lumbar vertebra to the first sacral vertebra at the base of the spine - in 2013, aged 39.

She had hoped it would let her return to normal life, but the surgery failed, with the bolts and screws causing yet more issues.

Four years later, another surgeon identified the issue as her sacroiliac joint instead. This led to three more surgeries, the most recent in September last year.

Howell has previously shared with media the details of her battle with ACC for compensation, with the Sunday Star Times reporting in 2018 she was awarded $84,797 in compensation, after her weekly payments were cancelled.

Speaking to RNZ now, she described this period as 14 lost years of her life - her relationship broke down, and she was still raising three sons while on high doses of prescription drugs like oxycodone, morphine, tramadol and codeine.

"I was like a zombie, basically, trying to work through my pain," she said.

An initial attempt at an ADHD diagnosis in 2022 was unsuccessful, with the doctor questioning why she would want to start medication in her forties.

RNZ has seen a letter from the psychiatrist, who wrote: "It is somewhat unusual to start treatment for ADHD at 48, given ADHD is conceptualised as a neuro developmental disorder, but not completely unheard of."

He also questioned whether prescribing a stimulant would be appropriate, given Howell's use of other medication.

But earlier this year, she saw a doctor who didn't share those concerns, and prescribed her Ritalin.

Howell said as soon as she started her course, the need for painkillers dropped off completely, and the brain fog lifted.

'Grief process immense'

But, there were downsides to her newfound mental clarity.

"To be honest, it's quite sad because everything comes back to light and everything that you because you weren't focused or you were in pain, you weren't able to think properly. Now my head's so clear and now I'm going, 'Oh my gosh, why did I do that? Or why did I do this? Or why didn't I do that?' The grief process is immense for me at the moment."

Psychiatrist Dr David Codyre, who is clinical director of the wellness support team at private healthcare group Tamaki Health in Auckland, said he had noticed a definite association between medication for ADHD and reduced severity of chronic pain among his own patients.

"I would see people who clearly had a history of lifelong ADHD, who had also along the way developed a chronic pain problem of some kind," he said.

"And there was a subset of them who reported not only were they doing better with their ADHD-caused symptoms and function as a result, but also they were managing their pain better."

So far, there was only "a smattering" of research on the topic, but what had been published indicated there was a link between treating ADHD and improvements in chronic pain.

Why? "That's the million-dollar question, isn't it?" said Codyre. "There's a lot of conjecture."

One possible explanation was that treating ADHD reduced stress, which was already known to help with pain management.

The other possibility was that the medication itself could be treating the underlying cause of the pain - but that was still unknown.

Howell said she was telling her story so that other people might find relief through a diagnosis.

World.title: Gisborne residents urged to be ready for flooding and slips
World.content:
Tairāwhiti Civil Defence is urging residents to be ready for potential surface flooding, slips and more as heavy rain moves in.

An orange heavy rain warning is in effect for Gisborne/Tai Rāwhiti, north of Tolaga Bay, until 8pm on Friday night.

Between 90 and 120mm of rain is expected, with potential peak rates of up to 20mm per hour.

The public are being told to clear gutters and drains, steer clear of low-lying areas while the heaviest rain comes through, and drive to the conditions.

A heavy rain watch is also in effect for Bay of Plenty, in and around Kawerau. Periods of heavy rain are possible through to 9am on Friday.

"Amounts may approach warning criteria with localised downpours possible," MetService said on Thursday night.

The wet weather is expected to continue through to Sunday.

Earlier, MetService issued a severe thunderstorm warning for the Far North.

World.title: Roosters force first NRL lead change in five months
World.content:
The Sydney Roosters have moved to the top of the NRL ladder for the first time in five years, leapfrogging Penrith with a 12-6 win over the Panthers.

With three rounds remaining, the Roosters are in the box seat to win the minor premiership thanks to a two-try showing from Daly Cherry-Evans and an electrifying performance from his halves partner Sam Walker at Parramatta Stadium on Thursday night.

Walker this week parked contract extension talks with the club until after their finals campaign and his clear mind helped Trent Robinson's men gain just their second win over Penrith in 14 meetings since the start of 2020.

The Tricolours produced a strong defensive performance in the highly-anticipated clash. (Getty Images: Matt King )

Cherry-Evans opened and finished the scoring and still looks every bit an NRL player as rumours swirl that the 37-year-old playmaker will head to the Super League for a career swansong next year.

The Roosters, who have won their last eight consecutive games, face Wests Tigers, the Dolphins and South Sydney to round out their regular season.

Penrith, meanwhile, could drop out of the top two by the end of the weekend after being the competition leaders since Round 4.

In their first hit-out since losing captain Isaah Yeo to a pectoral injury, Ivan Cleary's side lacked direction in attack and have now lost five of their past eight games.

The Panthers went desperately close to opening the scoring with a 14-pass move putting Brian To'o in the clear to touch down, only for the winger to step in to touch at the last minute.

The Roosters remained camped in their own half until a wayward Nathan Cleary pass fell to Mark Nawaqanitawase to relieve the pressure on Robinson's side.

In an instant, the Tricolours were up the other end and Cherry-Evans burst past a flat-footed Isaiah Papali'i to score in the 20th minute.

Walker converted and the Roosters should feel aggrieved for not doubling their lead as halftime approached when Rob Toia had a try chalked off.

Nawaqanitawase was penalised for a disruptor penalty that Canterbury football manager Phil Gould described in commentary for the Nine Network as "a disgraceful call and a disgraceful rule".

Walker kicked a penalty goal on halftime after a push and shove between Dylan Edwards and Connor Watson to make it 8-0 at the break, condemning Penrith to a scoreless first half for the second week running.

The Panthers were lacking spark, but with 15 minutes left Ivan Cleary threw Blaize Talagi on at five-eighth and they immediately reacted to the shake-up.

After pounding the Roosters' line, Lindsay Smith slipped an offload away to fellow forward Moses Leota who powered over with a 67th-minute try.

Cleary kicked the conversion to make it 8-6, but the Panthers were unable to come up with a late knockout blow as Cherry-Evans scampered over with a 77th-minute match winner.

AAP

World.title: Gardner breaks silence on affair with teammate, retains vice-captaincy
World.content:
Australia vice-captain Ash Gardner has apologised for the pain caused by her marriage breakdown and thanked Cricket Australia for backing her leadership.

Gardner's affair with Australian teammate Georgia Voll while married to ex-wife Monica Wright created headlines.

Wright publicly questioned the lack of action by CA in the wake of the affair, calling attention to "a clear power imbalance" when a senior member of staff has an affair with a junior.

Wright said Gardner should not be allowed to stay as vice-captain and questioned why CA had said nothing on the matter.

Gardner's marriage breakdown came as the result of an affair with teammate Georgia Voll (pictured). (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

Cricket Australia CEO Todd Greenberg, speaking on SEN on Thursday, said "additional policies" would be put in place in situations where perceived or real conflicts of interest existed, when relationships between players had been disclosed.

He confirmed CA had been made aware of the relationship between Gardner and Voll before it appeared in the press, but also backed Gardner to stay in her position.

"Ash is a highly regarded leader in our system. The CA board make leadership decisions and have oversight over all leadership decisions," Greenberg said.

"Ash is our vice-captain for a reason, because she's highly regarded, but what we will do is in situations where there are personal relationships is make sure there are additional guardrails, so the perception of conflict or conflict itself — talking about things like selection — are handled appropriately and respectfully."

Todd Greenberg (pictured) says Gardner remains a highly-valued leader within the Australian team. (AAP: James Ross)

"We've got policies in place but we will put additional ones in place given Ash is now vice-captain. If there are relationships that have been disclosed and they have been, then we will make sure that conflict — perceived or real — around selections are removed, so Ash is not involved in those things."

Greenberg said the relationship between Gardner and Voll was "new news" in the media.

"But for those that were in the team and leading the team, we've been well across this for a period of time," he said.

Gardner addressed her affair and the position of the hierarchy in a post on Instagram.

"While my separation from my wife is a personal matter, I understand my current relationship status needed to be addressed by Cricket Australia given my position as vice-captain," Gardner wrote.

"I am grateful that the CA Board has chosen to support my continued leadership. I look forward to playing a strong role as a leader and providing the best possible support for my teammates in the season to come.

"I am grateful for the time Monica and I shared and sorry for the pain this has caused. I wish her nothing but happiness and success in the future.

"I won't be making any further public comment on this matter at this time and ask that the privacy of those involved is respected."

Greenberg made the point "respect" for all concerned was paramount.

"It is a very personal matter for the player, and I think there's a level of respect that needs to go with that," he said.

"Cricket's got very strong respect-at-work policies, so we've got a policy that's been developed over time that can deal with these sorts of things."

AAP

World.title: Quick hits: A 'peanut' jibe, a Starc record and a brain explosion
World.content:
Steve Smith called a Bangladesh bowler a "peanut" for making an appeal, but he could probably have labelled a couple of his batting colleagues as such on a dire batting display for Australia.

Meanwhile, Mitch Starc collected another accolade with yet another top order wicket for the Aussies

As it happened: Bangladesh minnows humble Australia's giants on day one in Darwin

Here are the quick hits from day one of the first Test between Australia and Bangladesh.

1. Weatherald falls in front of hometown crowd

Weatherald was unable to impress in front of his home crowd. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/CA)

Local boy Jake Weatherald began the first Test under significant pressure, having clung onto his opening spot after struggling through his debut series against England.

And there was significant support for the Northern Territorian in Darwin, with the crowd rising and falling as he attempted to get his innings going.

But once again, Weatherald was unable to find his feet at Test level, eventually reaching and swiping and nicking off for an unconvincing 23 off 37 deliveries.

It was Weatherald's 10th sub-50 score from his 11 Test innings, and one that only raised more questions about his viability as a Test match opener

Weatherald, the first Australian men's Test cricketer born and raised in the Northern Territory and now the first Territorian to play Test cricket in Darwin, with three more opportunities to secure a spot on the plane to South Africa in October.

2. Green's pre-lunch brain explosion

Bangladesh was overjoyed to claim Green's wicket with the final ball before lunch. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

With Australia teetering at 3-61, the under-pressure Cam Green decided to take the game on.

Perhaps the Australian most in need of a score, the all-rounder began his innings with a pair of well-timed drives, before hooking Taskin Ahmed for a maximum over backward square leg.

However, Green's counterattack was short lived, with the big man playing one shot too many in the shadows of the first break.

With what turned out to be the final ball of the morning session, Green all but gave his wicket away, meekly chipping one to a grateful Mushfiqur Rahim on the on-side.

Australia headed to lunch at 4-74, Bangladesh couldn't believe their luck, and Green, having come out with such purpose, trudged off for a run-a-ball 13.

3. Smith's triple reprieve

So often the man for a crisis, Steve Smith is no stranger to standing tall as wickets tumble around him.

But Australia's idiosyncratic world beater was anything but convincing as he somehow managed to prod his way to lunch after coming to the crease at 2-52.

Smith should have been out on 2, with his thick edge falling through the fingers of a stooping second slip.

A matter of balls later, Smith was once again nicking towards the cordon — but this time, the ball flew through a gap between second slip and gully, with Bangladesh captain Najmul Hossain Shanto having only just removed a man from behind the wicket.

And it appeared that Smith's luck was well and truly in when he survived a line-ball DRS review.

With Smith swinging hard outside off, Bangladesh went up for caught behind with some confidence. Umpire Kumar Dharmasena was unmoved, and Shanto wasted no time in sending the decision upstairs.

The technology, however, showed no conclusive evidence of an edge, with the ball passing perilously close to Smith's blade but failing to make its mark on ultra edge.

Bangladesh couldn't believe it as Smith was handed his third reprieve of the morning.

4. Smith talks Bangladesh out of a review, lands "peanut" jibe

Smith talked Bangladesh out of a review before late in the second session. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Having burnt two reviews in the first session, Bangladesh had just one DRS Hail Mary to play with for the bulk of the Australian innings.

Late in the second session, seamer Ebadot Hussein was tempted to break the glass for one that he never should have been.

His LBW shout against Smith was clearly far too high, but that didn't stop the Bangladeshi brains trust gathering for a serious discussion in the middle.

Smith couldn't believe it.

"Knee roll you reckon? It was up here you peanut!" Smith could be heard saying through the stump mic, gesturing to his hip area.

"What game are you watching?"

Smith's derision was enough to talk Bangladesh out of the review, but his honesty didn't end up counting for much — the Australian vice-captain eventually top-edging a short ball to be caught for 71.

5. Starc makes history

Australia's Mitchell Starc added another record to his list. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/CA)

The records keep coming for Australia's top-order destroyer, Mitchell Starc.

Fresh from being named his country's Test player of the year last Friday, the 36-year-old carved out another piece of history, becoming the most lethal left arm bowler in the history of the format.

Starc procured a leading edge from opener Shadman Islam to claim the 434th wicket of his Test career, with Nathan Lyon making amends for an earlier dropped chance.

Starc's milestone scalp took him past former Sri Lanka spinner Rangana Herath.

However, that was the only breakthrough of the day in what was a humbling start to the season for Australia.

World.title: Pallister downs McIntosh to claim 200m gold medal at Pan Pacs
World.content:
Australia's freestyle star Lani Pallister has collected gold and silver medals in her arduous opening to the Pan Pacific championships in the United States.

Pallister triumphed in the women's 200m freestyle and then set a personal best when finishing behind American legend Katie Ledecky in the 1500m freestyle in Irvine, California on Wednesday (Thursday AEST).

Dolphins teammates Sam Short (men's 800m freestyle), Brittany Castelluzzo (women's 200m butterfly) and Ben Armbruster (men's 50m butterfly) also triumphed on the opening night of the Pan Pacs.

The Dolphins won four of 11 gold medals on offer, with Pallister's remarkable year continuing.

Sam Short claimed gold in the men's 800m freestyle. (Getty Images: Maddie Meyer)

Just weeks after winning four Commonwealth Games gold medals in Glasgow, Pallister pipped Canadian ace Summer McIntosh in the 200m final.

The Australian clocked one minute 53.67 seconds — just 0.02s outside her personal best in the event — with McIntosh second in 1:53.86.

About two hours later, Pallister then returned to the pool for the gruelling 1500m freestyle and set a her best time over the distance.

In what was essentially a match race against peerless American great Ledecky, who hasn't lost in the event in 16 years, Pallister put in a gallant effort.

Lani Pallister (left) and Moesha Johnson (right) were beaten out by Katie Ledecky (centre) in the 1500m freestyle. (Getty Images: Maddie Meyer)

The 26-year-old shadowed Ledecky, the winner of nine Olympic and 23 world championship gold medals, for the initial 500 metres.

The American great then produced her renowned burst to create a handy advantage en route to touching in 15:36.09.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Pallister's 15:38.62 eclipsed her previous best of 15:39.14 from June last year.

In the men's 800m freestyle, Short went close to a personal best as he edged American rival Bobby Finke.

Short clocked 7:37.02, just 0.71s shy of his best time in the event, with Finke finishing some five-and-a-half seconds behind in second.

Earlier, Armbruster claimed Australia's first gold medal of the pool meet, winning the men's 50m butterfly in 22.75 seconds, 0.02s outside the Australian record jointly held by Kyle Chalmers and Matt Targett.

And Castelluzzo took out the women's 200m 'fly in 2:06.24 from her Dolphins teammate Liz Dekkers (2:06.56).

AAP

World.title: 'I'll remember the people': Sidebottom among retiring AFL premiership duo
World.content:
Collingwood great Steele Sidebottom has officially told Magpies teammates he will be retiring at season's end.

The dual Magpies premiership hero's announcement on Thursday comes just hours after Richmond midfielder Dion Prestia also called it quits.

Debuting in 2009, Sidebottom has played 373 AFL games — the second most in Collingwood's storied history, only behind Scott Pendlebury.

A member of the Magpies' 2010 premiership side as a 19-year-old, Sidebottom then kicked a famous goal late in the 2023 grand final to help seal the club's next flag 13 years later.

Sidebottom (left) and Scott Pendlebury (right) have played the most matches together as teammates in VFL/AFL history. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

With Collingwood guaranteed to be in the wildcard round of the finals, at least, Sidebottom will be hoping for a fairytale farewell.

The versatile midfielder won Collingwood's Copeland Trophy in 2017 and 2018, also earning All-Australian honours once.

"As a young kid from 'Tally' [Tallygaroopna], I could never imagine I'd finish my AFL career with over 370 games, two premierships and 18 years of memories," Sidebottom said.

"When I look back on my time at Collingwood, I'll remember the people.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"So many teammates, coaches, staff and volunteers have invested their time and energy into helping me along the way."

Sidebottom might not be the only senior Collingwood player to retire this year, with Pendlebury also weighing up his future after breaking the VFL/AFL games record in May.

The Magpies have the oldest list in the AFL and are attempting to stay in premiership contention with a group in transition.

At Richmond, Prestia has joined premiership teammate Nathan Broad in ending his career.

After starting his career with Gold Coast, Prestia enjoyed instant success after making the switch to the Tigers in 2017.

Prestia won three premierships in his first four seasons with Richmond after joining at the end of 2016. (Getty Images: Mackenzie Sweetnam)

The midfielder played in three premierships (2017, 2019, 2020) in his first four seasons at Richmond.

Despite being riddled by injury in 2020 and restricted to just five games during the pandemic season, Prestia returned to play an important role in all four of the Tigers' finals.

"I felt like a Richmond man from the very beginning," Prestia said.

"My decision to come to Richmond was not to prove what I could do, but to be a part of a club that I saw potential for greatness, and didn't we prove that right?"

Prestia and Broad will be given a farewell in front of the Richmond army this Saturday when the Tigers host St Kilda at the MCG.

AAP

World.title: Solomon rubbishes rumours of rifts with Essendon coaching candidates
World.content:
Interim Essendon coach Dean Solomon has described a rumoured falling-out with Mark McVeigh as like an "episode of Home and Away".

After Solomon chose not to put his hand up to be the Bombers' full-time coach, Essendon are closing in on announcing a leader as soon as next week.

McVeigh has been tipped to win the job, even ahead of Essendon icon James Hird.

It has led to suggestions of a rift among the trio, something Solomon has strenuously denied.

Solomon (centre) says there is no ill-feeling towards either Hird (left) or McVeigh (right) after pulling out of the Essendon coaching race. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

"We don't know where they've come from — they're rumours," Solomon said.

"[McVeigh's has been] one of my best mates since the age of 15.

"I've known Hirdy since the age of 17.

"The talks with me potentially not being here next year, whether that stimulated a bit of that conversation, we're unsure.

"But I feel like it's a bit of an episode of [long-running Australian TV soapie] Home and Away.

McVeigh, currently an assistant with Sydney, has been touted as the favourte to win the Essendon job. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

"There's nothing there. We all want to see this club heading in the right direction."

Solomon, McVeigh and Hird all played together at the Bombers, with Solomon and Hird playing in Essendon's most recent premiership side in 2000. McVeigh played with the pair in a losing grand final in 2001.

The trio also worked together briefly at GWS when McVeigh was the Giants' interim coach in 2022.

Solomon initially declared he would stay on at the Bombers next year, even if he wasn't senior coach.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

But his family remains living in northern NSW, complicating matters for him.

"Part of the process of thinking about going in the process for the senior coaching role was sitting down with my family and talking about that," Solomon said.

"My wife and kids live in northern NSW.

"I've had 10 to 11 months away from them at the moment.

"Is that sustainable long-term? It's probably not."

Solomon stressed the next coach didn't need to be an Essendon person, referencing the legendary Kevin Sheedy, who grew up supporting the Bombers but whose playing career was at Richmond.

"He just needs to be the right person," Solomon said.

"A lot of people surrounding our football club are really frustrated.

"We want to be great, and we want to be great really quickly.

"This is a big job and it's an exciting challenge."

AAP

World.title: Hulking prop set to be 1,000th Wallaby as Kiss reshuffles deck
World.content:
The 1,000th Wallaby is poised to be capped in Townsville after hulking prop Massimo De Lutiis was named on the bench to face Japan.

Les Kiss, in his second game in charge, has also recalled fly half Carter Gordon at Declan Meredith's expense.

With Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii injured, he has given Isaac Henry a starting debut at outside centre a week after he earned his first minutes in a tight Osaka defeat of Eddie Jones's side.

Lukhan Salakaia-Loto's Test return has also been secured, the Queensland Reds firebrand set to partner Lachlan Shaw — in his starting debut — in the second row, with Jeremy Williams on the bench and Josh Canham rested.

The Kiss era has begun, and new coach Les is seeking the 'Wallaby way' The new Wallabies era under Les Kiss began with a win in tough conditions against an improving nation, but coach Les Kiss wants more than just wins to be the legacy of his tenure.

Kiss has also shaken up the back row, with Charlie Cale and Carlo Tizzano to partner skipper Harry Wilson, leaving Fraser McReight on the bench and Rob Valetini out of the 23.

Brandon Paenga-Amosa will get his chance under Kiss as replacement hooker while Filipo Daugunu has also been included on the bench as backline cover.

Angus Bell and Taniela Tupou also return to the starting side after stirring second-half cameos in Osaka, while the back three are unchanged and Tate McDermott and Ben Donaldson again provide play-making options on the bench.

It continues the theme of Kiss's tenure, with the new coach keen to assess his options before a long run of Tests ahead of next year's Rugby World Cup in Australia.

"The coaches have looked to find some balance in the selection after what was a physically taxing Test week in the heat in Japan," Kiss said.

"The whole group has worked hard this week and we know where we need to improve.

"This Saturday in Townsville gives us an opportunity to grow and strengthen our game on home soil in front of our supporters."

Gordon impressed at fly half against Ireland, before missing the next two Tests with a calf injury.

Meredith started in the past three Tests alongside Brumbies clubmate Ryan Lonergan, who has been retained the starting scrum half role.

WALLABIES (1-15): Angus Bell, Josh Nasser, Taniela Tupou, Lachlan Shaw, Lukhan Salakaia-Loto, Charlie Cale, Carlo Tizzano, Harry Wilson, Ryan Lonergan, Carter Gordon, Harry Potter, Hunter Paisami, Isaac Henry, Max Jorgensen, Tom Wright.

BENCH (16-23): Brandon Paenga-Amosa, Aidan Ross, Massimo De Lutiis, Jeremy Williams, Fraser McReight, Tate McDermott, Ben Donaldson, Filipo Daugunu

ABC Sport will have live blog coverage of the second Test between the Wallabies and Japan on Saturday afternoon from 2pm (AEST).

AAP

World.title: Cunningham's trans stance opens WNBA up to its latest hijacking atempt
World.content:
Pre-game press conferences are usually a bit of a nothingburger in the WNBA.

Coaches will answer questions about their starting line-ups, address recent trends and it is all very smooth and easy.

However, when Indiana Fever coach Stephanie White arrived at the podium prior to her team's clash against the New York Liberty this week, the mood was different.

White didn't let the journalists ask questions first, as is usually the case in these settings. Her press conference began and ended with a passionate two-minute address.

"The hate, the fear-mongering, the divisiveness, the stuff that's trying to hijack our league will not win. It won't win. We are united. We are connected. We will not be divided," White said in part.

"Every day, these women put their ass on the line … I stand by them. I will always stand by them. Everybody else can go to hell."

White's statement comes after another week where WNBA headlines have had very little to do with the on-court product.

It is sadly old news for a league that is undoubtedly growing but continues to be hijacked by different agendas, whether they be political, racial or financial.

WNBA player claims 'white privilege' saw her ejected after foul Chicago's DiJonai Carrington was ejected for a foul on Indiana Fever's Sophie Cunningham, but stormed off only to post "white privilege" on social media minutes later.

Racial tensions in the WNBA were heightened earlier this week when Chicago Sky defender DiJonai Carrington tweeted "WHITE PRIVILEGE" and tagged the Fever account after being ejected from a game against the Fever due to a hard foul on Fever guard Sophie Cunningham.

Cunningham believed the foul was "absolutely" intentional, adding that Carrington probably had some "pent-up stuff".

White, Cunningham's coach on the Fever, did not think Carrington intended to hurt Cunningham, and was criticised by some for not supporting her players. It was a criticism that left the Fever coach seething.

Cunningham is the WNBA's latest main character, and it is hardly her first time in the limelight.

Sophie Cunningham (right) first went viral after becoming Caitlin Clark's unofficial bodyguard on the court for the Fever. (Getty Images: Jess Rapfogel)

The 29-year-old isn't one of the WNBA's best players, but she is one of its most marketable.

A combination of a suite of endorsement deals, a Sports Illustrated Swimsuit cover, a guest UFC referee spot and an unofficial role as star teammate Caitlin Clark's bodyguard has all combined to net her 3.8 million Instagram followers.

For comparison, the WNBA's consensus best player and four-time league MVP A'ja Wilson has just 1.5 million followers.

Cunningham was the subject of an ESPN feature last month where she spoke out against the participation of transgender women in women's sports, saying "young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men".

Sophie Cunningham has no problems being the villain on her Fever team. (Melissa Tamez/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

When pressed about her comments a few days later, Cunningham did not back down, saying her stance is simply "common sense".

"I think I'll always believe in that," she said.

"I think it's really important to protect children, and that's little girls who are also involved in that category. I stand on what I said."

Cunningham has always presented her views on transgender athletes under the guise of protecting the sanctity of women's sport, and while she may be well-intentioned, the views are problematic in a league that prides itself on diversity and being a safe space for the trans community and other minorities.

Cheryl Reeve has shown her support to the transgender community in the wake of Sophie Cunningham's comments. (Jerry Holt/The Minnesota Star Tribune via Getty Images)

Her comments were met with a wave of support for the transgender community from within the WNBA.

Cheryl Reeve, the head coach and president of the Minnesota Lynx, wore a T-shirt reading "Trans Kids Belong" when her team faced Cunningham's Fever.

"I come from a space of inclusion," she said.

"The narrative that I think is problematic is to suggest that transgender athletes are the biggest problem in women's sports."

The WNBA's Player's Association also denounced "hate abuse and demonisation of the transgender community" in a statement.

While Cunningham cares about the league and its future, her views opened the door to people outside the WNBA to gatecrash and use it as a vehicle to push their agendas,an all too familiar a tale for the league.

Unsurprisingly, US President Donald Trump and his vice-president JD Vance wasted little time jumping on the Cunningham train, with Vance labelling her "inspiring".

Riley Gaines, a vocal campaigner against the participation of transgender women in women's sports, also took a sudden interest in Cunningham and the WNBA.

Two former NBA players, Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White, have taken the jig a step further by declaring their intentions to enter the 2027 WNBA draft, more as an attack on the league's current eligibility guidelines and gender inclusivity as a whole rather than a genuine attempt to commence women's basketball careers.

It is a shameless publicity stunt that will ultimately fail. Sadly, it is coming at the cost of both the transgender community and women's sport as a whole.

White has done multiple interviews in a long-haired wig since declaring his draft eligibility and has claimed he is in his "feminine era".

Like Gaines, neither Kanter nor White have previously displayed much public interest in the WNBA.

Perhaps realising the firestorm her comments caused, Cunningham took aim at media covering the WNBA, accusing reporters of covering "everything except basketball" in the days following her ESPN interview.

The irony of it is that Cunningham's comments regarding transgender women in the WNBA came despite there being no transgender players in the league currently, or none about to enter the draft.

She was the one who drove the conversation away from the league's on-court product.

There should be headlines about the 2027 draft class. USC's Juju Watkins is one of the most exciting draft prospects in WNBA history. Her teammate Jazzy Davidson is another star in the making and could also declare.

Instead, we're all here talking about Kanter, a player who spent 11 seasons in the NBA, and White, a former first-round NBA draft pick, threatening to finagle their way into the league while pretending to care about the women's game.

Republican party's bid to claim Clark

Caitlin Clark's arrival in the WNBA has seen the league's popularity skyrocket over the past two seasons. (Getty Images: Michael Hickey)

Clark's arrival in the WNBA as the top pick in 2024 supercharged the interest in the league.

While her sensational long-range shooting and playmaking have endeared her to basketball fans, a different set of traits — being a catholic white woman from Iowa — made her the top target of the Republican Party.

Being the Republican representative of the WNBA is not a role Clark has ever asked for.

That hasn't stopped the Republican Party from attempting to use Clark as a weapon to wield in order to try and stoke race wars within the league, given the majority of its players are of colour.

Last month, eleven Republican politicians wrote to the WNBA asking the league to protect Clark from fouls that they deemed to be "attacks" on her because she is white.

The politicians claimed they were worried that "attacks against Clark may be racially motivated".

The Fever said they were unaware of the Republican letter and added that neither "our organisation nor Caitlin has had any interaction with anyone in this congressional group".

Ironically, while the Republicans complained over so-called attacks on Clark, it was a black player who fouled her, Alyssa Thomas, who was subjected to racist attacks on social media. Thomas was suspended for one game for her collision with Clark.

As Cunningham's teammate, Clark has also been involuntarily dragged into the transgender debate and has said it wasn't a topic of discussion within the Fever locker room.

Clark was asked for her thoughts on the matter in a post-game press conference and said: "It's for leagues and governing bodies to work with their athletes to find solutions".

Conservatives are unimpressed that, unlike Cunningham, Clark has not publicly denounced the participation of transgender athletes in women's sport.

A bizarre sex toy invasion

The WNBA has also been used for financial gain, infamously for the betting company Polymarket.

Last season, multiple games were forced into stoppages after green coloured sex toys were thrown onto the court.

The toys were aimed at the court and towards the players, and one accidentally hit a man watching a game in the stands.

Eventually, members of a meme-coin group, Green Dildo Coin, took responsibility for the bizarre acts, claiming they were simply promotional stunts to promote the launch of their meme-coin.

Polymarket is a company that allows you to bet on pretty much anything, and as it turned out, people were betting on what games sex toys would be thrown on and what colour the toys would be, and then winning the money themselves by throwing the toys into the court.

One of the toys thrown came close to hitting Cunningham, and she denounced the actions on her podcast.

"Everyone's trying to make sure the W is not a joke and it's taken seriously, and then that happens," she said.

Reeve, as she did on the transgender topic, spoke out again, calling the sex toy saga the league's latest "distraction".

"The sexualisation of women. This is the latest version of that," she said.

"It's not funny and it should not be the butt of jokes on radio shows, or in print or any comments."

Loading...

The WNBA is now in its 30th season and continues to go from strength to strength, whether its detractors like it or not.

A host of brilliant young players, headlined by Clark, are bending the realms of what was previously thought possible in the women's game.

Sport and politics are always more intertwined than people think, or like to admit, and unfortunately sport will always be wielded as a political tool by bad-faith operators for as long as it exists.

That is not a good enough excuse for the WNBA to be treated the way it so regularly is.

Cunningham may be passionate about defending women's sport, but has to know that she opened the door for the latest attack on her own league.

Tech.title: OpenAI is losing its second executive this week
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Another OpenAI executive is departing. Denise Dresser, who joined OpenAI as its chief revenue officer in December after serving as CEO of Slack, will be leaving in the “coming weeks” to “pursue other opportunities,” she said in a team note posted to LinkedIn. Dali Rajic, president and COO of Wiz, will be taking over the CRO role, OpenAI says.

Dresser’s departure is just the latest in a string of major exits. Earlier this week, special projects lead and former COO Brad Lightcap announced he would be leaving. (Dresser had taken over some of Lightcap’s work when he moved to the special projects role.) Former AGI chief Fidji Simo and former CMO Kate Rouch also recently stepped down.

“We’re now at an inflection point: the next generation of models will change not just how work gets done but how companies are built and run,” OpenAI says. “Dali will build the revenue operating system needed to scale for this next phase.”

Dresser is also leaving ahead of OpenAI’s IPO; the company announced in June that it had submitted a confidential S-1 filing to the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Tech.title: The Trump admin will start letting private firms launch international cyberattacks
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The Trump administration is launching a new program that will allow private firms to perform cyberattacks against foreign criminals, as reported earlier by Bloomberg. The private firms would operate “under the control and oversight” of the federal government, giving them permission to surveil and disrupt criminal networks, according to a presidential memorandum published on Wednesday.

The Department of Justice and Department of Homeland Security will oversee the private firms, which must meet requirements in “technical proficiency, proven performance of cyber operations, facility security,” and more. Companies in the program must hold a bond or escrow of at least $1 million that they’ll forfeit if they don’t comply with their contractual agreement. The memorandum also says private firms will only hack groups that are “not an institutional part of a foreign government or wholly operated under a foreign government’s direction.”

The memo describes private businesses as “underutilized” forces for fighting criminal networks. “It is the policy of the United States to use all instruments of national power, including the innovative capabilities of the private sector, to combat cybercrime,” it says.

But as pointed out by Cybersecurity Dive, it can be difficult to identify which criminal groups are affiliated with foreign governments, which could put cybersecurity firms at risk of stoking geopolitical or legal conflicts. Jason Healey, a senior cyber conflict researcher at Columbia University, tells Cybersecurity Dive that “Anyone conducting these operations is doing so at substantial personal legal risk.” Jake Williams, the vice president of research and development at Hunter Strategy, similarly tells TechCrunch that “Americans participating in these operations could easily be classified as non-uniformed combatants while traveling overseas.”

Ben Bernstein, a manager for the cybersecurity advisers team at Huntress, also raises concerns about how this program will play out. “Threat actors don’t launch attacks from labeled servers in Moscow; they route traffic through compromised, innocent infrastructure, like a vulnerable router at an Ohio dental office or a hospital network,” Bernstein says. “That makes it practically impossible to ‘strike back’ without taking out innocent bystanders.”

The US government previously carried out its own cyber operations, rather than relying on third parties. President Donald Trump began making plans to get private cybersecurity companies involved last year, Bloomberg reported.

Tech.title: I finally found a robot lawnmower I’d trust with my yard
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer with over twenty years of experience. She covers smart home, IoT, and connected tech, and has written previously for Wirecutter, Wired, Dwell, BBC, and US News.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

All the smart home news, reviews, and gadgets you need to know about

Robot lawnmowers are finally good enough to take a lot of work out of maintaining a yard, but they’re still not set-it-and-forget-it machines. If you don’t want these autonomous cutting machines to tear up your lawn or go roaming in your neighbors’ yard, you’re still going to need to keep an eye on them. But with some oversight, they can take a big chore off your hands.

This summer I tested five bots on my flat, three-quarter-acre, coastal South Carolina property with sandy soil, centipede grass, and lots of trees. Things went much better than last year’s trials and tribulations, thanks to huge improvements in navigation and maneuverability. Basically, they stopped getting stuck. My lawn has never looked better, and my spouse — who had sworn off robot lawnmowers after a user-error injury — is now a convert. His riding lawnmower has been idle for over a month.

The consistency of robot mowers is impressive. Running daily and shaving just millimeters at a time, these mowers have created a noticeably lusher lawn. I walked out on it barefoot this morning — something I’ve never done before. The best part is that they work quietly around the clock, without bothering my pets, the wildlife, or the neighbors. I also love the professional-looking lawn lines they make.

My backyard has mostly been a dry, sandy, dusty landscape with patchy grass. Three months of robot lawnmowers have helped it look healthier. My chickens don’t appreciate the neat lines, but I do.

What’s better

The key upgrades this year are network RTK navigation, fallback navigation systems, and improved all-wheel-drive to tackle rougher terrain.

RTK — real-time kinematic positioning — is the satellite positioning tech most automowers switched to over the last few years as they’ve ditched boundary wires. It uses stationary ground-based reference stations (antennas), along with GPS, to provide very precise location data, down to a centimeter or two. It’s used for surveying, drone navigation, and anything that needs that fine level of precision.

Every mower I tested, apart from the Lidar-based Dreame, comes with its own RTK antenna that needs to be installed in your yard with a clear view of the sky; trees, a neighbor’s house, or your own roofline can all block the signal. In my previous testing, I didn’t get a single RTK mower to run successfully in my backyard, where I have very spotty GPS coverage.

This graphic shows how antenna-based RTK works versus network RTK. Image: Mammotion

This new crop all now offers NetRTK as an option. This taps into a network of existing RTK reference stations through a cloud connection, and requires a Wi-Fi or 4G connection on the mower. Most worked out of the box without me needing to install the antenna, but you’ll need to check if your house is covered, as coverage varies.

RTK mowers now also use a secondary navigation tech such as lidar or vSLAM to keep on track when the signal drops. This improvement in navigation, plus bigger, more capable machines, meant I no longer spent my summer dragging confused mowers out from under oak trees.

What still needs work

Previous Next

1 / 2 After a few days, the Mammotion had torn up most of this section of damper-than-normal lawn next to my neighbors’ yard.

However, automowers are far from perfect.

These are autonomous machines with blades, and leaving them to their own devices comes with risks. One spent three days methodically destroying a patch of my lawn before I noticed. Another took out two outdoor extension cords. Several models dug sandpits in bare patches, and another tried to climb up a small tree.

Obstacle detection is better across the board, but it still has a long way to go. Hoses, cables, and cars are still a challenge — my family now knows to check under the wheels before driving away.

No one has really solved gates yet, either (although they’re trying) — I still have to manually open mine to let the robot mow the full property. And, while every manufacturer currently advertises NetRTK coverage as free for the lifetime of the device, there are obvious downsides to relying on a cloud service to mow your lawn. Finally, automowers are still expensive, and I have concerns around long-term durability.

Obstacle avoidance is much better, but they still can’t reliably see cars.

Like their siblings, robot vacuums, there are myriad models on the market now; the right one for you will depend on the size of your yard and your landscape. To find the mower that worked best for me, I tested four top-of-the-line models with specs capable of tackling my challenging terrain and large expanse of my backyard: The Husqvarna 420 IQ ($3,299), Mammotion Luba 3 AWD 3000 ($2,799), Navimow X430 ($2,499), and the Dreame A3 AWD Pro 2500 ($3,099.99). I also tried the entry-level Roborock RockNeo Q110H ($1,299) on my front lawn, which is more like a standard suburban lawn.

Also like robot vacuums, robot lawnmowers fall under the new FCC robot ban, so while existing models can continue to be sold and supported in the US — including all the models reviewed here — the fate of new models is in question.

The robot I’d get for my yard

The Segway Navimow X430 ($2,499) is by far the best mower I tested. This 60-pound beast looks like Darth Vader’s dog, and was the only mower I tested that didn’t get stuck once. Its 4WD wheels combined with impressive suspension rolled through the potholes, over sticks and rocks, even small tree branches. It navigated around my chickens and across the tall, uneven transition from my front yard to back yards — it was the only bot that could mow both in one trip (with the gate open).

It uses a combination of RTK, vSLAM, and vision-based tech to navigate, and it covered my entire property without once getting lost or stuck. It features impressive “xero-turn” maneuverability enabling it to pivot smoothly with no lawn damage. Its dual-disc, 17-inch cutting width covers more ground, and it was able to mow most of my backyard in under three hours — nearly twice as fast as most competitors. I really liked the remote-control mowing feature, which was handy for tidying up the edges of the lawn and more sensitive areas such as around flower beds.

The Segway’s speed does mean a few blades go untrimmed, and its rain sensing relies on weather data from the internet, which meant it often didn’t mow because it predicted rain that never came. Setting up the NetRTK was a bit tricky, mostly because I had to put the charging station in an awkward spot to connect to the GPS (it can’t be under an awning or up against a building as the mower also needs a clear view of the sky).

A good lidar-based alternative

The Dreame A3 AWD Pro 2500 ($3,099.99) is the best option if you can’t rely on RTK. Its lidar and camera-based navigation performed nearly as well as the Segway in my backyard, only getting stuck a couple of times. It doesn’t need a clear view of the sky, so you can place it anywhere, and its sliding edge-cutting deck worked slightly better than the Segway’s EdgeSense feature in my testing. (Beware, it’s set to a fixed 1.2-inch minimum).

But in my testing, lidar was the least reliable navigation tech, and sometimes the A3 declared the job complete when it wasn’t. Lidar robots do best in a fenced-in yard, as they can more easily get lost and wander off into your neighbors’ yard, something that never happened with the RTK robots.

While the Dreame rarely got stuck, its turning mechanism wasn’t as smooth as the Segway, and it dug several sandpits in various spots where there was no grass. I do like its “Garden Guardian” mode that uses the camera as a roaming security guard, and it can also identify when people cross its path and warn them that it’s working. It’s been mildly hilarious watching it surprise the heck out of dog walkers passing by the front yard.

An expensive but reliable option for yards with no trees

Husqvarna Automower 420 IQ $ 3144 $ 3300 5 % off $ 3144 Navigation: EPOS (RTK), radar / Yard size: 1 acre / Cutting: 1” to 4” height, 9.4” width (single discs) / Terrain capabilities: 2WD, large wheels, 45% slope / Theft features: Out-of zone alarm, GPS anti-theft, PIN / Weatherproofing: IPX5 / Connectivity: 4G (free for life), Wi-Fi, BLE / Warranty: 4 yr mower, 3 yr battery Read More $3144 at Amazon$3300 at Husqvarna

Husqvarna’s Automower 420 IQ ($3,299) is a good option for a standard yard. It has the longest warranty (four years), the easiest app and controls, and a modular design for longevity. It’s 2WD, but its large wheels tackled uneven terrain well. It requires an RTK antenna and has the option of cloud-based RTK (in some areas), but its backup navigation for satellite dead spots requires installing physical boundary wire.

I tested this in my neighbor’s yard using the physical RTK antenna, as they have fewer trees and clearer views of the sky. It navigated well, but it uses radar for obstacle detection and has no camera at all. This meant it wasn’t as good at dodging objects as the others, and ran into the bushes once and tried to climb a small tree.

The Husqvarna mowing my neighbors’ lawn — I had to install it there as the RTK antenna didn’t work in my yard. There is the option of netRTK.

But if you have a large, uncomplicated, tree-free yard, it’s a good option thanks to Husqvarna’s broad support network, free-for-life cellular connectivity for both theft and NetRTK (should you need it), and impressive performance.

More reliable navigation, but spotty software

The Mammotion combines all three wireless navigation types — RTK, lidar, and vision — making it ideal for properties with spotty GPS coverage like mine. But it’s less nimble than the other AWD models thanks to lower ground clearance and weaker suspension.

While the Mammotion did great cutting the lawn, it had serious issues with turns and soft ground. It dug itself sandpits and tore up grass in a particularly soft spot.

Its turning mechanism also tore up a couple areas of my garden, particularly a shaded area near my neighbors’ sprinklers, which stayed damper than other spots.
